intro: Ordered practice ladders built from the AtCoder Categories problem tags. Each ladder walks one technique from its easiest AtCoder appearance to its hardest, picked so that every rung introduces a model the previous rungs did not cover — rather than ten variations of the same idea. Difficulty numbers are AtCoder's own estimated difficulty, coloured by the standard rating bands.
how_to_use: Sit with a rung for 30–45 minutes before opening anything. The "nudge" under each problem is the one idea the problem turns on, not a solution — read it only when you are genuinely stuck, and read the editorial after you have solved it either way. If a rung takes more than two sittings, drop back and do a second problem in the same model before continuing.

ladders.name: Two Pointers & Sliding Window
ladders.source_label: AtCoder Categories — Two Pointers / Sliding Window
ladders.blurb: Twenty problems that build the two-pointer and sliding-window toolkit from a single forward scan up to the point where a window is only one subroutine inside a much larger algorithm. The early rungs establish why a pointer never has to move backwards; the middle rungs make the window carry state - a sum, a minimum, a covering condition - and turn 'find one' into 'count them all'; the last rungs reuse the same walk inside geometry, offline query ordering, meet in the middle, and a counting DP.

tiers.name: Pointers that only move forward
tiers.note: The core move and the reason it is linear: on a sorted or otherwise ordered sequence the right pointer never has to go back. These rungs also introduce the two basic shapes - one window over one sequence, and one pointer per sequence.

problems.label: ABC 326 C
problems.title: Peak
problems.teaches: The base move: sort the values, then let a right pointer chase a left pointer so every candidate window is examined in one linear pass.
problems.nudge: An optimal half-open interval can always be slid until its left end sits exactly on some `A_i`, so only N candidate windows matter. Sort `A`, and for each left index advance the right index while `A[r] - A[l] < M` - the right index never moves backwards.

problems.label: ABC 358 D
problems.title: Souvenirs
problems.teaches: Two pointers over two different sorted sequences, where a greedy exchange argument is what makes the single forward pass correct.
problems.nudge: Sort both `A` and `B`. Handle the people in increasing order of `B_i`, always handing over the cheapest still-unused box that is large enough - one pointer per list, each moving forward only. If a pointer runs off the end of `A`, the answer is -1.

problems.label: ABC 466 C
problems.title: Count Close Pairs
problems.teaches: Why forward-only pointers are cheap: here the amortised argument is literally the problem, since you are allowed only 2N queries.
problems.nudge: The points are already given left to right, so for each `i` the set of `j` with distance at most 1 is a contiguous block `[i, r_i]`, and `r_i` is non-decreasing in `i`. Never rewind `r`: each step either advances `r` or advances `i`, which is where the 2N budget comes from.

problems.label: ABC 355 D
problems.title: Intersecting Intervals
problems.teaches: Turning 'count the pairs' into a single ordered sweep instead of an O(N^2) check over all pairs.
problems.nudge: Once the intervals are sorted by left endpoint, `i < j` intersect exactly when `l_j <= r_i`. Sweep the 2N endpoints in sorted order keeping a running count of currently open intervals: each opening event contributes that count, and the whole answer falls out of one pass.

problems.label: ABC 383 D
problems.title: 9 Divisors
problems.teaches: A two-pointer walk over a derived sorted sequence - the primes - rather than over the input itself.
problems.nudge: Exactly nine divisors means the number is `p^8` or `(p*q)^2` with `p != q` prime. The first case has only a handful of members; the second reduces to counting prime pairs `p < q` with `p*q <= sqrt(N)`. Sieve primes up to `sqrt(N)`; as `p` walks up the list, the largest allowed `q` walks down.

tiers.name: Windows that carry state
tiers.note: The window now holds something - a running sum, a matching, a feasibility test - so advancing a pointer means updating an aggregate rather than just comparing two values. Two rungs also show that the moving index need not be an array position at all.

problems.label: ABC 461 D
problems.title: Count Subgrid Sum = K
problems.teaches: Collapsing one dimension so the other becomes a plain one-dimensional window, and counting sums equal to K as at-most(K) minus at-most(K-1).
problems.nudge: Fix the top and bottom rows (H^2 / 2 pairs) and use row prefix sums to collapse each column to a single non-negative number. Because zero columns break strict monotonicity, do not chase sum exactly K directly: count windows with sum at most K and subtract those with sum at most K-1.

problems.label: ABC 388 E
problems.title: Simultaneous Kagamimochi
problems.teaches: A feasibility predicate that is monotone in the answer, checked by pairing a prefix against a suffix in one scan.
problems.nudge: If K pairs are possible, an optimal choice is the K smallest against the K largest, matched in order: `2*A[i] <= A[N-K+i]` for every `i`. Feasibility is monotone in K, so binary search K and verify with a single linear pass.

problems.label: ABC 246 D
problems.title: 2-variable Function
problems.teaches: Two pointers where the pointers index the arguments of a monotone function, not positions in a given array.
problems.nudge: Rewrite `X = (a+b)(a^2+b^2)`, which is non-decreasing in each of `a` and `b` separately. So the smallest valid `b` for a given `a` shrinks as `a` grows: walk `a` up from 0 to about 10^6 and let `b` slide down, never resetting it, recording the best value that is at least N.

problems.label: ABC 181 E
problems.title: Transformable Teacher
problems.teaches: Combining prefix and suffix precomputation with a merge pointer over a second sorted sequence, so every insertion point is evaluated in O(1).
problems.nudge: With everyone sorted by height, an optimal pairing always pairs adjacent people. Precompute the cost of pairing up a prefix and, separately, a suffix; then dropping the teacher into slot `i` costs `pre[i] + suf[i+1]` plus one pairing. Sort `W` too and let a pointer over `H` advance monotonically as you scan `W`.

problems.label: ABC 325 D
problems.title: Printing Machine
problems.teaches: The sweep-line cousin of the two-pointer scan: one forward pointer over sorted events feeding a heap that resolves the greedy choice.
problems.nudge: Product `i` is available on the interval `[T_i, T_i + D_i]` and prints are one microsecond apart, so this is deadline scheduling. Sort by start time; sweep the candidate print times upward, pushing every product whose interval has opened into a min-heap keyed by its deadline, discarding expired ones, and always printing the one that expires soonest.

tiers.name: Counting, not finding
tiers.note: Every left endpoint has a monotone boundary; the real work is turning those N boundaries into the quantity the problem actually asks for - a count per length, an 'exactly K', a DP value, a digit sum.

problems.label: ABC 258 E
problems.title: Packing Potatoes
problems.teaches: Using a two-pointer pass to build a next-state function, then exploiting the cycle that function necessarily creates.
problems.nudge: For each start index `i`, the number of potatoes the box swallows is found by prefix sums over two copies of `W`, and that count's endpoint is monotone in `i` - so one forward pass gives all N of them. That defines a map `i -> next start`; the box sequence is then a rho shape, so find its tail and cycle and index into it.

problems.label: ABC 452 F
problems.title: Interval Inversion Count
problems.teaches: The standard move for 'exactly K' under a monotone window predicate: count at-most-K and subtract at-most-(K-1).
problems.nudge: Inversion count of `[l, r]` grows when `r` grows and shrinks when `l` grows, so the boundary of 'at most K' is monotone in both directions. Slide two pointers while a BIT maintains the inversion count incrementally as elements enter and leave; run it for K and for K-1 and subtract.

problems.label: ABC 260 E
problems.title: At Least One
problems.teaches: The minimal covering window for every left endpoint, and how to convert those N answers into a count for each window length at once.
problems.nudge: For each `l` let `r(l)` be the smallest right end whose window hits every pair; `r(l)` is non-decreasing, so two pointers plus a counter of still-uncovered pairs finds all of them. Then the window starting at `l` of length `k` is good exactly when `l + k - 1 >= r(l)` - a range increment over `k`, so accumulate with a difference array.

problems.label: ABC 334 F
problems.title: Christmas Present 2
problems.teaches: A DP transition restricted to a window of the last K indices, made linear by a sliding window minimum.
problems.nudge: Let `dp[i]` be the cheapest way to have served the first `i` children. Going home after child `j` and serving `j+1..i` in one trip has a cost that splits into a part depending only on `i` and a part depending only on `j`, so `dp[i] = f(i) + min over j in [i-K, i-1] of (dp[j] + g(j))` - a monotone deque gives that minimum in O(1) amortised.

problems.label: ARC 158 C
problems.title: All Pair Digit Sums
problems.teaches: A change of representation - counting carries instead of digits - that converts a sum of digit sums into a threshold pair-count.
problems.nudge: `f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) - 9 * (number of carries in x + y)`. A carry leaves digit position `k` exactly when `(x mod 10^k) + (y mod 10^k) >= 10^k`, so for each of the ~16 positions sort the residues and count pairs above the threshold with two pointers.

tiers.name: Two pointers inside something bigger
tiers.note: Here the forward walk is the inner loop of a larger algorithm: a geometric search around a polygon, a two-dimensional window, an offline query order, a meet-in-the-middle count, a counting DP.

problems.label: ABC 250 F
problems.title: One Fourth
problems.teaches: Two pointers on a cyclic structure, where convexity rather than sorting is what supplies the monotonicity.
problems.nudge: Fix one endpoint `i` and let `j` run forward; the area of the fan `i..j` increases with `j`, so the best `j` for `i` never moves backwards as `i` advances around the polygon. Walk both pointers once around, using prefix sums of cross products to get any fan's doubled area in O(1), and compare against a quarter of the total.

problems.label: ABC 228 F
problems.title: Stamp Game
problems.teaches: Sliding window maximum in two dimensions, used as the inner solve of a minimax game.
problems.nudge: Aoki's reply is forced: he erases the best `min(h1,h2) x min(w1,w2)` block that fits inside the black rectangle. So precompute a 2D sliding window maximum of white-stamp sums (a row pass with a deque, then a column pass), and the answer is the maximum over black placements of its prefix-sum total minus that stored maximum.

problems.label: ABC 238 G
problems.title: Cubic?
problems.teaches: Mo's algorithm: two pointers walking over reordered offline queries, requiring only an O(1) add/remove invariant.
problems.nudge: Factor every `A_i` (all under 10^6) and track, for the current window, each prime's exponent sum mod 3 plus a single counter of how many primes are currently nonzero - the window is a cube exactly when that counter is 0. Adding or removing one element touches only its own primes, so sort the queries in Mo's order and let the two pointers do the rest.

problems.label: ABC 300 G
problems.title: P-smooth number
problems.teaches: Meet in the middle followed by a merge-count, so the pointers walk two generated sorted lists rather than the input.
problems.nudge: You cannot enumerate all P-smooth numbers (there can be billions), but you can split the prime list: numbers built only from the small primes form a short sorted list, and numbers built only from the remaining primes are far fewer than the total. Sort both and count pairs with product at most N - as one factor grows, the largest allowed partner shrinks, so one two-pointer sweep counts them all.

problems.label: ABC 262 Ex
problems.title: Max Limited Sequence
problems.teaches: A counting DP whose set of valid predecessors slides forward, combining the 'at least one per interval' idea with a running window sum.
problems.nudge: First push every constraint down to an upper bound `ub[i] = min X_j over constraints covering i` (range-chmin, then read off). Then group positions by `ub` value: within value X, each constraint of that value needs at least one of its positions to actually equal X while the rest are free in `[0, X)`. Counting that is a DP over the compressed positions whose earliest allowed predecessor only moves forward, so maintain a window sum of `dp` values, and multiply the groups together.

ladders.name: Subarrays & Subsequences
ladders.blurb: Twenty AtCoder problems built around the distinction the whole category rests on: a contiguous subarray is pinned down the moment you choose two endpoints, so a window or a prefix aggregate handles it, while a subsequence is chosen element by element and almost always needs a DP over positions. The ladder starts with one-pass counting of both kinds, moves through sliding windows, greedy splits and greedy subsequence matching, and finishes with problems whose answer is a sum over every subsequence or every string at once.

tiers.name: Contiguous or Not
tiers.note: The split everything else builds on. These five drill counting each kind in a single pass: prefix aggregates and two pointers for the contiguous case, a small state-carrying DP for the non-contiguous one.

problems.label: ABC 346 B
problems.title: Piano
problems.teaches: A contiguous substring is determined by its two endpoints, so when the search space is tiny you enumerate every pair and stop thinking.
problems.nudge: The infinite string repeats with period 12, and W + B is at most 200, so build a few dozen copies and check the letter counts of every window (l, r) — the only real care is making the built string longer than any window you might need.

problems.label: ABC 369 C
problems.title: Count Arithmetic Subarrays
problems.teaches: Counting subarrays with a property that is closed under taking sub-subarrays: fix the right end and count how far left it can reach.
problems.nudge: Every subarray of an arithmetic subarray is arithmetic, so for each right end r the valid left ends form a contiguous block. Track the length of the longest arithmetic subarray ending at r (it extends the one ending at r-1 exactly when `A[r]-A[r-1]` equals the previous difference) and add that length to the answer.

problems.label: ARC 104 B
problems.title: DNA Sequence
problems.teaches: The core trick for counting subarrays: turn the condition into 'two prefix aggregates are equal' and count equal pairs.
problems.nudge: A substring works exactly when it holds as many `A` as `T` and as many `C` as `G`. Encode each letter as a step in two running counters, and the answer is the number of pairs of prefix positions where both counters agree.

problems.label: ABC 456 D
problems.title: Not Adjacent 2
problems.teaches: The contrast rung: the same kind of counting question, but non-contiguous, so you carry the one piece of state the constraint needs.
problems.nudge: Keep, for each of the three letters, how many valid subsequences currently end in that letter. When you read letter x, every valid subsequence not already ending in x can be extended by it, plus the new length-one one — so f[x] gains the sum of the other two plus 1.

problems.label: ABC 430 C
problems.title: Truck Driver
problems.teaches: When a subarray condition is monotone in each endpoint, the valid right ends for a fixed left end form an interval you can slide instead of recompute.
problems.nudge: For a fixed l, the r with at least A `a`s form a suffix and the r with fewer than B `b`s form a prefix, so the valid r are one interval. Both of its endpoints only move right as l moves right, so two pointers give the whole count in one sweep.

tiers.name: Windows and Matches
tiers.note: Now the property inside the window has structure. These rungs cover a greedy split into contiguous blocks, an invariant a sliding window can maintain, and greedy subsequence matching that turns a pair-counting problem into two independent scans.

problems.label: ABC 414 D
problems.title: Transmission Mission
problems.teaches: Splitting a sorted line into contiguous blocks: the cost of a partition is the total span minus the gaps you choose to cut at.
problems.nudge: Sort the houses. An optimal station covers a contiguous block and costs exactly (max - min) of that block, so the total over M blocks is the whole span minus the M-1 gaps you cut — cut at the M-1 largest gaps.

problems.label: ABC 381 D
problems.title: 1122 Substring
problems.teaches: Best-subarray optimisation where the window carries a violation you can repair by advancing the left end.
problems.nudge: A valid subarray is a chain of adjacent equal pairs `A[i]=A[i+1]`, `A[i+2]=A[i+3]`, ... whose values are all distinct. Precompute the positions where `A[i]=A[i+1]`, then slide a window over chains of such pairs spaced two apart, shrinking from the left whenever a value repeats.

problems.label: ABC 324 E
problems.title: Joint Two Strings
problems.teaches: Greedy subsequence matching is optimal prefix-wise, which lets a pair problem split into one number per string.
problems.nudge: Matching a subsequence greedily from the left gets you as far into T as possible, so compute for each S_i how far forward into T it reaches and how far backward from the end of T it reaches. Pair (i, j) works exactly when the forward reach of i plus the backward reach of j covers |T| — then count pairs with a sorted array or a suffix-count table.

problems.label: ARC 126 B
problems.title: Cross-free Matching
problems.teaches: Recognising a longest-increasing-subsequence in disguise: a geometric non-crossing condition is exactly 'increasing in both coordinates'.
problems.nudge: Two chosen segments may not cross or share an endpoint, which means one must be strictly to the left of the other on both rows. Sort by a, breaking ties by b descending so two segments with the same a can never both be picked, then take a strictly increasing longest subsequence of the b values.

problems.label: ABC 271 E
problems.title: Subsequence Path
problems.teaches: When the allowed order of moves is fixed by a sequence, shortest paths need no priority queue — the sequence itself is the processing order.
problems.nudge: The road numbers used must appear in E's order, so walk E once from left to right and relax only that one edge each time. After processing a prefix of E, `dist[v]` is already the best cost reachable using a subsequence of that prefix.

tiers.name: Aggregates and Bounded Search
tiers.note: Two competing instincts, and when each one applies: enumerate when the constraints secretly bound the search space, and replace the enumeration with a prefix aggregate or a monotone pointer when they do not.

problems.label: ABC 386 E
problems.title: Maximize XOR
problems.teaches: An odd-looking constraint like C(N,K) <= 10^6 is an invitation to enumerate — but read carefully which side of the choice is cheap to build.
problems.nudge: C(N,K) bounds the number of subsets but not their size, so enumerating K elements each time is still too slow when K is large. XOR of the chosen equals the XOR of everything XOR the unchosen, so enumerate whichever of K and N-K is smaller by DFS.

problems.label: ARC 196 A
problems.title: Adjacent Delete
problems.teaches: Reasoning about which elements can be paired: a parity invariant on indices reduces an operation game to a sorted-half sum.
problems.nudge: For even N the score can reach (sum of the larger half) minus (sum of the smaller half) after sorting. For odd N exactly one element survives, and since everything left of it is deleted in pairs its index must be odd — so sweep the odd candidate indices while maintaining the half-split incrementally instead of recomputing it.

problems.label: ABC 427 F
problems.title: Not Adjacent
problems.teaches: N around 60 with a modular sum condition means splitting the sequence in half and joining the halves by residue.
problems.nudge: Enumerate the non-adjacent subsets of each half — there are only Fibonacci-many — recording each sum mod M, then join the halves with a hash map on the residue. The only subtlety is the seam: split each half's list by whether its boundary index is used, so you never glue two adjacent picks together.

problems.label: ABC 452 F
problems.title: Interval Inversion Count
problems.teaches: Counting subarrays whose aggregate hits an exact value, by exploiting that the aggregate is monotone in both endpoints.
problems.nudge: The inversion count grows as r grows and shrinks as l grows, so for each l the r with exactly K inversions form one contiguous block, and both of its ends only move right as l increases. Maintain two pointers and update the inversion count with a Fenwick tree as elements enter or leave the window.

problems.label: ABC 288 D
problems.title: Range Add Query
problems.teaches: Turning 'can these operations zero out this subarray' into an invariant that prefix sums can answer per query in O(K).
problems.nudge: One operation touches K consecutive positions, so it shifts every residue class mod K by the same amount. That makes the differences between the K residue-class sums invariant, so the subarray is good exactly when all K of those sums are equal — precompute a prefix sum per residue class and answer each query directly.

tiers.name: Counting Over All Subsequences
tiers.note: The answer is now a sum over every split, every subsequence, or every string at once, so the work is designing the DP state. Partition DP, gluing tokens before counting arrangements, uniqueness of an extraction, and an automaton for a pattern that must never appear.

problems.label: ABC 207 E
problems.title: Mod i
problems.teaches: Counting all ways to cut a sequence into contiguous blocks, when each block's condition depends only on prefix sums.
problems.nudge: Let dp[k][i] count splits of the first i elements into k blocks. The k-th block's condition is just that `prefix[i] - prefix[j]` is divisible by k, so as you sweep i bucket the dp[k-1][j] values by `prefix[j] mod k` — that makes each layer linear and the whole table O(N^2).

problems.label: ABC 266 G
problems.title: Yet Another RGB Sequence
problems.teaches: Counting strings with an exact number of occurrences of a two-letter substring: glue the required occurrences into tokens, then forbid accidental extras.
problems.nudge: Fuse K of the `G`s onto an `R` to make K indivisible `RG` tokens, and arrange those tokens with the remaining `R`s and the `B`s freely. Then drop the leftover `G`s into the gaps of that arrangement by stars and bars — every gap is allowed except the ones immediately after a bare `R`, which would create an extra `RG`.

problems.label: ARC 125 D
problems.title: Unique Subsequence
problems.teaches: Distinct-subsequence counting done by index set: pin each subsequence to one canonical set of positions so nothing is double counted.
problems.nudge: An extraction is the only one exactly when it is simultaneously the leftmost and the rightmost match, which means between two consecutive chosen indices there is no other copy of the later value, and the final index is the last occurrence of its value in A. Do a DP over the ending index with a Fenwick tree for the sliding range sum.

problems.label: ABC 345 E
problems.title: Colorful Subsequence
problems.teaches: Optimising over subsequences when the state you 'need' is unbounded: keep only the best two candidates that differ in that state.
problems.nudge: dp over (index, number removed so far) wants the colour of the last kept ball as extra state, which is too many colours. Notice you only ever need the best value overall and the best value whose last colour differs from the current one — so keep the top two entries by distinct last colour per removal count and each step is O(1).

problems.label: ABC 301 F
problems.title: Anti-DDoS
problems.teaches: Counting strings that avoid a pattern as a subsequence: build the automaton of 'how much of the pattern is already matched' and never let it finish.
problems.nudge: Track how far along the forbidden pattern you are: how many distinct uppercase letters have been seen (repeating any of them completes the `XX` prefix), whether that `XX` has happened, and whether a lowercase has followed it — from that last state any further uppercase is fatal. Each `?` branches into 26 uppercase choices split by whether the letter is one already seen, plus 26 lowercase ones.

ladders.name: Prefix Sums & Range Queries
ladders.blurb: A climb from the plain running total to the data structures that replace it. The early rungs build the two reflexes — accumulate once and answer range queries in O(1), and record only the endpoints of a range update — then the ladder pushes the same idea onto counts, XORs, digit places, residue classes and DP transitions. The last tier is where a single accumulated array stops being enough: second-order differences, two dimensions, and Fenwick or segment trees once updates interleave with the queries.

tiers.name: The running total
tiers.note: One pass, one array, O(1) queries. These rungs establish the two directions the idea runs in: accumulate values so a range costs one subtraction, and record only what changes so a range update costs two writes.

problems.label: ABC 419 D
problems.title: Substr Swap
problems.teaches: Range updates whose result is only read at the end collapse into one difference array plus a single sweep.
problems.nudge: A position only cares how many of the M ranges cover it, not in what order they came. Write `+1` at `L_i` and `-1` at `R_i+1`, sweep once, and take the count mod 2 to decide whether that character ends up from S or from T.

problems.label: ABC 425 C
problems.title: Rotate and Sum Query
problems.teaches: The base case: never move the data, keep one prefix-sum array and translate the query indices instead.
problems.nudge: Build the prefix sums of `A` concatenated with itself. A rotation is just an offset `s` kept mod N, so a sum query on `[l, r]` becomes the sum of the window `[s+l-1, s+r-1]` in the doubled array — one subtraction.

problems.label: ABC 318 C
problems.title: Blue Spring
problems.teaches: Enumerating how much of a resource you buy turns an optimisation into one accumulated-array lookup per candidate.
problems.nudge: Sort the fares descending — a pass should always cover the most expensive remaining day. Then for each number of batches `k`, the cost is `k*P` plus the sum of every fare after the first `k*D`, which is a single suffix-sum lookup. Try all `k` from 0 to ceil(N/D).

problems.label: ABC 186 D
problems.title: Sum of difference
problems.teaches: Sorting removes the absolute value, and then each element's whole contribution to an O(N^2) double sum is a rank times itself minus a prefix sum.
problems.nudge: After sorting, `|A_i - A_j|` for `i < j` is simply `A_j - A_i`. The element at 0-indexed sorted position `j` is the larger one in exactly `j` pairs, so it contributes `j*A_j` minus the sum of everything before it. One pass with a running total; the answer needs 64-bit.

problems.label: ABC 267 C
problems.title: Index x A(Continuous ver.)
problems.teaches: Some quantities need two accumulators at once: sliding a position-weighted window costs exactly one ordinary window sum.
problems.nudge: Let `V` be the weighted value of the window starting at `l` and `S` its plain sum. Moving one step right gives `V' = V - S + M*A_{l+M}`. Maintain both and update them together in a single pass.

tiers.name: Difference arrays and prefix counts
tiers.note: The accumulated array stops holding values and starts holding events, character counts, or DP mass. Two rungs here are the first time a prefix sum is what makes a DP transition O(1).

problems.label: ABC 334 D
problems.title: Reindeer and Sleigh
problems.teaches: A sorted prefix-sum array is monotone, so 'how many can I afford' becomes one binary search per query.
problems.nudge: Cheapest sleighs first is optimal, so sort `R` ascending and prefix-sum it. That array is strictly increasing, so a query `X` is answered by the largest `m` with `prefix[m] <= X` — binary search, `O((N+Q) log N)` total. Sums reach 2*10^14, so use 64-bit.

problems.label: ABC 183 D
problems.title: Water Heater
problems.teaches: The canonical range-update sweep: N interval demands become a pointwise curve by recording only the two endpoints of each.
problems.nudge: Add `P_i` at index `S_i` and subtract `P_i` at index `T_i` in one array over the time axis 0..2*10^5, then accumulate left to right. The answer is No exactly when that running total ever exceeds `W`; note the interval is half-open, so the subtraction goes at `T_i`, not `T_i+1`.

problems.label: ABC 229 D
problems.title: Longest X
problems.teaches: Counting occurrences of a character is itself a prefix sum, which reduces a window's feasibility test to one comparison.
problems.nudge: Let `d[i]` be the number of `.` among the first `i` characters. The window `(l, r]` can be made all `X` when `d[r] - d[l] <= K`. Since `d` is non-decreasing, sweep `r` and only ever advance `l` — or binary search the smallest valid `l` for each `r`.

problems.label: ABC 248 C
problems.title: Dice Sum
problems.teaches: The first DP rung: a transition that sums over a contiguous block of predecessors is exactly one prefix-sum lookup.
problems.nudge: `dp[i][s]` counts length-`i` sequences with sum `s`, and `dp[i][s] = dp[i-1][s-M] + ... + dp[i-1][s-1]` — a fixed-width window over the previous row. Prefix-sum each row once so every state costs `O(1)` instead of `O(M)`. Work mod 998244353.

problems.label: ABC 222 D
problems.title: Between Two Arrays
problems.teaches: When the DP is indexed by a value and the transition sums everything at most that value, the prefix sum runs along the value axis rather than the position axis.
problems.nudge: Let `dp[i][v]` be the number of valid prefixes with `c_i = v`. Then `dp[i][v]` is the sum of `dp[i-1][u]` for all `u <= v`, restricted to `a_i <= v <= b_i`. Replace each finished row by its running total over `v` and the transition is a single read.

tiers.name: Prefixes of things that are not values
tiers.note: Accumulate a prefix sum, an XOR, a digit place, a probability, or a residue class — whatever the problem's algebra actually needs. The rungs here are about recognising which quantity telescopes.

problems.label: ABC 468 E
problems.title: Sum of Average
problems.teaches: Grouping all subarrays by length makes the inner sum a difference of prefix-sums-of-prefix-sums — the array gets accumulated twice.
problems.nudge: Group by length `L`: the contribution is `inv(L)` times `sum over r of (P[r] - P[r-L])` where `P` is the prefix sum. Accumulate `P` itself into `Q`, and that whole inner sum is `Q[N] - Q[L-1] - Q[N-L]`. Precompute the modular inverses of 1..N in one pass.

problems.label: ABC 365 E
problems.title: Xor Sigma Problem
problems.teaches: XOR telescopes exactly like addition, and once you split by bit the double sum becomes a count of unequal pairs.
problems.nudge: With `X_i` the XOR of the first `i` elements, the XOR of `A_i..A_j` is `X_j ^ X_{i-1}`. For each bit, count how many of `X_0..X_N` have it set; the pairs contributing are (set count)*(unset count). That counts all subarrays, so subtract the length-1 ones, which are just the `A_i`.

problems.label: ABC 379 E
problems.title: Sum of All Substrings
problems.teaches: When each element contributes with a positional weight, accumulate the weights per place and normalise the carries once at the end.
problems.nudge: The digit at 1-indexed position `i` has `i` possible left endpoints, and for right endpoint `j` it sits in place `10^(j-i)`. So the total coefficient of `10^p` is the sum of `i*S_i` over `i <= N-p` — one prefix sum of `i*S_i`. Build that array of place totals, then carry once; the answer has up to ~2*10^5 digits.

problems.label: ABC 183 E
problems.title: Queen on Grid
problems.teaches: A DP transition that sums an entire ray behind the cell is three running accumulators that reset when they hit a wall.
problems.nudge: `dp[i][j]` is the sum of `dp` over every reachable cell to the left, above, and up-left. Carry one accumulator per direction: each equals the previous cell's accumulator in that direction plus that cell's `dp`, and resets to 0 the moment the predecessor is a wall. Modulo 10^9+7, `O(HW)`.

problems.label: ABC 263 E
problems.title: Sugoroku 3
problems.teaches: A backward expectation DP whose transition averages a contiguous block of future states — plus the self-reference you clear algebraically first.
problems.nudge: `E[i] = 1 + (1/(A_i+1)) * (E[i] + E[i+1] + ... + E[i+A_i])`. The die can roll 0, so `E[i]` appears on both sides; solve to get `E[i] = (A_i + 1 + S)/A_i` with `S = E[i+1]+...+E[i+A_i]`. Fill right to left keeping a suffix sum of `E` so each `S` is one subtraction, mod 998244353.

problems.label: ABC 288 D
problems.title: Range Add Query
problems.teaches: The invariant of a K-wide range operation lives in residue classes mod K, so you keep K separate accumulated arrays.
problems.nudge: One operation adds the same `c` to exactly one element of each residue class mod `K`. So the differences between the class sums never change, and the subarray is good precisely when its `K` class sums are all equal. Precompute one prefix-sum array per residue and each query is `K <= 10` lookups.

tiers.name: Extra dimensions and live updates
tiers.note: Where one accumulated array runs out. Periodic input, ramps added over ranges, two dimensions, and finally the point where updates interleave with queries and the prefix sum has to become a Fenwick or segment tree.

problems.label: ABC 300 F
problems.title: More Holidays
problems.model: Prefix counts on a repeated string
problems.teaches: When the array is a huge periodic repetition, prefix counts over two copies plus arithmetic stand in for the whole thing.
problems.nudge: Any window is a suffix of one copy, then some whole copies, then a prefix of another. Fix the left endpoint inside the first copy; whole copies each cost `X` (the number of `x` in `S`), so take `K/X` of them by division, then finish the tail with prefix counts on `S+S`. Cap the answer at `N*M`.

problems.label: ABC 268 E
problems.title: Chinese Restaurant (Three-Star Version)
problems.teaches: Adding a linear ramp over a range of indices is the difference-array trick applied twice: write slope changes, then accumulate twice.
problems.nudge: Answer the question for every rotation `k` at once. One person's frustration as a function of `k` is a triangular wave — it falls to 0 at one rotation, rises by 1 per step away, and turns around near `N/2`, wrapping. Record only the slope changes at the few breakpoints, then prefix-sum the array once for slopes and once more for totals.

problems.label: ABC 256 F
problems.title: Cumulative Cumulative Cumulative Sum
problems.teaches: The step up: when point updates interleave with prefix-of-prefix queries, expand the coefficient into a polynomial and keep one Fenwick tree per power.
problems.nudge: Triple accumulation gives `D_x = sum over i <= x of A_i * (x-i+1)(x-i+2)/2`. Expand that in `i` and it is a fixed combination of the running sums of `A_i`, `i*A_i` and `i^2*A_i`. Keep three Fenwick trees, update all three on a point change, combine them per query mod 998244353 with `inv(2)`.

problems.label: ABC 292 Ex
problems.title: Rating Estimator
problems.teaches: Finding the first prefix that crosses a threshold, under point updates — a segment tree storing sums and best prefix sums, searched by descent.
problems.nudge: The rating freezes at the smallest `k` with `(A_1+...+A_k)/k >= B`, i.e. with `(A_1-B)+...+(A_k-B) >= 0`. Subtract `B` from every term and store the sequence in a segment tree holding each node's sum and maximum prefix sum. An update is `O(log N)`, and the first non-negative prefix is found by descending left-child-first.

problems.label: ARC 157 D
problems.title: YY Garden
problems.teaches: The two-dimensional accumulation: any rectangle's count in O(1), with the search space cut down first by a counting identity.
problems.nudge: If the fences make `a` row bands and `b` column bands, every one of the `ab` blocks holds exactly two `Y`, so the total number of `Y` equals `2ab` — enumerate divisor pairs. For a fixed `(a, b)` the cut positions are forced (cut a band as soon as its running `Y` count hits `2b`), and then you only have to verify each block with one 2D prefix-sum rectangle query.

ladders.name: Sorting, Inversions & Binary Search
ladders.guide_label: Sorting & Binary Search — Binary Search on the Answer
ladders.blurb: Twenty rungs that start with sorting a short list and end with a feasibility check that is a minimum cut. The first half builds the two habits the whole topic rests on: counting pairs (i, j) under a comparison, which is what an inversion is, and rewriting 'maximise the answer' as 'is this answer achievable'. The second half pushes both, through inversion counts that update incrementally, live inside a segment tree or drive a bitmask DP, and through binary searches whose monotone check is itself a greedy, a DP, or a flow.

tiers.name: Order and Feasibility
tiers.note: Sorting as a first move, and the habit of turning 'what is the best answer' into 'is this answer achievable'. By the end of this tier the binary-search-on-the-answer template should feel mechanical.

problems.label: ABC 196 C
problems.title: Doubled
problems.teaches: When the answer space is huge but every valid object is generated by a small parameter, search the parameter instead.
problems.nudge: Every valid x is some k written twice, i.e. `k * 10^d + k` where d is the number of digits of k. That value strictly increases with k, so you only need to count the k up to about 10^6 whose doubled form is at most N.

problems.label: ARC 147 A
problems.title: Max Mod Min
problems.teaches: Keeping a collection sorted under updates lets you read off the current min and max in O(log N) while a process runs.
problems.nudge: Simulate it literally with an ordered multiset: take the current max and min, replace the max with `max mod min`, and delete it if it hits 0. Each step either removes an element or drops that element strictly below the current minimum, which is the same Euclidean-style shrinkage that bounds gcd, so the total number of steps stays small.

problems.label: ABC 195 B
problems.title: Many Oranges
problems.teaches: Writing 'is this count achievable' as a two-sided inequality is the first half of every binary search on the answer.
problems.nudge: Work in grams, so the target is `1000 * W`. A count of n oranges can hit it exactly if and only if `n * A <= 1000 * W <= n * B`, since the weights are real numbers in the range. The feasible n form one contiguous block, so scan or bound it directly.

problems.label: ABC 319 D
problems.title: Minimum Width
problems.teaches: The core template: guess the answer, write a check that is monotone in the guess, and let a greedy do the verifying.
problems.nudge: For a fixed width W, the greedy line break (put the next word on the current line if it fits, otherwise start a new line) uses the fewest lines possible, and that line count is non-increasing in W. So binary search W between `max L_i` and `sum L_i + N - 1`.

problems.label: ABC 457 D
problems.title: Raise Minimum
problems.teaches: 'Make the smallest element as large as possible' is always a binary search whose check is a sum of independent per-element costs.
problems.nudge: Binary search the target X. Index i needs `ceil((X - A_i) / i)` operations when `A_i < X` and none otherwise, so the total cost is non-decreasing in X; compare it against K. Cap or short-circuit the running sum, since it can overflow long before it stops being a valid answer.

tiers.name: Counting Pairs
tiers.note: Inversions arrive here. Every rung counts pairs (i, j) under a comparison, using prefix sums, a Fenwick tree, a truncated sorted list, or a canonical sort key.

problems.label: ABC 461 D
problems.title: Count Subgrid Sum = K
problems.teaches: Counting pairs of prefix sums that satisfy a relation is the shape every inversion-style count reduces to.
problems.nudge: Fix the top and bottom row of the rectangle, which is only O(H^2) choices, and collapse that horizontal strip into a 1-D array of column sums. Counting subarrays of that array with sum exactly K is then the classic prefix-sum frequency count.

problems.label: ABC 441 E
problems.title: A > B substring
problems.teaches: Counting index pairs i < j whose values compare a given way is exactly an inversion count, and a BIT over values does it in O(N log N).
problems.nudge: Score A as +1, B as -1 and C as 0, and take prefix sums `P_0 .. P_N`. The substring (l, r] qualifies exactly when `P_r > P_l`, so the answer is the number of pairs l < r with `P_l < P_r` — sweep r and query a Fenwick tree indexed by the shifted prefix value, the same sweep that counts inversions.

problems.label: ABC 372 E
problems.title: K-th Largest Connected Components
problems.teaches: When only the top few order statistics are ever queried, carry a truncated sorted list per component instead of the whole set.
problems.nudge: k never exceeds 10, so each DSU component only needs its 10 largest vertex labels kept in sorted order. A union merges two lists of length at most 10 and truncates back to 10, so the whole thing is O((N + Q) * 10) plus the DSU.

problems.label: ARC 118 B
problems.title: Village of M People
problems.teaches: An exchange argument: once you write down each item's cost of being rounded up, sorting by that cost makes the optimal choice obvious.
problems.nudge: Write `A_i * M = b_i * N + r_i` with `b_i = floor(A_i * M / N)`. Setting `B_i = b_i` costs `r_i` in the numerator `|B_i * N - A_i * M|` and setting `B_i = b_i + 1` costs `N - r_i`, and you must round exactly `M - sum(b_i)` of them up. To minimise the maximum cost, round up the ones with the largest `r_i`.

problems.label: ABC 418 E
problems.title: Trapezium
problems.teaches: Canonicalising a comparison key so equal things sort together is what turns an O(N^2) set of objects into groups you can count within.
problems.nudge: Take all O(N^2) segments and reduce each direction `(dx, dy)` by its gcd with a fixed sign convention, then group by that key: two segments in the same group that are not on the same line give a trapezoid. Then fix the double counting — a parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, and parallelograms are exactly the segment pairs sharing a midpoint.

tiers.name: Searching the Answer Space
tiers.note: Binary search stops being a library call. The thing you guess is a value, a rank, a median, or a ratio, and each feasibility check is a small algorithm of its own.

problems.label: ABC 396 F
problems.title: Rotated Inversions
problems.teaches: Recomputing an inversion count M times is too slow; find the O(1)-per-affected-element delta between consecutive states instead.
problems.nudge: Compute the k = 0 inversion count with a Fenwick tree, then move incrementally. Raising k by one only wraps the elements whose value is `M - 1 - k`, from the largest value to the smallest. Such an element stops inverting with everything after it and starts inverting with everything before it, so its contribution changes by `(elements before it) - (elements after it)`, ignoring the others that share its value.

problems.label: ABC 391 F
problems.title: K-th Largest Triplet
problems.teaches: K-th largest over a product of sorted lists is a best-first expansion, not an enumeration of the product.
problems.nudge: All values are positive, so `A_i * B_j + B_j * C_k + C_k * A_i` is increasing in each of the three chosen values separately. Sort A, B, C descending and run a best-first search: push index triple (0,0,0) into a max-heap, and on popping (i, j, k) push (i+1, j, k), (i, j+1, k) and (i, j, k+1) with deduplication. K is at most 5 * 10^5, so the K-th pop is the answer.

problems.label: ABC 373 E
problems.title: How to Win the Election
problems.teaches: A binary search per element is affordable when the feasibility check is itself O(log N) off a sorted prefix-sum table built once.
problems.nudge: For each candidate, binary search the extra votes X — safety is monotone in X. For the check, the opponents worth pushing past `A_i + X` are the ones already closest to it, so sort A once with prefix sums and use them to compute how many opponents the remaining `K - sum(A) - X` votes can lift strictly above that total. The candidate is safe when that number is at most M - 1.

problems.label: ABC 203 D
problems.title: Pond
problems.teaches: A median condition becomes a plain counting condition the moment you threshold the values to 0 and 1.
problems.nudge: Binary search the answer x over the distinct values. Mark each cell 1 if `A[i][j] > x` and 0 otherwise, take 2-D prefix sums, and ask whether some K by K window contains at most `floor(K*K / 2)` ones — that is exactly 'this window's median is at most x', and it is monotone in x.

problems.label: ABC 324 F
problems.title: Beautiful Path
problems.teaches: A fractional objective (sum over sum) becomes a linear one once you binary search the ratio and subtract it out.
problems.nudge: Binary search the ratio lambda and reweight edge i to `b_i - lambda * c_i`. A path with ratio at least lambda exists exactly when the maximum-weight 1 to N path under those weights is at least 0. Every edge runs from a smaller vertex to a larger one, so that maximum is one DP in increasing vertex order.

tiers.name: Inversions as Structure, Checks as Algorithms
tiers.note: The top of the pool. Inversions stop being a number to compute and become an encoding you reason about or maintain, while the feasibility checks grow into greedy tree DPs and minimum cuts.

problems.label: AGC 054 C
problems.title: Roughly Sorted
problems.teaches: The inversion table is a bijective encoding of a permutation, and one adjacent swap moves exactly one of its entries by exactly one.
problems.nudge: Encode a permutation by `v_i = #{ j < i : P_j > P_i }`; this table determines the permutation uniquely, and swapping an adjacent out-of-order pair lowers exactly one `v_i` by 1. The given P' has every `v'_i <= K`, so the originals are exactly the tables agreeing with v' wherever `v'_i < K` and sitting anywhere in `[K, i-1]` where `v'_i = K`. Count those tables with a DP over positions.

problems.label: ARC 116 E
problems.title: Spread of Information
problems.teaches: A minimax objective on a tree becomes a decision problem whose check is a bottom-up greedy — the first real 'the check is itself an algorithm' rung.
problems.nudge: Binary search the time D, then check greedily. Root the tree and DFS; each subtree reports either the depth of its deepest still-uncovered vertex or how far up an already-placed centre still reaches. Place a centre at a vertex exactly when its deepest uncovered descendant is at distance D, and the check passes if the number of centres placed is at most K.

problems.label: ARC 126 D
problems.title: Pure Straight
problems.teaches: Minimum adjacent swaps is an inversion count; once you say that out loud, the remaining choice is a bitmask DP.
problems.nudge: Split the cost in two: sorting the chosen K elements among themselves, which is the inversion count of the chosen value sequence, plus pulling them together. Sweep positions with a DP over the bitmask S of which of 1..K are already chosen: picking value v adds the number of already-chosen values greater than v, and skipping an element adds `min(popcount(S), K - popcount(S))`, because it gets shifted past whichever side is smaller.

problems.label: ABC 265 G
problems.title: 012 Inversion
problems.teaches: With a tiny alphabet an inversion count is a small matrix of pair counts that merges associatively, and a value remap is a composable lazy tag.
problems.nudge: Store in each node the 3 value counts plus the 9 numbers `c[a][b] = #{ i < j in this node : A_i = a, A_j = b }`; merging children adds `cntL[a] * cntR[b]` to `c[a][b]`, and the inversion count is `c[1][0] + c[2][0] + c[2][1]`. A range remap is just a function from {0,1,2} to itself, and functions compose, so it is a legal lazy tag that regroups the 9 buckets.

problems.label: ABC 397 G
problems.title: Maximize Distance
problems.teaches: Parametric search reaches problems no greedy check could, once you accept that the check for a guessed answer may be an entire flow computation.
problems.nudge: The answer is at most N - 1, so test each candidate d separately. Distance at least d is achievable exactly when you can assign every vertex a level `l(v)` in 0..d with `l(1) = 0`, `l(N) = d` and `l(v) - l(u) <= 1` on every edge, and the edges you must pay for are precisely those with `l(v) > l(u)`. Minimising that count over level assignments is a minimum cut in the d-layer graph; take the largest d whose cut is at most K.

ladders.name: Monotonic Structures & Heaps
ladders.guide_label: Data Structures for CP — Monotonic Stack / Queue
ladders.blurb: A climb through the containers that decide what to look at next: queues and deques that hold items in arrival order, and priority queues that hand you the extreme element on demand. The early rungs use the structure directly to simulate a process; the middle rungs turn it into a search engine, where the design work is choosing the state and the edge weight so that a heap or a 0-1 deque relaxes them in the right order; the last rungs keep one heap alive across rounds, run several in parallel, or use it to drive a greedy exchange argument.

tiers.name: Order In, Order Out
tiers.note: Direct simulation with a queue, a deque, or a single heap. The point is fluency with the container: what it costs to push, to pop, and to keep an aggregate up to date while it changes.

problems.label: ABC 329 D
problems.title: Election Quick Report
problems.teaches: Maintaining the current extremum of a changing collection online, without rescanning it after every update.
problems.nudge: Only the candidate who just received a vote can become the new winner. Compare that one candidate against the stored leader (count first, then smaller index) and you never need to look at the other N-1.

problems.label: ABC 247 D
problems.title: Cylinder
problems.teaches: Compressing a queue of up to 10^9 identical items into (value, count) blocks so each query still costs amortised O(1).
problems.nudge: You can never afford to push `c` balls one at a time, but they are all identical: store the queue as a deque of `(x, c)` pairs and let a type-2 query eat whole blocks from the front, splitting only the last one it partially consumes.

problems.label: ABC 450 D
problems.title: Minimize Range
problems.teaches: Using a priority queue as a greedy driver: repeatedly act on the current extreme element and record the best state seen along the way.
problems.nudge: Adding K never changes `A_i mod K`, so every element is pinned to its residue class and only its offset is free. Put everything in a min-heap and repeat N times: read off `max - min`, then pop the minimum, add K to it, push it back — the maximum only ever grows, so the answer is the best range you saw.

problems.label: ABC 423 D
problems.title: Long Waiting
problems.teaches: Running two structures at once — a queue for arrival order and a heap for the event timeline — which is the shape of most scheduling simulations.
problems.nudge: Groups enter strictly in arrival order, so process them in input order; the only question is when. Keep a min-heap of departure times of the groups currently inside, and while the next group does not fit, pop the earliest departure and advance the clock to it.

problems.label: ABC 298 D
problems.title: Writing a Numeral
problems.teaches: Carrying a derived aggregate alongside a deque so that both ends can be updated in O(1) instead of recomputing from scratch.
problems.nudge: Store the digits in a deque and the value mod 998244353 in a single variable. Appending `x` is `v = v * 10 + x`; dropping the front digit `d` from a string of length L is `v -= d * 10^(L-1)`, so precompute the powers of 10 and their arithmetic mod the prime.

tiers.name: The Heap as a Search Engine
tiers.note: The container stops being the answer and becomes the machinery. Each rung is really about choosing the state and the cost so that popping in key order visits things in the order you need.

problems.label: ABC 384 E
problems.title: Takahashi is Slime 2
problems.teaches: Growing a region best-first: keep the frontier in a min-heap so you always test the cheapest candidate, and a failure there is a proof that nothing else on the frontier works either.
problems.nudge: Your strength only increases, so a slime you could absorb stays absorbable forever. Keep the boundary cells in a min-heap by strength: if the weakest neighbour cannot be eaten, none can and you stop; otherwise eat it, add its neighbours to the heap, and repeat.

problems.label: ABC 305 E
problems.title: Art Gallery on Graph
problems.teaches: Turning many independent searches into one by making the search key 'best remaining budget' and letting the strongest claim on a vertex win.
problems.nudge: Do not BFS from each guard. Give every vertex a value 'most stamina anyone can still have while standing here', seed it with `h_i` at each `p_i`, and expand from the largest value first — a vertex reached with stamina `s` passes `s-1` to its neighbours, and reaching it again with less stamina is useless.

problems.label: ABC 277 E
problems.title: Crystal Switches
problems.teaches: Duplicating the graph over an extra piece of state, and handling a zero-cost transition between the copies.
problems.nudge: A switch flips every edge, so the whole world has only two configurations. Search over states `(vertex, parity)`: a move along a currently-passable edge costs 1 and keeps the parity, and pressing a switch at a switch vertex costs 0 and jumps to `(vertex, parity xor 1)` — a free edge, so use a deque (0-1 BFS) rather than a plain queue.

problems.label: ABC 237 E
problems.title: Skiing
problems.teaches: Rewriting an objective with negative edges as a telescoping potential plus non-negative residual costs, which is exactly what makes Dijkstra legal.
problems.nudge: The gain of moving from X to Y is `(H_X - H_Y) - max(0, H_Y - H_X)`. The first part telescopes along any path to `H_1 - H_end`, and the second part is a non-negative edge weight, so run Dijkstra with `w(X,Y) = max(0, H_Y - H_X)` and answer `max over v of (H_1 - H_v - dist[v])`.

problems.label: ABC 176 D
problems.title: Wizard in Maze
problems.teaches: The 0-1 BFS itself: when every edge costs 0 or 1, a deque replaces the heap and drops the log factor.
problems.nudge: Walking to an adjacent road cell costs 0 and warping anywhere in the 5x5 block costs 1. Use a deque: push a 0-cost move onto the front and a 1-cost move onto the back, and the deque stays sorted by distance with at most two distinct values in it.

tiers.name: Picking the Structure the Problem Wants
tiers.note: Here the structure is not handed to you. A monotonic stack builds a recursion tree, two heaps split a multiset in half, a heap enumerates the top X of an exponential set, and a counter decides when a BFS vertex is finished.

problems.label: ABC 435 F
problems.title: Cat exercise
problems.teaches: The monotonic stack as a tree builder: recursing on the maximum of a range gives the Cartesian tree, and many 'divide at the max' DPs live on it.
problems.nudge: Removing the tower the cat stands on splits the row at that position, and the cat jumps to the tallest tower on one side — that is a recursion 'split at the maximum'. Build the Cartesian tree of P with a monotonic stack in O(N) and take `dp[v] = max over children c of dp[c] + |pos(v) - pos(c)|`.

problems.label: ABC 431 E
problems.title: Reflection on Grid
problems.teaches: Designing a state space out of a physical process: position alone is not enough, and the extra coordinate is what makes the edge weights 0/1.
problems.nudge: A state is `(cell, direction of travel)`, so there are 4HW of them. Entering a cell, you may leave in any of the three directions its mirror types allow: cost 0 if the grid already has that mirror there, cost 1 if you change it. That is a 0-1 BFS from `((1,1), right)` to `((H,W), right)`.

problems.label: ARC 210 B
problems.title: Remove Median Operations
problems.teaches: The two-heap median split, and reading off from it a characterisation stable enough to survive point updates and Q re-queries.
problems.nudge: Cut X into its lower N/2 and upper N/2 and watch a single step. If the inserted b lands in the lower half it pushes out that half's largest; if it lands in the upper half it pushes out that half's smallest; if it sits between them it is removed immediately. So the two halves evolve independently, and each one keeps only its own extremes over `A` and `B` combined — maintain those with an order-statistic structure so a query is not a re-simulation.

problems.label: ABC 440 E
problems.title: Cookies
problems.teaches: Enumerating the X best elements of an exponentially large set by popping a max-heap and pushing only the canonical successors of what you popped.
problems.nudge: Sort A descending; the best multiset is K copies of A_1, and every other multiset is reached by downgrading some cookies. Represent a selection as a sorted list of type indices and define one canonical way to generate each selection from a better one (advance the last index, or split off a new one) — then a max-heap of X+K states emits the answers in order with no duplicates.

problems.label: ABC 413 F
problems.title: No Passage
problems.teaches: A BFS where a vertex is not finalised on first contact: it needs a counter, because its value depends on the second neighbour to settle, not the first.
problems.nudge: Aoki will always ban whichever direction Takahashi most wants, so from a cell Takahashi effectively gets his second-best neighbour: `d[cell] = 1 + (second smallest d among the four neighbours)`. Run a multi-source BFS from the goals, but only finalise a cell when its second neighbour becomes final — keep a per-cell counter and push on the second hit.

tiers.name: Heaps Inside Bigger Algorithms
tiers.note: Contest-hard rungs where the priority queue is a component of something larger: it is reused across rounds, run once per bit, replaced by a set of unvisited vertices, or used to justify a greedy exchange argument.

problems.label: ABC 359 F
problems.title: Tree Degree Optimization
problems.teaches: Greedy over marginal costs: when the objective is convex in each variable, a heap of 'cost of the next unit' gives the optimum unit by unit.
problems.nudge: Any degree sequence with every `d_i >= 1` and `sum d_i = 2N-2` is realisable by some tree, so forget the tree. Start all degrees at 1 and hand out the remaining N-2 units one at a time; raising `d_i` to `d_i+1` costs `(2*d_i + 1) * A_i`, and since that cost grows with `d_i`, always spend on the cheapest next unit from a min-heap.

problems.label: ABC 307 F
problems.title: Virus 2
problems.teaches: Keeping one priority queue alive across D phases instead of restarting a multi-source Dijkstra each phase — the amortisation is the whole solution.
problems.nudge: Re-running a multi-source Dijkstra on every one of the D days is far too slow, but the infected set only grows. Carry a single priority queue of candidate `(distance from this day's sources, room)` entries across days: each day pop only while the key is at most X_i, mark those rooms infected on that day, and push their neighbours as candidates for the days that follow.

problems.label: ABC 319 G
problems.title: Counting Shortest Paths
problems.teaches: BFS on a dense complement without ever building it, by replacing the frontier's neighbour list with a global set of not-yet-visited vertices.
problems.nudge: The graph has about N^2 edges but only M are missing, so hold the unvisited vertices in a `std::set` and, when expanding u, sweep that set skipping u's at most `deg(u)` deleted partners. Every vertex is erased once, so the total work is O((N + M) log N); for the counts, `cnt[v]` is the layer total minus the counts of the previous-layer vertices joined to v by a deleted edge.

problems.label: ABC 245 G
problems.title: Foreign Friends
problems.teaches: Answering a 'must differ' constraint with about log K multi-source runs instead of K, by splitting on one bit of the label at a time.
problems.nudge: Two nations differ exactly when their numbers differ in some bit. For each bit b, run two multi-source Dijkstras: one seeded with all popular people whose `A_i` has bit b equal to 0, one with bit b equal to 1. Person i's answer is the minimum, over all b, of the run seeded from the side opposite to i's own bit b — any valid pair is caught by at least one of these.

problems.label: ABC 254 Ex
problems.title: Multiply or Divide by 2
problems.teaches: A greedy exchange argument driven by two heaps: look only at the largest surviving element, and the operation it forces is unique.
problems.nudge: Keep A and B in two max-heaps and look at the two tops. If they are equal, cancel both — nothing else can ever match that value. If A's top is larger, it can only be brought down, so halve it and pay one operation. If B's top is larger, it can only have been produced by doubling, so halve it instead and pay for that doubling; if this bottoms out with a positive B value and nothing in A to grow, the answer is -1.

ladders.name: Greedy Algorithms
ladders.blurb: Twenty rungs on the discipline of taking the locally best move and being able to say why it is safe. It starts with greedy choices you can read off a single scan, moves to exchange arguments that pin down a sort order, then to problems where the greedy step only appears after you restate the problem, and finishes with greedy driven by a heap, a DSU, or a descent through the bits.

tiers.name: Local Moves
tiers.note: The greedy choice is visible from one pass over the data. The work here is naming the invariant that makes the obvious move safe rather than guessing at it.

problems.label: ARC 133 A
problems.title: Erase by Value
problems.teaches: That a lexicographic minimum is usually decided at the first position where the input stops behaving, so you only need to find that position.
problems.nudge: The result differs from A first at the earliest index you delete, so you want the deleted value to be one that is immediately followed by something smaller. Scan for the first `i` with `A[i] > A[i+1]` and erase that value; if A is non-decreasing, erase its maximum.

problems.label: ABC 399 C
problems.title: Make it Forest
problems.teaches: The Kruskal skeleton: walk the edges once and keep an edge only when it joins two different components.
problems.nudge: A forest on N vertices with c components has exactly N - c edges, so the answer is M - (N - c). Feed every edge into a DSU and count how many merges actually happened; the rest are the edges you delete.

problems.label: ARC 195 A
problems.title: Twice Subsequence
problems.teaches: That greedy matching gives you extremal witnesses, and comparing the two extremes answers a counting question without any counting.
problems.nudge: Build the greedy leftmost embedding of B in A (scan left to right, take the first match for each B element) and the greedy rightmost embedding. If the leftmost one fails, the answer is No; otherwise there are two distinct subsequences exactly when those two index sets are not identical.

problems.label: ARC 227 A
problems.title: Fermat Point of Binary Strings
problems.teaches: Turning a swap-distance objective into a coordinatewise sum of absolute values, where the optimum is the median at every coordinate independently.
problems.nudge: Adjacent-swap distance between two good strings equals the sum over all prefixes of the absolute difference in their counts of `1`. So each prefix contributes independently, and the sum of three absolute deviations is minimised at the median — take the pointwise median of the three prefix-count sequences and check it is still a legal prefix-count sequence.

problems.label: ABC 307 D
problems.title: Mismatched Parentheses
problems.teaches: That an order-independent deletion process can be run in one left-to-right pass with a stack, which is the standard greedy shape for bracket problems.
problems.nudge: Push characters onto a stack; when you read `)`, pop back to the nearest `(` if one is still on the stack, otherwise keep the `)`. The statement's guarantee that the result is unique is what licenses this fixed order.

tiers.name: Exchange Arguments
tiers.note: Each rung is settled by an exchange: assume an optimal solution disagrees with your rule, swap two elements, and show the cost does not go up. This is where the sort order or the priority comes from.

problems.label: ABC 415 D
problems.title: Get Many Stickers
problems.teaches: Ranking options by their marginal effect on the resource rather than by their face value, and batching identical greedy steps arithmetically when N is astronomically large.
problems.nudge: Every exchange i burns A_i - B_i bottles net, so to squeeze out the most exchanges you always want the affordable option with the smallest A_i - B_i. Sort options by A_i, keep a running best A_i - B_i over the affordable prefix, and use division to apply the same exchange many times at once instead of simulating up to 10^18 steps.

problems.label: ARC 175 B
problems.title: Parenthesis Arrangement
problems.teaches: Comparing two repair operations head-to-head and collapsing them into one effective price before doing any counting.
problems.nudge: One swap fixes a `)` that is too early together with a `(` that is too late; doing the same repair with two replacements costs 2B. So the real price of that repair is min(A, 2B). Count from the prefix balance how many such crossed pairs there are, then handle any leftover imbalance in the total counts with plain replacements.

problems.label: ABC 447 E
problems.title: Divide Graph
problems.teaches: That weights of 2^i make the objective lexicographic, so the answer is a sequence of independent yes/no decisions taken from the top down.
problems.nudge: Since 2^i exceeds the sum of every smaller power, avoiding one big edge beats anything you gain later. Process edges from index M down to 1 and keep an edge unless the merge would drop the DSU's component count below 2; the rejected edges are exactly the ones you delete. Sum their 2^i modulo 998244353 at the end, not during the comparisons.

problems.label: ABC 334 C
problems.title: Socks 2
problems.teaches: The non-crossing exchange argument on a line, plus the one place a pure greedy is not enough and a small search over the leftover takes over.
problems.nudge: Only the K lonely colours matter — everything else pairs with itself for free. In an optimal pairing of points on a line no two pairs cross, so pairs are consecutive. If K is even that fixes the answer; if K is odd, exactly one colour at an odd position is left out, so try each of those with prefix and suffix sums.

problems.label: ARC 191 A
problems.title: Replace Digits
problems.teaches: Reformulating a sequence of forced operations into a selection problem: figure out which inputs can be made irrelevant before you optimise.
problems.nudge: Later writes overwrite earlier ones, so every character of T except the final one can be dumped onto a cell you overwrite afterwards — but T's last character is stuck wherever you put it. Decide T's last character separately, then sort the rest in descending order and walk S from the most significant position, spending them only where they beat the digit already there.

tiers.name: Reformulate First
tiers.note: The greedy step is not visible in the statement as written. Each of these needs a change of object — a graph, a binary search, a fixed centre — before the obvious move becomes obvious.

problems.label: ABC 256 E
problems.title: Takahashi's Anguish
problems.teaches: That an ordering problem with one constraint per element is a functional graph, and the only unavoidable costs are the cheapest edge of each cycle.
problems.nudge: Draw an edge X_i -> i with weight C_i: every vertex has out-degree one, so the graph is a set of cycles with trees hanging off them. Every constraint outside a cycle can be satisfied by a topological order for free; inside each cycle you must break exactly one, so pay the minimum C on that cycle.

problems.label: ABC 267 E
problems.title: Erasing Vertices 2
problems.teaches: The minimax-to-feasibility conversion, and the monotone peeling argument that makes the feasibility check a plain greedy.
problems.nudge: Minimising a maximum invites binary search: fix X and ask whether every vertex can be removed at cost at most X. Removing a vertex only lowers other vertices' costs, so if a vertex is ever removable it stays removable — repeatedly delete any vertex whose current neighbour-sum is at most X and see whether the graph empties. A priority queue does the same thing without the binary search.

problems.label: ABC 385 E
problems.title: Snowflake Tree
problems.teaches: Enumerating the one parameter that unlocks a greedy, and keeping the total work near-linear because degrees sum to O(N).
problems.nudge: Maximise kept vertices instead of minimising deleted ones. Try every vertex as the centre; for a chosen leaf count y, a neighbour is usable exactly when its degree minus 1 is at least y, so sort the neighbours' degrees descending and sweep y — the k-th entry in that sorted list tells you the best x for that y. Summing over all centres costs O(sum of degrees) times a log.

problems.label: ABC 407 E
problems.title: Most Valuable Parentheses
problems.teaches: The take-then-regret pattern: commit greedily, keep the commitments in a min-heap, and undo the worst one when a constraint bites.
problems.nudge: The only real constraint is that among the first 2i positions at most i can be `(`. So walk left to right pushing every A_i into a min-heap of currently chosen opens, and after each even position pop the smallest. Whatever is left in the heap at the end is a valid choice and its sum is the answer.

problems.label: ABC 383 E
problems.title: Sum of Max Matching
problems.teaches: That bottleneck path weights are read off the Kruskal process, and that pairing greedily at the earliest possible weight is optimal.
problems.nudge: f(x, y) is the smallest w such that x and y are connected using only edges of weight at most w — that is the moment they merge while running Kruskal. So sort edges by weight, and each time two DSU components merge, immediately match as many unpaired A's on one side with unpaired B's on the other as you can, charging the current edge weight. Carry the leftover counts of A's and B's in the DSU root.

tiers.name: Greedy With Machinery
tiers.note: The greedy rule is still simple, but making it correct and fast needs a heap, a DSU, a comparator you have to prove transitive, or a descent through bits and mediants.

problems.label: ABC 359 F
problems.title: Tree Degree Optimization
problems.teaches: Separating feasibility (which degree sequences are trees) from optimisation, then spending a budget one unit at a time by marginal cost.
problems.nudge: Any sequence of positive degrees summing to 2N - 2 is realisable as a tree, so forget the tree and just choose degrees. Start every vertex at degree 1 and hand out the remaining N - 2 units one at a time; raising vertex i from d to d+1 costs A_i * (2d + 1), which only grows, so a min-heap on that marginal cost is safe.

problems.label: ABC 471 F
problems.title: Concat (maximize)
problems.teaches: The canonical exchange argument for concatenation order (compare a+b against b+a) and the fact that choosing which items to take is a separate, earlier decision.
problems.nudge: Two decisions, in this order. First the length: a longer digit string is never worse, so fix which K strings to take by maximising the total length, breaking ties by value. Second the order: for two adjacent strings the only thing that matters is whether a+b beats b+a, and that comparator is a valid sort key.

problems.label: ABC 333 G
problems.title: Nearest Fraction
problems.teaches: Greedy descent over the Stern-Brocot tree, and accelerating a run of identical steps with binary search — which is exactly the continued-fraction expansion.
problems.nudge: Read r as an exact fraction (at most 18 decimals) so nothing is approximate. Keep bounds p1/q1 < r < p2/q2 starting at 0/1 and 1/1 and repeatedly move to the mediant; a naive walk is O(r's partial quotients summed), so binary search how many times in a row you go the same direction and jump. Stop when the denominator would pass N, then compare the two surviving bounds.

problems.label: ABC 349 G
problems.title: Palindrome Construction
problems.teaches: Compiling constraints into equality classes with a DSU and only then reading off the lexicographically smallest assignment left to right.
problems.nudge: Each A_i gives equalities S[i-k] = S[i+k] for k up to A_i, and one inequality S[i-A_i-1] != S[i+A_i+1]. Union the equalities — naively that is quadratic, so keep a 'next position not yet merged' pointer so each merge is charged once. Then check no inequality lands inside a single class, and walk left to right giving each class the smallest positive integer not banned by an already-assigned class it must differ from.

problems.label: ABC 249 G
problems.title: Xor Cards
problems.teaches: Splitting an 'at most K' condition into 30 disjoint prefix cases, and maximising a xor greedily from the highest bit using a linear basis.
problems.nudge: Split 'xor of A at most K' by the highest bit where the xor differs from K: either the xor equals K, or it agrees with K above some bit b where K has a 1 and the xor has a 0. That is 31 independent cases, each fixing a prefix of bits. In each case build a basis over the pairs (A_i, B_i) with the A-part reduced against the fixed prefix, then walk the B-part from the top bit down, taking a basis vector whenever it raises the answer.

ladders.name: Subsets & Exhaustive Search
ladders.blurb: Eighteen problems about searching a space of subsets: when 2^n is simply affordable, when a bitmask becomes DP state, and what to do when 2^n is one size too big. It opens with plain enumeration, all-pairs brute force and constructions built from a tiny prime set, works through bitmask TSP, submask partition DP and Steiner trees, and closes with meet-in-the-middle on the bits themselves, a min cut that collapses an exponential family of subsets to one number, and inclusion-exclusion over set partitions.

tiers.name: Deciding what to enumerate
tiers.note: Search spaces small enough to walk directly, plus the first cases where the right move is to bound the answer or fix an order rather than enumerate blindly.

problems.label: ABC 263 C
problems.title: Monotonically Increasing
problems.teaches: The base skill: generate every size-N subset of 1..M in lexicographic order with a recursion that carries the last value chosen.
problems.nudge: Recurse on the position, passing down a lower bound: A_i must exceed A_{i-1} and still leave room for the remaining elements below M. Trying candidates in increasing order at every level makes the output lexicographic for free.

problems.label: ABC 392 D
problems.title: Doubles
problems.teaches: Knowing when N^2 pairs is affordable, and how to bound the per-pair work so the total stays linear in the input size.
problems.nudge: For a fixed pair the probability of a match is the sum over values v of cnt_i(v) * cnt_j(v), divided by K_i * K_j. Store each die's value counts in a hash map and iterate over the shorter die's entries, so a pair costs min(K_i, K_j) rather than 10^5.

problems.label: ABC 447 E
problems.title: Divide Graph
problems.teaches: With weights 2^i, minimizing a sum over subsets is lexicographic minimization of the indicator bits, so the highest index is decided first and never revisited.
problems.nudge: Exactly two components means choosing a vertex set S with both S and its complement connected and deleting the cut. Any connected graph can be split that way whenever at least two contracted blobs remain, so sweep edges from the largest index down, union the endpoints whenever that still leaves two or more DSU components, and pay 2^i only for the edges you are forced to cut.

problems.label: ARC 118 C
problems.title: Coprime Set
problems.teaches: Building an object out of the two-element subsets of a tiny prime set, so that every pair shares a prime yet no prime is common to all.
problems.nudge: Label each number by which of 2, 3, 5 divide it. Multiples of 6, 10 and 15 pairwise share a prime; include 6, 10 and 15 themselves so the overall gcd drops to 1. Then count how many such numbers sit below 10000 and check it clears 2500.

problems.label: ARC 190 A
problems.title: Inside or Outside
problems.teaches: Proving the optimum is at most a small constant collapses the search to checking a handful of shapes instead of exploring a space.
problems.nudge: A type-2 move covers everything outside its interval, so two moves on disjoint intervals already finish. If no two intervals are disjoint they all share a common point, and only a type-1 move can cover that point. That caps the answer at 3, so all you actually search is whether 1 or 2 moves suffice.

problems.label: ABC 328 F
problems.title: Good Set Query
problems.teaches: Greedy online subset building: a constraint joins the set exactly when it does not contradict what is already fixed, and the check must be near-constant time.
problems.nudge: X_a - X_b = d constrains a difference, so store a potential for every vertex relative to its DSU root. If a and b already share a root, accept only when the stored potential difference equals d; otherwise merge and set the offset so the equation holds.

tiers.name: Subsets as state
tiers.note: The bitmask stops being an enumeration and becomes a DP index, and one problem shows the opposite move: recognising when a sum over 2^n subsets folds into a linear recurrence.

problems.label: ABC 190 E
problems.title: Magical Ornament
problems.teaches: Compressing a large graph down to the K <= 17 vertices you actually care about, then running a 2^K Hamiltonian-path DP over the compressed distances.
problems.nudge: A valid sequence is a walk that visits all K required gems, and its cost is the sum of shortest-path distances in the visiting order. BFS from each of the K gems to get pairwise distances, then dp[mask][last] over 2^K masks gives the best order; a walk with e edges uses e+1 gems.

problems.label: ABC 282 F
problems.title: Union of Two Sets
problems.teaches: Designing a set system so that every possible query is the union of exactly two members - the sparse table seen from the construction side.
problems.nudge: Emit every interval of length 2^k, for all starts and all k: about N log N of them, comfortably under 50000. Then [L, R] is the union of the length-2^k block starting at L and the one ending at R, with k = floor(log2(R - L + 1)).

problems.label: ABC 332 E
problems.title: Lucky bag
problems.teaches: Partitioning 15 items into D labelled groups by submask enumeration, where 3^N is the cost of visiting every (mask, submask) pair.
