problems.nudge: The mean bag weight is fixed at total/D, so minimizing variance is the same as minimizing the sum of squared bag weights. Precompute sum(mask) for all 2^15 masks, then dp[d][mask] = min over submasks sub of dp[d-1][mask ^ sub] + sum(sub)^2.

problems.label: ABC 288 F
problems.title: Integer Division
problems.teaches: A sum over all 2^(N-1) subsets collapses into a linear DP once you see each subset as a set of cut positions and let the last piece grow one digit at a time.
problems.nudge: Let dp[i] be the total of f(S) over all ways to split the first i digits. Adding digit i either extends the last piece (its value multiplies by 10) or starts a new one, so carry a second running sum of `dp[j] times the value of the piece ending at i` and update both in O(1).

tiers.name: When 2^n needs help
tiers.note: The exponent is now too large to touch directly. Split the bits, sign-flip over a smaller index set, or restrict the subset DP to structures where only a few masks matter.

problems.label: ARC 205 E
problems.title: Subset Product Problem
problems.teaches: Meet in the middle applied to the bits themselves: split 20 bits into two halves so that both the update and the query cost 2^10 instead of 2^20.
problems.nudge: (A_i OR A_k) = A_k just says A_i is a submask of A_k, so you need to insert masks and query the product of all inserted submasks of a given mask. Split each value into a high half and a low half: on insert, write the value into every superset of its high half; on query, scan every submask of the low half.

problems.label: ABC 462 G
problems.title: Completely Wrong
problems.teaches: Counting permutations with forbidden position-value pairs by inclusion-exclusion on how many forbidden pairs are used, when those pairs form disjoint complete bipartite blocks.
problems.nudge: Score 0 means the ball drawn at step k never has colour G_k. Inclusion-exclusion over the number j of matching steps gives sum (-1)^j r_j (N-j)!, and because forbidden pairs group by colour, r_j is a coefficient of a product of small per-colour polynomials - multiply them with divide and conquer plus NTT.

problems.label: ARC 171 D
problems.title: Rolling Hash
problems.teaches: Rewriting 'these two prefix values must differ' as graph colouring, then getting the chromatic number from a subset DP over independent sets.
problems.nudge: The hash of [L, R] equals B^R times (g_R - g_{L-1}), where g_k is the k-th prefix hash divided by B^k. So every condition is just g_{L-1} != g_R on N+1 <= 17 free values, and the answer is Yes exactly when that graph is P-colourable - compute its chromatic number with a 2^17 DP over independent sets.

problems.label: ABC 364 G
problems.title: Last Major City
problems.teaches: The Steiner tree DP over subsets of at most 10 terminals, with its two moves: merge two submasks at a vertex, then relax along edges.
problems.nudge: Run dp[S][v] = minimum cost of a tree spanning terminal set S plus vertex v, combining dp[A][v] + dp[S ^ A][v] over submasks and relaxing over edges with Dijkstra. Take cities 1..K-1 as the terminals; then dp[full][i] answers every query i at once, with no per-i rerun.

tiers.name: Partitions, cuts and compression
tiers.note: The hardest rungs, where the subset structure is buried: inclusion-exclusion driven by a tree DP, a graph shrunk to a searchable core, a min cut indexed by subsets, and finally set partitions themselves.

problems.label: ARC 121 E
problems.title: Directed Tree
problems.teaches: Inclusion-exclusion over violated conditions, where the count of ways to violate exactly k of them comes from a tree knapsack rather than a closed form.
problems.nudge: Group permutations by how many indices i have `a_i` a proper ancestor of i: the answer is sum (-1)^k f_k (N-k)!, with f_k the number of ways to pick k disjoint (ancestor, descendant) assignments. Compute f by a subtree DP that merges children knapsack-style and, at each vertex, lets that vertex be the ancestor of one so-far-unmatched descendant below it.

problems.label: ABC 419 G
problems.title: Count Simple Paths 2
problems.teaches: When M - N is tiny the graph is a tree plus a few extra edges; shrinking it to its branching core turns an unbounded path enumeration into a finite one.
problems.nudge: M <= N + 20 leaves at most 21 edges beyond a spanning tree. Repeatedly delete degree-1 vertices other than 1 and N, then contract every degree-2 chain into a weighted edge: only O(40) branching vertices survive. Enumerate simple paths from 1 to N in that core and combine the chain lengths as a polynomial in k.

problems.label: ABC 332 G
problems.title: Not Too Many Balls
problems.teaches: A min cut described by a subset of one side, where the exponential family of subsets collapses because the cut value depends on the subset only through a single number.
problems.nudge: Model it as a flow: source to colour i with capacity A_i, colour i to box j with capacity i*j, box j to sink with capacity B_j. A cut that keeps colour set S costs (sum of A_i outside S) + sum_j min(B_j, j * T) where T = sum of i in S - so knapsack over T to maximise the retained A-sum, and precompute the box term for every reachable T.

problems.label: ABC 236 Ex
problems.title: Distinct Multiples
problems.teaches: Removing an all-distinct condition by summing over set partitions with Mobius weights - the canonical way to enumerate partitions of an n-element set.
problems.nudge: Forget distinctness and use inclusion-exclusion over which indices are forced equal: a block of size s contributes (-1)^(s-1) * (s-1)! * floor(M / lcm of its D values). Enumerate partitions with a submask DP that always starts the new block at the lowest index not yet used, so each partition is built exactly once.

ladders.name: LIS, LCS & Sequence DP
ladders.source_label: AtCoder Categories — LIS / LCS / Sequence DP
ladders.blurb: A climb through DP that runs along a sequence: start by carrying one small piece of state through a single left-to-right pass, then learn to recognise LIS hiding inside problems that never mention it, then widen the state until it counts instead of optimises. The last tier makes the state itself the interesting object - a bitmask of reachable sums, an LCS row, an interval, a decomposition of a convex sequence - and leans on segment trees and string matching to keep the transitions fast.

tiers.name: Carrying state along one pass
tiers.note: Every problem here is one sweep over a sequence with a small amount of extra information carried along: how far a pattern has matched, a parity bit, a bounded value, a Fenwick tree of best-so-far. Get comfortable naming the state before writing the transition.

problems.label: ABC 452 D
problems.title: No-Subsequence Substring
problems.teaches: The most basic sequence state there is: how much of a pattern a scan has matched so far, and how that state moves as you extend the window.
problems.nudge: For a fixed left endpoint, extending the right endpoint can only push the greedy match of `T` forward, so there is a first position where the substring goes bad - and that position is non-decreasing in the left endpoint. Two pointers plus a `next occurrence of character c at or after index i` table counts everything.

problems.label: ARC 206 B
problems.title: Slime Swap
problems.teaches: A sorting-by-swaps condition can decompose into independent longest-increasing-subsequence problems, one per equivalence class.
problems.nudge: Two slimes of the same color can never swap past each other, so their relative order is frozen: the sequence is good exactly when each color's slimes already appear in increasing size order. So within each color keep a longest increasing subsequence and repaint the rest - and there are always enough spare colors to give each repainted slime its own.

problems.label: ABC 244 E
problems.title: King Bombee
problems.teaches: Counting walks of a fixed length while one extra bit of history rides along in the state.
problems.nudge: `dp[step][vertex][parity of how many times X has been visited]`. The parity flips only on the transitions that land on `X`, so the recurrence is the plain edge relation with a flag attached - `K` and `N` are both 2000, so `O(K*M)` states-times-edges is the budget.

problems.label: ABC 417 D
problems.title: Takahashi's Expectation
problems.teaches: When the running value collapses into a small range, precompute the whole function of the starting value instead of answering queries one at a time.
problems.nudge: All `P_i` are at most 500, so once the mood is at or below 500 it stays there. Sweep the presents right to left computing, for every starting mood in `0..500`, the final mood of that suffix. A query with `X` above 500 only ever decreases, so prefix sums of `B` tell you where it first drops into the precomputed range.

problems.label: ABC 393 F
problems.title: Prefix LIS Query
problems.teaches: The Fenwick-tree formulation of LIS - best length over values below the current one - answers prefix-and-value-capped queries for free if you process them offline.
problems.nudge: Run the `O(n log n)` LIS where a BIT indexed by compressed value stores the best length ending at each value. Sort the queries by `R` and answer them mid-scan: after `R` elements have been inserted, query `(R, X)` is just the maximum stored at values at most `X`.

tiers.name: Reductions to a known DP
tiers.note: Here the DP is standard but the problem does not say so. The work is the reduction - a non-crossing condition that is really strict increase, a graph that is really a DAG, an expectation that is really a backward recurrence.

problems.label: ARC 126 B
problems.title: Cross-free Matching
problems.teaches: A geometric compatibility condition restated as 'both coordinates strictly increase' - the canonical way LIS shows up in disguise.
problems.nudge: Two segments are compatible exactly when `a` and `b` increase together, and sharing an endpoint is forbidden too. Sort by `a` ascending with ties broken by `b` descending, then take a strictly increasing longest subsequence on `b`.

problems.label: ABC 375 E
problems.title: 3 Team Division
problems.teaches: Splitting items into three groups needs only two running sums in the state - the third is implied - and the objective rides along as the DP value.
problems.nudge: The total must be divisible by 3, and each team ends at `S/3`. Let `dp[i][s1][s2]` be the fewest people moved after deciding the first `i` people, where `s1` and `s2` are the totals of teams 1 and 2; team 3 is forced. The bound `sum B_i <= 1500` is what makes the table fit.

problems.label: ABC 335 E
problems.title: Non-Decreasing Colorful Path
problems.model: Longest path on a value DAG
problems.teaches: An LIS-shaped objective on a graph: once the non-decreasing constraint is imposed the graph becomes acyclic, and linear DP generalises to DAG DP.
problems.nudge: Contract every edge whose two endpoints have equal values with a DSU - walking along such edges is free and changes nothing. What remains, keeping only edges from a smaller value to a larger one, is a DAG, and the answer is the longest path in vertices from 1's component to `N`'s.

problems.label: ABC 354 F
problems.title: Useless for LIS
problems.teaches: Characterising which elements can lie on *some* optimal subsequence, not just the optimum's length - the prefix-plus-suffix trick.
problems.nudge: Compute `f[i]`, the longest increasing subsequence ending at `i`, and `g[i]`, the longest increasing subsequence starting at `i` (run the same LIS on the reversed, negated array). Element `i` is usable exactly when `f[i] + g[i] - 1` equals the global LIS length.

problems.label: ABC 263 E
problems.title: Sugoroku 3
problems.teaches: A backward expectation DP whose transition can stay in place - you solve for the state algebraically instead of iterating.
problems.nudge: `E[i] = 1 + (E[i] + E[i+1] + ... + E[i+A_i]) / (A_i + 1)` because rolling 0 leaves you where you are. Move the `E[i]` term to the left and solve; keep a running suffix sum of `E` so each square costs `O(1)`.

tiers.name: Wider state, and counting
tiers.note: The state stops being a single number. It becomes a bitmask, a run length, a rejected-so-far frontier - and the answer is often a count or a construction rather than a maximum.

problems.label: ARC 125 C
problems.title: LIS to Original Sequence
problems.model: Build a sequence from its LIS
problems.teaches: Inverting the problem: given the optimal subsequence, reconstruct the lexicographically smallest sequence that has it - which means reasoning about what must *not* be extendable.
problems.nudge: Nothing you insert may lengthen `A`: a leftover value `v` can never sit both after `A_i` in position and strictly between `A_i` and `A_{i+1}` in value, or you get an increasing subsequence of length `K+1`. Inside a gap the leftovers must therefore go in decreasing order; with that rule fixed, walk the output positions and take the smallest still-legal value each time.

problems.label: ABC 310 F
problems.title: Make 10 Again
problems.teaches: Compressing everything that matters about a prefix into a small bitmask - here, the set of subset sums still worth tracking.
problems.nudge: Only sums up to 10 can ever matter, so the state after some dice is the 10-bit set of subset sums they can make. Every face above 10 is interchangeable with 'unusable', so a die contributes 1/`A_i` weight per face in `1..min(A_i,10)` and one lumped transition for the rest.

problems.label: ARC 169 C
problems.title: Not So Consecutive
problems.teaches: Counting sequences under a 'no run longer than L' constraint by making the start of the current maximal run part of the state.
problems.nudge: Define the state by where the current maximal run began and what value it holds: `dp[i][v]` = ways where positions `j+1..i` are all `v` and position `j` is not. The fixed entries just forbid some `(v, run)` pairs, and prefix sums over the run start collapse each transition to `O(1)` - `N <= 5000` is the hint that `O(N^2)` is intended.

problems.label: ARC 159 D
problems.title: LIS 2
problems.teaches: A DP whose transition is a range update rather than a point update - the case where LIS needs a data structure beyond the usual multiset.
problems.nudge: An optimal subsequence takes a contiguous run of values from each appended block, so you never need the individual elements. Keep the best LIS length as a function of the last value used over compressed coordinates, and process each block `[l, r]` as one range update on that function with a lazy segment tree.

problems.label: ABC 238 F
problems.title: Two Exams
problems.teaches: Counting selections that are closed under 2D dominance by scanning one coordinate and remembering only the frontier the other coordinate has left behind.
problems.nudge: Sort people by `P`. Then a rejected person only ever blocks later people with a larger `Q`, so the whole history compresses to the smallest `Q` among those rejected so far: `dp[i][chosen so far][that minimum]`, which is `O(N^3)` at `N <= 300`.

tiers.name: Reshaping the state
tiers.note: The final tier is about choosing a representation. The state may be a whole DP row, an interval, or a decomposition of the sequence into structural pieces - and string matching or a monotonicity argument is usually what keeps it fast enough.

problems.label: ABC 257 G
problems.title: Prefix Concatenation
problems.teaches: A covering DP over a string where a linear-time matching algorithm supplies the transitions and monotonicity removes the range-minimum query.
problems.nudge: Run the Z-algorithm on `S + '#' + T` to get, for each position of `T`, the longest prefix of `S` that starts there. Then `dp[j]` = fewest pieces covering the first `j` characters is a shortest-path over intervals - and since `dp` is non-decreasing you can sweep it left to right with a pointer instead of a segment tree.

problems.label: ABC 391 G
problems.title: Many LCS
problems.teaches: Making the LCS DP row itself the state - the standard move when you must count strings grouped by their LCS with a fixed short string.
problems.nudge: `N <= 10`. The LCS row of `S` against a growing string is non-decreasing and increases by at most 1 per step, so encode it as a 10-bit difference mask. Transition that mask over each of the 26 letters and count strings of length `M` ending in each mask; the answer for `k` is the total weight of masks with popcount `k`.

problems.label: ABC 273 F
problems.title: Hammer 2
problems.teaches: When the reachable set is always a contiguous interval, the state becomes (interval, which end you stand at) - the classic interval DP shape.
problems.nudge: Compress all coordinates. Let `dp[l][r][0/1]` be the least distance walked to have made the whole compressed interval `[l, r]` reachable while standing at its left or right end; you may only push an end outward when the wall there has already had its hammer collected, which is exactly the condition to check on each transition.

problems.label: AGC 049 D
problems.title: Convex Sequence
problems.teaches: Counting under a structural constraint by decomposing the sequence into basis pieces whose sums grow quadratically, which caps how many can be used.
problems.nudge: Convexity says the difference sequence is non-decreasing, so any valid sequence is a non-negative combination of 'wedge' sequences that fall then rise linearly from a chosen bottom. A wedge of half-width `k` already contributes on the order of `k^2` to the total, so only `O(sqrt M)` distinct wedge sizes can ever fit inside `M` - and the count becomes a knapsack over those weights.

problems.label: AGC 061 C
problems.title: First Come First Serve
problems.teaches: Counting distinct results rather than distinct choice vectors: identify exactly when two choices collide, and subtract that with a prefix DP.
problems.nudge: There are `2^N` choice vectors but many give the same list. Flipping customer `i` from `A_i` to `B_i` changes nothing exactly when no other name is written strictly between `A_i` and `B_i`. Since `A` and `B` are both increasing, that is a prefix condition - so `dp[i] = 2*dp[i-1]` minus the number of ways in which customer `i`'s two options collide.

ladders.name: Knapsack & Counting DP
ladders.blurb: Twenty rungs from a first reachability table to knapsacks whose capacity no longer fits in an array. The early tiers settle the mechanics - bounded copies, the in-place backward loop, and choosing what the DP axis should be - and then the ladder turns to counting: contributions, partitions, distinct multisets, and a subset-sum table you can both add to and delete from. The last tier is knapsack under pressure: capacities near 10^15, per-range queries, and knapsacks hiding inside a tree or a coordinate rotation.

tiers.name: The table and what goes in it
tiers.note: Basic recurrences and the 0/1 knapsack table, plus the two moves that make everything later possible: bounding the copies of an item, and deciding which quantity the table is indexed by.

problems.label: ABC 260 C
problems.title: Changing Jewels
problems.teaches: Turning a described process into two mutually recursive value functions and evaluating them bottom-up.
problems.nudge: Let `r(n)` and `b(n)` be the number of level-1 blue jewels one red / one blue jewel of level n eventually yields. Each rule rewrites one of them in terms of values you already have - note the red rule produces blue jewels at the same level, so compute `b(n)` before `r(n)`.

problems.label: ABC 286 D
problems.title: Money in Hand
problems.teaches: The reachability table when each item comes in a limited number of copies - the first place the plain 0/1 loop breaks.
problems.nudge: Reachability over amounts 0..X, one coin type at a time. The unbounded (forward) loop would silently use a type more than `B_i` times, so carry a count: for each amount record the fewest coins of the current type needed to reach it, or binary-split the `B_i` copies into powers of two.

problems.label: ABC 431 D
problems.title: Robot Customize
problems.teaches: A two-group assignment becomes an ordinary knapsack once you index by the weight of one of the groups.
problems.nudge: Every part is used, so start from the total of all `B_i` and treat moving part i to the head as a swap worth `H_i - B_i` that costs `W_i` on the head axis. Then take the best head weight satisfying `2 * head <= total weight`.

problems.label: ARC 122 A
problems.title: Many Formulae
problems.teaches: Summing over exponentially many objects by asking, per element, how many objects give it a plus and how many give it a minus.
problems.nudge: Never enumerate formulae. For each `A_i`, count the good sign patterns in which it ends up added and those in which it ends up subtracted, using a prefix count and a suffix count of sign sequences with no two consecutive minuses.

problems.label: ABC 317 D
problems.title: President
problems.teaches: Knapsack where the axis is the thing you must accumulate and the value being optimised is the cost of getting there.
problems.nudge: Each district has a fixed price - `max(0, (X_i + Y_i + 1) / 2 - X_i)` converted voters - and a fixed payoff of `Z_i` seats. Minimise cost along the seat axis, then read off the cheapest entry at or past half of `sum Z_i`.

tiers.name: Choosing the axis
tiers.note: Five problems where the work is deciding what the DP is indexed by: residue chains, calories against vitamin amount, bit positions, prefix sums, and prefixes glued to suffixes.

problems.label: ABC 403 D
problems.title: Forbidden Difference
problems.teaches: Recognising that a global constraint splits into independent chains, each of which is the no-two-adjacent DP.
problems.nudge: Bucket the values by count. For `D > 0` the constraint only ever links `v` with `v + D`, so values fall into chains `r, r + D, r + 2D, ...`; on each chain keep the largest total count with no two neighbours chosen. `D = 0` is a separate and easier case.

problems.label: ABC 390 E
problems.title: Vitamin Balance
problems.teaches: Maximising a minimum across groups: binary search the answer and let each group's knapsack say how cheaply that level is reached.
problems.nudge: Run one knapsack per vitamin over calorie budgets 0..X, giving the best amount obtainable for each budget. Then binary search the target `m` and check that the cheapest budget reaching `m` in each of the three groups sums to at most X.

problems.label: ABC 406 E
problems.title: Popcount Sum 3
problems.teaches: A digit DP that carries two aggregates at once - how many numbers a state stands for, and what those numbers sum to.
problems.nudge: Walk the bits of N from the top with the usual tight/free flag and a counter of ones placed. Keep the pair (count, sum) in each state: setting a bit adds `2^bit * count` to the sum as well as advancing the ones counter.

problems.label: ABC 370 E
problems.title: Avoid K Partition
problems.teaches: Counting partitions with a forbidden transition by subtracting the bad predecessors from a running total instead of enumerating good ones.
problems.nudge: `dp[i]` counts valid partitions of the first i elements and equals (sum of all earlier `dp[j]`) minus (sum of `dp[j]` where `prefix[i] - prefix[j] = K`). Maintain the running total and a hash map from prefix sum to accumulated dp.

problems.label: ABC 441 F
problems.title: Must Buy
problems.teaches: Answering "what is the optimum without item i" for every i at once, by gluing a prefix knapsack to a suffix knapsack.
problems.nudge: Build `pre[i][w]` over items 1..i and `suf[i][w]` over items i..N. The best value with item i banned is the max over w of `pre[i-1][w] + suf[i+1][M-w]`; compare it against the overall optimum, and against the best value that is forced to buy item i.

tiers.name: Counting, undoing, two-sided states
tiers.note: The table starts holding counts rather than maxima, learns to run backwards so an item can be removed, and grows a second dimension when one sweep has to model two journeys.

problems.label: ABC 234 F
problems.title: Reordering
problems.teaches: Counting distinct results rather than distinct choices - process the alphabet and interleave with binomials so each object is counted exactly once.
problems.nudge: A distinct outcome is exactly a multiset of letters, so index the DP by letters used so far. With `dp[j]` strings of length j from the first k letters, adding i copies of the next letter contributes `dp[j] * C(j + i, i)` to `dp[j + i]`.

problems.label: ABC 321 F
problems.title: #(subset sum = K) with Add and Erase
problems.teaches: The subset-sum counting table is invertible: inserting an item is the backward loop, deleting the same item is the forward loop with a subtraction.
problems.nudge: Insert x with `dp[k] += dp[k-x]` scanning k downward from K. Deletion is the exact inverse - scan k upward from x and do `dp[k] -= dp[k-x]` - so each operation costs O(K) and you never rebuild.

problems.label: ABC 450 F
problems.title: Strongly Connected 2
problems.teaches: Reducing a graph property to interval coverage, then counting the covering subsets with a sweep DP over positions.
problems.nudge: The backbone edges already let you walk downward, so the graph is strongly connected exactly when every gap between i and i+1 is crossed by some kept edge with `X <= i < Y`. You are counting subsets of intervals that cover `[1, N-1]`: sweep the gaps with a DP indexed by the furthest right end reached so far.

problems.label: ABC 373 F
problems.title: Knapsack with Diminishing Values
problems.teaches: When the value of k copies is concave, copies can be taken greedily by marginal gain, which collapses the inner loop of an unbounded knapsack.
problems.nudge: The j-th copy of type i is worth `v_i - (2j - 1)`, a decreasing sequence. Within each weight class, take the largest marginal gains first to get the best value for taking k items of that weight; then it is a plain knapsack over weight classes, and `sum over w of W/w` transitions is small.

problems.label: ABC 320 F
problems.title: Fuel Round Trip
problems.teaches: Two passes over the same line sharing a use-once resource, handled by sweeping once with both passes' state in the table.
problems.nudge: Sweep the coordinates left to right with the state (fuel on the outbound leg, fuel on the return leg at this point). Each station is assigned to at most one of the two legs, and buying `F_i` on the return leg means you are allowed to arrive back at that point with `F_i` less.

tiers.name: Knapsack under pressure
tiers.note: The final tier attacks knapsacks that do not fit: many queries over ranges, capacity near 10^15, item counts that must be grouped, and knapsacks embedded in a tree or in rotated coordinates.

problems.label: ABC 426 G
problems.title: Range Knapsack Query
problems.teaches: Making a knapsack per query affordable by answering all queries offline on a divide-and-conquer over the index range.
problems.nudge: Recurse on `[l, r]`. Queries straddling the midpoint are served by two knapsack tables built outward from mid - one growing leftwards, one rightwards - merged in O(C) per query by splitting the capacity between the two halves.

problems.label: ABC 415 G
problems.title: Get Many Cola
problems.teaches: Unbounded knapsack whose capacity dwarfs any table: the best-ratio item covers the bulk and a DP only handles the remainder.
problems.nudge: Drink everything first: one exchange then nets `B_i` extra drinks for a cost of `A_i - B_i` empties, so this is unbounded knapsack with capacity about N and every cost under 300. Use the best drinks-per-empty option for almost all the capacity and DP only over the last O(max A squared) of it.

problems.label: ABC 269 G
problems.title: Reversible Cards 2
problems.teaches: A hidden bound on the input - the item sizes sum to M, so only O(sqrt M) distinct sizes exist - turns a hopeless knapsack into a grouped bounded one.
problems.nudge: Flipping card i shifts the visible sum by `B_i - A_i`, and since all `A_i + B_i` add up to M there are only O(sqrt M) distinct shift magnitudes. Group equal shifts, handle positive and negative directions separately, and run a min-flips bounded knapsack that tracks how many copies of the current shift are already spent.

problems.label: ARC 165 E
problems.title: Random Isolation
problems.teaches: Expectation computed by summing over structures, where each structure's probability depends only on two counts that a tree knapsack can tabulate.
problems.nudge: Charge each operation to the component it acted on. A vertex set S is that component exactly when every neighbour outside S was picked before any vertex of S, a probability determined only by `|S|` and the number of outside neighbours - so count connected subtrees by (size, boundary size) with a tree knapsack and sum the sizes above K.

problems.label: ABC 221 G
problems.title: Jumping sequence
problems.teaches: A 45-degree change of coordinates splits two-dimensional reachability into two independent subset sums, each small enough for a bitset.
problems.nudge: Set `u = x + y` and `v = x - y`: every jump adds `+D_i` or `-D_i` to u and, independently, `+D_i` or `-D_i` to v. Each coordinate is then "choose a subset summing to `(sum D + target) / 2`", solvable with a bitset, and the two subsets recombine into the four directions.

ladders.name: Bitmask DP & DP on Subsets
ladders.blurb: A climb through exponential-state DP, starting where the mask simply records which items you have already used and the popcount tells you how far along you are. It then adds order (tours over (mask, last)), sliding windows and grid profiles, submask enumeration and the 3^n bound, and finally the counting identities — sum over subsets, and the 'fix the lowest vertex and subtract the disconnected splits' trick that powers connectivity counting. Along the way several rungs are about the reformulation itself: seeing that a 300x300 grid, a range of 10^18-sized integers, or a huge sequence is secretly an 18-bit problem.

tiers.name: The mask as the set you have used
tiers.note: Every rung here stores one bit per item and builds masks up (or tears them down) one bit at a time. The goal is to get comfortable with dp indexed by 2^n states, popcount as the step counter, and the habit of reading 'N <= 18' as an instruction.

problems.label: ABC 415 C
problems.title: Mixture
problems.teaches: The plainest possible subset DP: a boolean per mask, transitions that add exactly one bit, and forbidden states pruned by the input.
problems.nudge: The mask is the set of chemicals currently in the bottle, and the string tells you directly whether that state is safe. A mask is reachable exactly when it is safe and some mask with one bit removed is reachable — and removing a bit always makes the number smaller, so a single loop over masks in increasing order is enough.

problems.label: ABC 407 D
problems.title: Domino Covering XOR
problems.teaches: Bits standing for cells on a moving frontier rather than for items, which is the entry point to profile DP.
problems.nudge: `HW <= 20` means the smaller side is at most 4, so transpose until the width is tiny. Sweep the cells in row-major order carrying a mask of which of the next W cells are already covered by a domino you placed earlier; at each cell you either leave it uncovered (XOR its value into the running score) or start a domino going right or down.

problems.label: ABC 318 D
problems.title: General Weighted Max Matching
problems.teaches: Pairing up a small set: the canonical way to remove the ordering redundancy when elements are consumed two at a time.
problems.nudge: dp[mask] is the best matching using only the vertices in mask. Do not loop over all pairs inside the mask — always deal with the lowest set bit: either drop it unmatched, or pair it with one of the other set bits. That makes each matching be built in exactly one way.

problems.label: ABC 424 D
problems.title: 2x2 Erasing 2
problems.teaches: Grid DP where the whole state is the previous row, and the constraint only ever couples two consecutive rows.
problems.nudge: With W <= 7, let the state be the mask of black cells you keep in the current row (necessarily a submask of that row's blacks). Two consecutive kept masks p and c are compatible exactly when `p & c & (p >> 1) & (c >> 1)` is zero, i.e. no column pair is black in both rows; maximise kept cells and subtract.

problems.label: ABC 354 E
problems.title: Remove Pairs
problems.teaches: Win/lose evaluation over 2^n positions — the same subset lattice, now read backwards from terminal states.
problems.nudge: The position is exactly the set of remaining cards, so dp[mask] = 'the player to move wins'. It is true iff some legal removal of a matching pair (i, j) from mask leads to a losing dp[mask without i and j]; masks with fewer bits are smaller numbers, so recurse with memoisation or iterate downward.

tiers.name: Order, windows and submasks
tiers.note: Now the mask alone is not a state. These rungs pair it with 'where you are' for tour-shaped DP, slide it along as a window over a string, or split it into submasks — and two of them are really about noticing that a huge instance is an 18-bit instance in disguise.

problems.label: ABC 359 D
problems.title: Avoid K Palindrome
problems.teaches: That a bitmask can encode a window of recent decisions instead of a set — the bridge from subset DP to profile DP.
problems.nudge: K <= 10, so the only thing you need to remember about the prefix is its last K-1 characters, packed as a (K-1)-bit mask over A/B. Appending a character forms one K-length window you can test for being a palindrome, then you shift the mask and drop the oldest bit.

problems.label: ABC 274 E
problems.title: Booster
problems.teaches: The travelling-salesman shape: a mask of visited nodes plus the node you are standing on, with the mask also determining a side quantity.
problems.nudge: Put the N towns and the M chests into one mask of at most 17 bits and let the state be (mask, current point). The current speed is not extra state — it is `2^(number of chest bits in mask)` — so a move of length d costs d divided by that. Only masks containing all town bits may return to the origin.

problems.label: ABC 301 E
problems.title: Pac-Takahashi
problems.teaches: The reformulation move: a 300x300 grid is not maskable, but the at most 20 interesting squares in it are.
problems.nudge: Run a BFS from the start, from the goal, and from each of the <= 18 candies to get all pairwise shortest distances; the grid is then irrelevant. What remains is dp[mask][last] = minimum moves to have eaten the candy set mask and be standing on `last`, keeping any state whose distance plus dist(last, goal) is at most T.

problems.label: ABC 381 F
problems.title: 1122 Subsequence
problems.teaches: Masking the value alphabet rather than the positions, with the DP value being a greedy position instead of a count.
problems.nudge: N is huge but `A_i <= 20`, so the mask is over values, not indices. dp[mask] = the earliest prefix length in which you can already have laid down the pairs for exactly the values in mask; to add value v, jump to its next two occurrences after dp[mask] using precomputed occurrence lists. Earliest position is always the best position.

problems.label: ABC 187 F
problems.title: Close Group
problems.teaches: Enumerating submasks and why the total work is 3^n rather than 4^n — the standard partition-into-groups skeleton.
problems.nudge: First mark, for every mask, whether it induces a clique: mask is a clique iff mask without its lowest vertex is a clique and that vertex is adjacent to all the others. Then dp[mask] = 1 + min over clique submasks that contain mask's lowest bit, using the `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` submask loop.

tiers.name: What the bits are allowed to mean
tiers.note: Here the hard part is deciding what a bit stands for: a reachable subset sum, a prime, a maximal prime power. Two heavier tour DPs sit in the middle to show the (mask, last) pattern used for counting and for string overlaps.

problems.label: ABC 310 F
problems.title: Make 10 Again
problems.teaches: Compressing an unbounded DP into a mask of its own reachable set — N is 100, but the state space is only 2^9.
problems.nudge: Everything you need to know about the dice seen so far is which sums in 1..9 some subset of them already makes: a 9-bit mask. A die showing v <= 10 updates it to `mask | (mask << v) | bit(v)` (with sum 10 meaning success), and every roll above 10 is useless, so lump all of those into one probability per die.

problems.label: ABC 195 F
problems.title: Coprime Present
problems.teaches: Turning a 10^18-scale range into a 20-bit problem by bounding which primes can ever cause a conflict.
problems.nudge: If a prime p divides two chosen cards then p divides their difference, which is at most 72 — so only primes up to 72 matter, and there are 20 of them. Give each of the <= 73 cards the mask of those primes dividing it and count subsets with dp[mask of primes already spent].

problems.label: ABC 411 G
problems.title: Count Cycles
problems.teaches: The (mask, last) DP used to count rather than optimise, plus the anchoring trick that stops each object being counted many times.
problems.nudge: Anchor every cycle at its smallest vertex: dp[mask][v] = number of paths from lowbit(mask) to v visiting exactly the vertices of mask, multiplying in edge multiplicities. Close a cycle by adding the count of edges from v back to the anchor; each cycle of length >= 3 is produced twice (once per direction), and cycles of length 2 come from parallel edges, so count those as C(c, 2) separately.

problems.label: ABC 343 G
problems.title: Compress Strings
problems.teaches: A named NP-hard problem in its maskable regime, with a string-algorithm preprocessing step feeding the DP costs.
problems.nudge: First delete every string that already occurs inside another (otherwise the DP overcounts). Then precompute overlap(i, j) = the longest suffix of S_i that is a prefix of S_j, via KMP failure function on `S_j + '#' + S_i`. What is left is dp[mask][last] minimising total length minus overlaps.

problems.label: ABC 349 F
problems.title: Subsequence LCM
problems.teaches: Sum-over-subsets and inclusion-exclusion over supersets — counting subsets whose OR is the full mask.
problems.nudge: Throw away every A_i that does not divide M. For the remaining ones only the maximal prime powers of M matter: bit j means 'this element is divisible by p_j^(e_j)', and the condition is that the OR of the chosen masks is the full mask. Bucket elements by mask, run an SOS transform to get how many elements are submasks of each mask, then inclusion-exclude `2^count - 1` over subsets of the full mask.

tiers.name: Partition, connect, and count
tiers.note: The top of the ladder is subset counting: splitting a set into groups, and the recurring identity that isolates the component containing the lowest element in order to subtract off the disconnected configurations.

problems.label: ABC 432 F
problems.title: Candy Redistribution
problems.teaches: That a minimum-operations question can become 'maximise the number of parts', and that sum(mask) makes the partial-group state free.
problems.nudge: The total must be divisible by N, and a group of k children that already averages out internally needs k - 1 transfers — so the answer is N minus the largest number of groups whose sums each equal the average. Build masks by always adding the lowest unused index, and note that sum(mask) alone tells you how full the group in progress is, so no second state dimension is needed.

problems.label: ABC 321 G
problems.title: Electric Circuit
problems.teaches: Linearity of expectation over subsets, combined with the subtract-the-disconnected-splits recurrence.
problems.nudge: Expected components = sum over vertex subsets S of P(S is exactly one connected component). That needs S to contain equally many red and blue terminals, say k, which happens with probability k!(M - k)!/M!, times the number of the k! internal matchings that actually connect S. Get that connected count as k! minus the splits, peeled off by fixing which sub-subset holds S's lowest part.

problems.label: ABC 319 F
problems.title: Fighter Takahashi
problems.teaches: Masking only the handful of genuinely special objects and letting a greedy handle the other 490 vertices.
problems.nudge: Only the <= 10 medicine vertices need bits; note also that strength can only be multiplied about 30 times before it dwarfs 10^9. For a fixed set of medicines taken your strength is fixed, so sweep enemies greedily with a priority queue keyed on required strength, and let dp[mask] record whether that set of medicines is unlockable.

problems.label: ABC 213 G
problems.title: Connectivity 2
problems.teaches: The workhorse identity of subset counting: connected count = all count minus (component of the lowest vertex) times the rest.
problems.nudge: Let e(S) be the number of edges inside S and f[S] the number of edge subsets of S that make S connected. Then f[S] = 2^e(S) - sum over proper submasks T containing S's lowest vertex of f[T] * 2^e(S minus T). Vertex 1's component being exactly S then contributes f[S] * 2^e(complement of S), which you add to every k in S.

problems.label: ABC 253 Ex
problems.title: We Love Forest
problems.teaches: Assembling a global structure out of per-subset counts — Matrix-Tree for the pieces, subset DP for gluing them together.
problems.nudge: Give each unordered pair (u, v) weight c(u,v) = how many of the M indices produce it, and use the Matrix-Tree theorem to get the weighted spanning-tree count of every induced subgraph (N <= 14, so 2^14 determinants). Combine them with a subset DP that always places the lowest remaining vertex into the next tree; a forest with K edges has N - K trees, and the ordered sequences give a factor K! over M^K.

ladders.name: Digit DP
ladders.blurb: Digit DP is one idea worn many ways: walk a number's representation one position at a time, carry a tight-vs-free flag against the upper bound, and drag along whatever extra state the question needs. This ladder starts from the bare position-by-digit table with no bound at all, adds the tight flag and then residues, digit sums, digit products and distinct-digit masks, moves the same machinery into base 2 and base 16 and onto several bounds at once, and finishes where the carries themselves are the state and the DP runs over a whole array of numbers.

tiers.name: Position, last digit, tight flag
tiers.note: The skeleton every later rung reuses: a table indexed by digit position, plus whatever must be remembered about the prefix. These four introduce the tight-vs-free flag, extra predicates riding in the same state, and a transition that is a game rather than a sum.

problems.label: ABC 242 C
problems.title: 1111gal password
problems.teaches: The bare skeleton of digit DP - a table over (position, last digit) - before any upper bound exists to complicate it.
problems.nudge: Let `dp[i][d]` be the number of valid length-`i` prefixes ending in digit `d`; from `d` you may only go to `d-1`, `d`, `d+1`, all clamped to 1..9. There is no bound like `x <= N` here, so no tight flag appears at all - that is the point of starting here.

problems.label: ABC 465 E
problems.title: Digit Circus
problems.teaches: Independent digit predicates can all ride in one state vector, with the final condition read off at the last position instead of woven into the transitions.
problems.nudge: Carry four things through the positions at once: the tight flag against `N`, the running sum mod 3, whether a digit 3 has appeared, and a 10-bit mask of which digits have been used. 'Satisfies exactly one of the three' is decided only when you reach the end, from the mask's popcount and the two flags. Leading zeros must not enter the mask.

problems.label: ABC 336 E
problems.title: Digit Sum Divisible
problems.teaches: When the modulus depends on the number you are building, guess it with an outer loop and carry both the running digit sum and the running residue.
problems.nudge: You cannot reduce mod the digit sum while building, because you do not know it yet. So fix it: for each candidate sum `s` in 1..126, run a DP over (position, tight, digit sum so far, value mod `s`) and keep only the completions whose digit sum is exactly `s`.

problems.label: ABC 195 E
problems.title: Lucky 7 Battle
problems.teaches: The same per-position table works when the transition is a min/max over an opponent's choice rather than a sum over digits.
problems.nudge: The only thing worth remembering about `T` is its value mod 7, and appending digit `d` sends `r` to `(10*r + d) mod 7`. Work backwards from the last position: `dp[i][r]` = 'Takahashi wins from here', an OR over his two options when `X_i = 'T'` and an AND over Aoki's when it is `'A'`.

tiers.name: No upper bound - the digit string is the structure
tiers.note: Three problems where nothing is bounded by an `N` you sweep against, yet the answer is still per-digit. The work is spotting that a carry rule, a monotonicity rule, or a split rule is really a statement about individual positions.

problems.label: ARC 136 D
problems.title: Without Carry
problems.teaches: A digit-wise inequality turns pair counting into a multidimensional cumulative sum - the base-10 cousin of a subset-sum (SOS) transform.
problems.nudge: Adding `x` and `y` carries nowhere exactly when `y_d <= 9 - x_d` in every one of the six decimal positions. So each `x` needs the count of array values inside a 6-dimensional box. Build cumulative sums one digit position at a time across the whole `10^6`-sized count array (six passes), then fix up the `i = j` case and halve.

problems.label: ABC 443 F
problems.title: Non-Increasing Number
problems.teaches: A digit-monotonicity constraint can be re-encoded as a tiny additive basis, turning something that reads as number theory into a small state search over residues.
problems.nudge: Digits non-decreasing from the most significant end means the number is a sum of repunits `1, 11, 111, ...`, and because the leading digit is at most 9, at most nine of them. So search over (how many repunits used, 0..9) x (residue mod `N`) using repunit residues mod `N`; minimising the value means preferring fewer and shorter repunits.

problems.label: ABC 288 F
problems.title: Integer Division
problems.teaches: A DP that walks the digit string where the transition weight is itself built digit by digit, letting a quadratic sum collapse to a rolling accumulator.
problems.nudge: Let `dp[i]` be the sum of `f(S)` over all ways to cut the first `i` digits. The honest transition sums `dp[j] * value(j+1..i)` over every `j`, which is quadratic - but `value(j+1..i) = 10*value(j+1..i-1) + d_i`, so keep that whole sum as one rolling quantity: `S_i = 10*S_{i-1} + d_i * (dp[0] + ... + dp[i-1])`.

tiers.name: Bigger states, other bases, two bounds
tiers.note: The state stops being a small integer range: a digit product, three simultaneous tight flags in binary, a set of distinct hexadecimal digits. Each one forces a different trick for keeping the state space finite.

problems.label: ABC 208 E
problems.title: Digit Products
problems.teaches: When the state is an unbounded value, count the values that are actually reachable - here only 2,3,5,7-smooth numbers - and memoize on the value itself.
problems.nudge: The state is the product of the digits chosen so far. It looks unbounded, but every reachable product is a product of digits 1..9, so the reachable set is small enough to key a hash map on. Handle shorter numbers and the leading-zero prefix separately, or a leading zero will wipe the product to 0.

problems.label: ABC 317 F
problems.title: Nim
problems.teaches: Digit DP against several upper bounds at once: one tight flag per number, all sweeping the same bit positions.
problems.nudge: `X1 xor X2 xor X3 = 0` means the three bits at each position sum to an even number, so only 4 of the 8 bit-triples are legal. Sweep bits from the top carrying three tight-vs-`N` flags and three residues updated as `r_i = (2*r_i + bit) mod A_i` - that is `8 * 10 * 10 * 10` states per bit.

problems.label: ABC 194 F
problems.title: Digits Paradise in Hexadecimal
problems.teaches: The same machinery in base 16, with a set-valued state compressed to its size and the free suffix finished off by combinatorics.
problems.nudge: The natural state is the 16-bit mask of digits seen, which is far too big - but only its popcount matters. Once a position goes free with `j` distinct digits already used, the number of completions depends only on `j`, the digits remaining, and `K`, so precompute that table. 'No leading zeros' is its own state.

tiers.name: Digits of a whole collection, and carries as state
tiers.note: The final tier stops sweeping a single number. Here the digit positions belong to a whole array or to every term of a huge sum, and the carries between positions become the thing the DP is actually about.

problems.label: ABC 292 G
problems.title: Count Strictly Increasing Sequences
problems.teaches: Comparing many numbers digit by digit at once: equal prefixes form blocks, and each digit position is a chance to split a block.
problems.nudge: All strings have length `M`, so numeric order is plain lexicographic order. Strings still equal on the first `p` digits form a contiguous block, and at position `p` that block must break into consecutive groups whose digits strictly increase. That gives an interval DP over `(l, r, position, digit)`.

problems.label: ARC 156 D
problems.title: Xor Sum 5
problems.teaches: Kummer's theorem says a multinomial coefficient is odd exactly when its parts add without binary carries - which turns an XOR over N^K objects into a base-2 DP with a carry.
problems.nudge: Group the `N^K` sequences by their count vector `(c_1..c_N)`; the multiplicity is a multinomial coefficient, and it is odd exactly when the `c_i` sum to `K` with no carries in binary - i.e. each set bit of `K` is handed to exactly one index. Now XOR the sums `sum 2^b * A_{i_b}` with a DP over bit positions carrying the addition carry, tracking only parities of counts.

problems.label: ARC 153 D
problems.title: Sum of Sum of Digits
problems.teaches: The identity relating digit sums to carry counts converts a digit-sum objective into a carry-maximisation that a bottom-up digit DP can drive.
problems.nudge: Use `f(a) + f(x) - f(a+x) = 9 * (number of carries when adding a and x)`, so minimising the total digit sum is maximising the total carry count. A carry into position `j` happens exactly when `(A_i mod 10^j) + (x mod 10^j) >= 10^j`, so build `x` digit by digit from the bottom and count the qualifying `A_i` by binary search on sorted suffixes.

ladders.name: Tree DP
ladders.blurb: Twenty problems out of the 102 tagged Tree DP, from 704 to 2920. The progression is deliberate: one DFS returning one number, then a returned state, then rerooting, then the knapsack merge, then a DP with something wrapped around it, and finally the named machinery (Steiner trees, virtual trees, dynamic tree DP) that shows up in ARC/AGC.

tiers.name: Foundations
tiers.note: One DFS, one value per subtree. The goal here is to stop thinking about the tree and start thinking about what a child hands back to its parent.

problems.label: ABC 333 D
problems.title: Erase Leaves
problems.teaches: The single most reused primitive: root the tree, compute size[v] in one post-order pass.
problems.nudge: Root at vertex 1. Each neighbour of the root heads an independent subtree, and you must delete every one of them except the largest.

problems.label: ABC 348 E
problems.title: Minimize Sum of Distances
problems.teaches: The canonical introduction to rerooting: compute the answer at the root, then slide it to every other vertex in O(1) per edge.
problems.nudge: Get f(1) = sum of C_i * dist(1,i) with one DFS. Moving the root across edge (u,v) changes it by `total weight - 2 * (subtree weight of v)`.

problems.label: ABC 397 E
problems.title: Path Decomposition of a Tree
problems.teaches: A child hands back more than a number — here it hands back how many loose path-ends it still has. Feasibility DP rather than optimisation.
problems.nudge: Any vertex with three or more children still needing to extend a path is immediately impossible. Track the count of dangling ends and close them greedily as you unwind.

problems.label: ABC 222 E
problems.title: Red and Blue Tree
problems.teaches: Reducing a tree problem to a sequence problem. Half the difficulty of tree DP is spotting when the tree stops mattering.
problems.nudge: Walk the given route once and count how many times each edge is traversed. What remains is a subset-sum over those counts hitting a fixed target.

problems.label: ABC 394 F
problems.title: Alkane
problems.teaches: Merging children is not always a knapsack — often you just sort their values and take the top few. Learn to recognise that shape.
problems.nudge: Every internal vertex needs exactly four incident edges, so dp[v] keeps the best chain downward and you sum the three largest positive child contributions.

tiers.name: Core patterns
tiers.note: The workhorses: counting with subtree sizes, rerooting a non-trivial state, and the tree knapsack. Almost every harder problem is one of these wearing a costume.

problems.label: ABC 312 G
problems.title: Avoid Straight Line
problems.teaches: Counting triples on a tree by fixing the meeting vertex — and by counting the bad cases instead of the good ones.
problems.nudge: Total triples minus the collinear ones. For each vertex, the paths through it split the rest of the tree into its child subtrees plus everything above it.

problems.label: ABC 222 F
problems.title: Expensive Expense
problems.teaches: The same rerooting machinery, but max instead of sum — so you need the best and second-best child in order to exclude the one you came from.
problems.nudge: Keep the top two downward values at each vertex; when descending into child c, pass down the best value that is not c's own.

problems.label: ABC 259 F
problems.title: Select Edges
problems.teaches: Two states per vertex — edge to parent used or not — with a degree cap that turns the merge into a sort-and-take.
problems.nudge: dp[v][0/1] = best weight in v's subtree. For each child, taking its edge gains `w + dp[c][0] - dp[c][1]`; keep the positive gains, sort, take as many as the degree limit allows.

problems.label: ABC 287 F
problems.title: Components
problems.teaches: The O(n^2) subtree knapsack, and the amortisation argument that proves it is quadratic and not cubic. Non-negotiable to know.
problems.nudge: dp[v][k][0/1] = ways to get k components in v's subtree, with v chosen or not. Merge children one at a time, looping only up to the sizes already accumulated.

problems.label: ABC 369 G
problems.title: As far as possible
problems.teaches: Decompose the tree into vertex-disjoint downward chains; answering for every K at once falls out of sorting the chain lengths.
problems.nudge: Each vertex keeps its deepest downward path and the leftover branches become separate chains. Sort all chain lengths descending — the answer for K is a prefix sum.

tiers.name: An outer loop around the DP
tiers.note: The DP is no longer the whole solution. Here it sits inside a binary search, a game-theoretic argument, a rerooting of a two-state DP, or a compressed tree.

problems.label: ABC 218 G
problems.title: Game on Tree 2
problems.teaches: Game DP where the optimising player alternates by depth, plus maintaining a running median down the DFS path.
problems.nudge: Leaves are terminal; internal vertices take max or min of their children by parity. Keep the median of the root-to-current path with two heaps, pushing on entry and popping on exit.

problems.label: ABC 246 G
problems.title: Game on Tree 3
problems.teaches: Parametric search: guess the answer X, rewrite the problem as a boolean, and let a much simpler DP decide it.
problems.nudge: Fix X and mark vertices with value >= X as dangerous. dp[v] = how many dangerous vertices in v's subtree cannot be erased in time; monotone in X, so binary search.

problems.label: ABC 223 G
problems.title: Vertex Deletion
problems.teaches: Rerooting where the state is itself a DP (maximum matching), not just a number. The real test of whether you understand rerooting.
problems.nudge: dp[v][0/1] = matching size in v's subtree with v unmatched / matched. A vertex is removable iff the whole tree keeps the same maximum matching without it — reroot to test all n at once.

problems.label: ABC 207 F
problems.title: Tree Patrolling
problems.teaches: The classic dominating-set state set — chosen / covered by a child / not yet covered — used for counting rather than minimising.
problems.nudge: dp[v][0] = v not covered, [1] = v covered by a child's guard, [2] = guard on v. Merge children as a convolution over the number of covered vertices.

problems.label: ABC 340 G
problems.title: Leaf Color
problems.teaches: When a DP has to run once per colour, build the compressed tree over just that colour's vertices. Total size stays O(n log n).
problems.nudge: Sort a colour's vertices by DFS order, add pairwise LCAs, rebuild the edges with a stack. Then count connected subtrees whose leaf set is exactly that colour.

problems.label: ARC 130 D
problems.title: Zigzag Tree
problems.teaches: A naive child merge is quadratic per vertex here. Rewriting it as cumulative sums is the standard rescue for rank-indexed tree DP.
problems.nudge: dp[v][i] = ways in which v is the i-th smallest among v and its used children. Merging with binomials plus prefix sums keeps the whole thing quadratic overall.

tiers.name: Advanced machinery
tiers.note: Named techniques worth reusing for years: Steiner trees, inclusion–exclusion over a knapsack, multi-dimensional traversal states, and a DP that has to survive updates.

problems.label: ABC 364 G
problems.title: Last Major City
problems.teaches: Bitmask over terminals times vertices, with the two transitions — subset split and edge relax — that define the Steiner tree DP.
problems.nudge: dp[S][v] = cheapest tree connecting terminal set S and containing v. Split S into two halves at v, then relax over edges with Dijkstra for each fixed S.

problems.label: ARC 121 E
problems.title: Directed Tree
problems.teaches: Counting permutations with forbidden positions: count arrangements with at least k bad pairs via a tree knapsack, then alternate signs.
problems.nudge: f[k] = ways to choose k disjoint ancestor–descendant pairs, which is a subtree knapsack. The answer is the alternating sum of f[k] * (n-k)!.

problems.label: ARC 179 D
problems.title: Portable Gate
problems.teaches: Traversal DP where the state carries both a budget and whether you come back to the vertex. The dimension people forget to add.
problems.nudge: dp[v][k][0/1] over v's subtree, k = gate uses, last flag = whether the walk returns to v. Merge children like a knapsack, allowing exactly one non-returning branch.

problems.label: ABC 351 G
problems.title: Hash on Tree
problems.teaches: The DP has to survive point updates. Express each vertex's transition as an affine map and hang it off a heavy-light decomposition.
problems.nudge: dp[v] = A[v] + X[v] * (product of dp over children). Linearise along heavy paths, keep the light-child products aside, and put a segment tree of composed affine maps on each path.

ladders.name: Graphs: Traversal, DSU, MST & Shortest Paths
ladders.blurb: Twenty rungs that build graph technique from the ground up: reachability and connected components, then search on graphs the statement never draws, then Dijkstra, DSU and MST used as tools rather than templates. The climb ends with problems where the graph is the answer to a modelling question - cycle spaces, difference constraints, functional graphs and counting over forests.

tiers.name: Walking the graph you are given
tiers.note: The graph is handed to you, or is one rewrite away. These rungs drill the four primitives everything else is built from: reachability, component counting, BFS distance, and a first weighted shortest path.

problems.label: ABC 454 C
problems.title: Straw Millionaire
problems.teaches: That 'what can I end up with' is almost always the reachable set of a directed graph, not a simulation.
problems.nudge: Each friend is a directed edge from item A_i to item B_i. Nothing about the order of trades matters - run one BFS or DFS from item 1 and count what you can reach.

problems.label: ABC 399 C
problems.title: Make it Forest
problems.teaches: The vertex/edge/component identity for forests, and DSU as the cheapest way to count components.
problems.nudge: A forest on N vertices with k connected components has exactly N - k edges, so you must delete M - (N - k). Union-find over the M edges just to get k.

problems.label: ABC 309 D
problems.title: Add One Edge
problems.teaches: Decomposing a path through a chosen edge into two independent BFS distances you can maximise separately.
problems.nudge: If you add edge (u, v) the distance becomes `d(1,u) + 1 + d(v, N1+N2)`. Since u and v are free, run one BFS from vertex 1 and one from vertex N1+N2 and add the two largest distances, plus one.

problems.label: ABC 340 D
problems.title: Super Takahashi Bros.
problems.teaches: Recognising a plain weighted shortest path inside a statement written as a sequence of choices.
problems.nudge: Stage i is a node with exactly two outgoing edges: cost A_i to stage i+1 and cost B_i to stage X_i. That is 2N weighted edges - Dijkstra from 1 to N. Greedily taking the cheaper option fails because a jump can skip many stages.

problems.label: ABC 235 D
problems.title: Multiply and Rotate
problems.teaches: That the vertex set can be a range of values rather than a given list, and unit-cost operations make it a BFS.
problems.nudge: Every integer below 10^6 is a vertex; multiply-by-a and rotate are unit-cost edges. BFS from 1 and prune any value that reaches 10^6 or more - the reachable state space stays small enough to visit each state once.

tiers.name: Cycles, parity and edge order
tiers.note: Now the structure of the graph is the point: whether a cycle is odd, where the unique cycle of a functional graph sits, and what changes when you process edges in sorted order instead of arbitrary order.

problems.label: ABC 472 E
problems.title: Odd Cycle
problems.teaches: That two-colouring is not just a yes/no test - the failing edge plus its tree path is a constructive witness.
problems.nudge: Two-colour the graph with a DFS or BFS tree. An odd cycle exists exactly when some edge joins two vertices of the same colour; take that edge together with the tree path between its endpoints up to their meeting vertex, and the resulting simple cycle has odd length.

problems.label: ARC 177 C
problems.title: Routing
problems.teaches: Shortest path when every edge costs 0 or 1, using a deque instead of a heap.
problems.nudge: Stepping onto a cell whose colour already suits your route costs 0, otherwise it costs 1 (repaint it purple). That is 0-1 BFS with a deque: push 0-cost moves to the front, 1-cost moves to the back. Solve the red route and the blue route independently and add the two answers.

problems.label: ABC 208 D
problems.title: Shortest Path Queries 2
problems.teaches: What the outer loop of Floyd-Warshall actually means: the set of permitted intermediate vertices.
problems.nudge: After the k-th iteration of Floyd-Warshall's outer loop, the table holds exactly `f(s,t,k)` - the shortest paths allowed to pass only through vertices 1..k. So run the standard triple loop and add the whole table into the running total at the end of every outer step.

problems.label: ABC 256 E
problems.title: Takahashi's Anguish
problems.teaches: That one out-edge per vertex means every component holds exactly one cycle, and only cycles obstruct a topological order.
problems.nudge: Each person i forces the constraint 'i before X_i', so the graph i -> X_i has out-degree one everywhere: a functional graph whose every component has a single cycle. Constraints off the cycles can always be satisfied for free; on each cycle exactly one must break, and you pay the minimum C_i on that cycle.

problems.label: ABC 235 E
problems.title: MST + 1
problems.teaches: The cycle property of minimum spanning trees, and answering edge queries offline by folding them into Kruskal.
problems.nudge: A candidate edge (u, v, w) belongs to the MST exactly when w is smaller than the largest edge on the current MST path between u and v. Sort the real edges and the queries together by weight and run Kruskal: a query is `Yes` iff u and v are still in different DSU components when it comes up.

tiers.name: Building the graph the problem hides
tiers.note: The hard part stops being the algorithm and becomes the modelling: which vertices, which edges, which direction, and what extra nodes you have to invent so a textbook routine applies.

problems.label: ABC 342 E
problems.title: Last Train
problems.teaches: Running Dijkstra backwards with a max-heap when the quantity to optimise is a latest time rather than an earliest one.
problems.nudge: Let `f(B)` be the latest moment you may still be standing at station B. Work backwards from station N with a max-heap over the reversed graph: for a train A -> B, the best usable departure is the largest `l + j*d` with `j < k` and `l + j*d + c <= f(B)`, which is one division to compute - relax A with it.

problems.label: ABC 469 F
problems.title: GCD Maximum Spanning Tree
problems.teaches: Running Kruskal over candidate weights rather than over edges, when the edge set is a dense implicit clique.
problems.nudge: Never enumerate the N^2 pairs. Sweep d from 10^6 down to 1; all indices whose A_i is a multiple of d are pairwise joined by an edge of weight at least d, so union them all in DSU and charge d for each union that actually merges. The harmonic sum of multiples keeps this near `10^6 log`.

problems.label: ABC 204 E
problems.title: Rush Hour 2
problems.teaches: That Dijkstra survives edge costs that depend on the current time, as long as arrival time is still monotone and each relaxation can be minimised in O(1).
problems.nudge: Waiting can pay: relaxing an edge means minimising `t + C + floor(D/(t+1))` over departure times t at or after your arrival. That function is convex in t with its minimum near `sqrt(D) - 1`, so test only the arrival time itself and a couple of integers around `sqrt(D) - 1`, then run Dijkstra unchanged.

problems.label: ABC 413 G
problems.title: Big Banned Grid
problems.teaches: Searching the obstacles instead of the cells - the planar duality between 'a path exists' and 'no barrier exists'.
problems.nudge: The grid has up to 4*10^10 cells but only 2*10^5 obstacles, so search those. A path from (1,1) to (H,W) is blocked exactly when obstacles, adjacent in any of the 8 directions, chain the top-right boundary (row 1 or column W) to the bottom-left boundary (column 1 or row H). Hash the obstacle coordinates, union 8-neighbours, and add one virtual node per boundary side.

problems.label: ABC 364 F
problems.title: Range Connect MST
problems.teaches: Handling an MST over an implicit range-to-vertex edge set by sorting operations and merging each consecutive pair only once.
problems.nudge: Sort the Q operations by C ascending and run Kruskal. Operation i always spends C_i once to attach vertex N+i to the range. Beyond that, every pair of consecutive vertices inside [L_i, R_i] still in different components costs another C_i to merge - keep a 'next unmerged index' DSU so the total number of merges over all operations is O(N).

tiers.name: Graph structure as algebra
tiers.note: The final tier treats a graph as an algebraic object: paths as potentials, cycles as a linear space, constraints as edges, and forests as things to count. Each rung needs a correct model before any code helps.

problems.label: ABC 295 G
problems.title: Minimum Reachable City
problems.teaches: Amortised path collapsing in a DSU: each vertex is absorbed into an ancestor blob at most once over the whole run.
problems.nudge: G_S is a rooted tree with edges parent -> child, and a type-1 edge u -> v is only offered when v is an ancestor of u, so it makes the whole tree path from u up to v mutually reachable. Keep a DSU whose representative is the shallowest vertex of each blob; to add the edge, jump from u to the parent of its representative repeatedly until you land in v's blob, merging as you go. Since ancestors carry smaller labels, a type-2 answer is just the representative.

problems.label: ABC 451 G
problems.title: Minimum XOR Walk
problems.teaches: That walk values in a XOR-weighted graph are a coset: a spanning-tree potential plus the linear span of the fundamental cycles.
problems.nudge: Root a spanning tree and set `d[v]` to the XOR of edges from the root to v. Every walk from x to y has value `d[x] xor d[y] xor c` where c ranges over the XOR span of the fundamental cycles, and every such c is achievable. Build that linear basis, reduce each `d[v]` by it, and count pairs whose reduced XOR is at most K with a binary trie.

problems.label: AGC 056 C
problems.title: 01 Balanced
problems.teaches: Turning a system of inequalities on prefix sums into a graph, so that a shortest-path run produces the extremal feasible assignment.
problems.nudge: Let `x_i` be the number of ones in the first i characters. Adjacent positions force `0 <= x_i - x_{i-1} <= 1`, and each condition forces `x_R - x_{L-1} = (R-L+1)/2`, i.e. two opposite inequalities. That is a difference-constraint system, so its extremal solution is a shortest-path computation over N+1 nodes - and every constraint edge has weight 0 or 1, so 0-1 BFS handles N up to 10^6.

problems.label: ABC 306 G
problems.title: Return to 1
problems.teaches: That the set of closed-walk lengths through a vertex is generated by a single gcd, computable from DFS potentials inside one strongly connected component.
problems.nudge: Only the strongly connected component containing vertex 1 matters. Give each of its vertices a DFS depth `pot[v]`, and let g be the gcd of `pot[u] + 1 - pot[v]` over all edges inside that component - g generates every closed-walk length through vertex 1. The answer is Yes exactly when g divides `10^(10^100)`, that is, when g has no prime factor other than 2 and 5.

problems.label: ABC 253 Ex
problems.title: We Love Forest
problems.teaches: Counting labelled forests over a fixed edge list with subset DP, and converting an ordered random process into a count of edge sets.
problems.nudge: Picking the same index twice creates a multi-edge, which is a cycle, so the K picks must be K distinct edges forming a forest: the probability is `K! * (number of K-edge forests) / M^K`. With N at most 14, count forests by subset DP - first spanning trees of each vertex subset using only the given edges, then glue components together, always fixing the lowest-numbered remaining vertex so each forest is counted once.

ladders.name: Trees: Diameter, LCA & Path Queries
ladders.blurb: This ladder is about tree shape rather than tree DP: rooting, depth, ancestors, and the paths between vertices. It opens on graphs you have to root yourself — a parent function, a DFS tree, a functional graph — then meets trees hiding inside arrays and near-trees carrying one extra edge, before installing the standard toolkit: the Euler tour that turns a subtree into an interval, root-to-node prefixes that collapse a path aggregate into a two-term formula, and binary lifting for LCA and k-th ancestor. The last tier is where one root pass stops being enough — centroid decomposition, an undoable union-find carried down the DFS, and queries answered by cutting a path at its midpoint.

tiers.name: Root it and read off depth
tiers.note: Every rung here is a graph you have to root yourself. The habits to take away: a parent function defines a tree even when nobody draws one, DFS depth behaves better than BFS depth, and a doubling table turns "follow the parent T times" into O(log T).

problems.label: ABC 465 D
problems.title: X to Y
problems.teaches: A parent function is enough to define a tree, and the shortest edit sequence between two values is just the tree distance.
problems.nudge: Each value y has exactly one parent, `floor(y/K)`, so all reachable values form a tree rooted at 0 and every operation is one edge of it. Depth is at most about 60 because `K >= 2`, so lift the deeper of X and Y until the depths match, then step both up in lockstep until they collide.

problems.label: ARC 224 C
problems.title: Ascending Labels
problems.teaches: The DFS tree of an undirected graph has no cross edges, which is exactly the property that makes DFS depth a valid label where BFS depth is not.
problems.nudge: BFS levels fail: a vertex can have several neighbours one level up. Run a DFS from vertex 1 and set `A_v` to the DFS depth — every non-tree edge of an undirected DFS tree joins an ancestor to a descendant, and the only ancestor sitting at depth `A_v - 1` is the parent, so the "exactly one" condition is automatic.

problems.label: ABC 438 E
problems.title: Heavy Buckets
problems.teaches: Binary lifting is not only for ancestors — carry an aggregate in the table alongside the destination and you can sum a path of length T in O(log T).
problems.nudge: Bucket B is held by person B, then by `A_B`, then by `A[A_B]`, and each holder adds its own number, so the answer is the sum of the first T iterates of A starting at B. Build two doubling tables side by side: where a vertex lands after `2^j` steps, and the total added over those `2^j` steps.

problems.label: ABC 398 E
problems.title: Tree Game
problems.teaches: A tree's bipartition is just depth parity, and when no move can ever block another the whole game reduces to counting the moves.
problems.nudge: Forbidding odd cycles means keeping the graph bipartite, and the tree already fixes the 2-colouring by depth parity — an edge is legal exactly when its endpoints have different parity, and adding one never invalidates another. So the number of moves is fixed at `a*b - (N-1)` for colour class sizes a and b; its parity alone decides whether to go first, and then you may play any remaining legal pair.

tiers.name: Trees that arrive disguised
tiers.note: Objects that are not presented as trees but behave like one: a permutation split at its maximum, a graph with exactly one cycle, a functional graph, a binary tree far too large to store. The skill is spotting the tree and deciding where to root it.

problems.label: ABC 435 F
problems.title: Cat exercise
problems.teaches: Recursively splitting an array at its maximum is a tree construction, and once you name it the problem becomes a walk down that tree.
problems.nudge: Removing the tallest tower first cuts the line at its position, and the cat then has to jump to the tallest tower of the left part or of the right part — recurse on each. That recursion is the Cartesian tree of P built on maxima; the answer is the best root-to-leaf descent where the cost of an edge is the index gap between a node and the child it moves to.

problems.label: ABC 266 F
problems.title: Well-defined Path Queries on a Namori
problems.teaches: A connected graph with one extra edge is a cycle with trees hanging off it, and labelling each vertex by its cycle root answers a whole class of queries.
problems.nudge: N vertices and N edges means exactly one cycle. Strip it out by repeatedly deleting degree-1 vertices, then label every vertex with the cycle vertex whose hanging tree it belongs to. The simple path from x to y is unique exactly when those two labels agree — otherwise you can round the cycle either way.

problems.label: ABC 258 E
problems.title: Packing Potatoes
problems.teaches: When a state transition is a function on N states, indices as large as 10^12 collapse to a tail plus a cycle.
problems.nudge: One two-pointer sweep over the doubled prefix sums gives, for every start index i, how many potatoes that box takes and where the next box starts. That makes `next` a function on N states, so the sequence of box starts is a tail into a cycle — find the entry point and the cycle length once, then reduce every `K_i` into it.

problems.label: ABC 321 E
problems.title: Complete Binary Tree
problems.teaches: With N up to 10^18 the tree is never built, but its shape is regular enough that depth-level counts are closed-form intervals.
problems.nudge: You can only afford about 60 steps, so walk up the at most 60 ancestors of X. From the ancestor at distance d you want vertices exactly `K-d` further down that do not re-enter the child you came from, and the count of nodes at a fixed depth below a node of a complete binary tree is a contiguous index range clamped against `[1, N]`.

tiers.name: Euler tour, root prefix, binary lifting
tiers.note: The core toolkit. One DFS gives `tin`/`tout`, so a subtree becomes an interval; a root-to-node prefix turns a path aggregate into two or three lookups once you can locate the LCA.

problems.label: ABC 202 E
problems.title: Count Descendants
problems.teaches: The Euler tour turns "is u in U's subtree" into an interval test, so a subtree-and-depth query becomes a binary search.
problems.nudge: One DFS gives `tin` and `tout`, and u lies in U's subtree exactly when `tin[U] <= tin[u] < tout[U]`. Bucket vertices by depth, sort each bucket's `tin` values, and each query is two binary searches inside the bucket for depth D.

problems.label: ABC 201 E
problems.title: Xor Distances
problems.teaches: For any group operation, a path aggregate is the root prefix of one endpoint combined with the root prefix of the other — the part above the LCA cancels.
problems.nudge: Root at 1 and let `X_v` be the XOR of edge weights from the root down to v. Then `dist(i,j) = X_i xor X_j`, because the shared stretch above the LCA appears twice and cancels — no LCA computation needed. Finish bitwise: bit b contributes `2^b` times (count of v with the bit set) times (count without).

problems.label: ABC 294 G
problems.title: Distance Queries on a Tree
problems.teaches: Once edge weights change between queries, the root prefix has to live in a Fenwick tree over the Euler tour instead of a plain array.
problems.nudge: Give each edge to its deeper endpoint and store `+w` at that vertex's `tin` and `-w` at its `tout` in a Fenwick tree — a prefix sum up to `tin[v]` is then `dist(root, v)`, and changing an edge weight is two point updates. Answer a query with `d(u) + d(v) - 2*d(lca(u,v))`.

problems.label: ABC 267 F
problems.title: Exactly K Steps
problems.teaches: The farthest vertex from any starting point is always an endpoint of a diameter — combine that with binary lifting and every "walk exactly K" query is O(log N).
problems.nudge: Two BFS runs give a diameter with endpoints A and B, and the vertex farthest from any U is one of them, so the answer is -1 exactly when K exceeds both `d(U,A)` and `d(U,B)`. Otherwise head toward an endpoint that is far enough: split the U-to-endpoint walk at their LCA and use binary lifting to land on the K-th vertex.

tiers.name: Decompose, or answer offline
tiers.note: Where a single root pass runs out. These rungs decompose the tree itself, carry an undoable structure down the DFS, or cut a path at its middle to split the tree in two.

problems.label: ABC 291 Ex
problems.title: Balanced Tree
problems.teaches: Centroid decomposition is exactly a rooted tree whose LCA of any two vertices lies on their path in the original — this problem asks you to output that object.
problems.nudge: Build the centroid decomposition tree: the centroid of a component becomes the parent of the centroids of the pieces it splits into.
