Halving component sizes gives the factor-2 subtree condition directly, and the LCA condition holds because the LCA in R of x and y is the first centroid that separates them, which by definition sits on their path in T.

problems.label: ABC 302 Ex
problems.title: Ball Collector
problems.teaches: Answering a query for every root-to-vertex path at once means maintaining a structure that supports undo, so the DFS can push and pop path elements.
problems.nudge: Turn the path into a graph on ball values, with one edge `(A_i, B_i)` per vertex: a connected component with k values and at least k edges yields all k, while a tree component yields `k-1`. DFS the tree keeping a union-find over values plus a per-component "has a cycle" flag, and undo each merge on the way back up — union by size with no path compression, so rollback is exact.

problems.label: ABC 298 Ex
problems.title: Sum of Min of Length
problems.teaches: A min over two endpoints partitions the tree at the middle of the path joining them, which reduces the query to two precomputed half-tree aggregates.
problems.nudge: Every vertex is closer to L or to R according to which side of the middle of the L-R path it sits on, so find that midpoint by binary lifting and the query becomes one cut edge. Precompute the sum of distances from every vertex by rerooting, and for each directed edge the vertex count and distance sum on the far side; then each half is a couple of lookups plus a count times a known distance.

problems.label: AGC 047 D
problems.title: Twin Binary Trees
problems.teaches: In a tree of height H every vertex has only H ancestors, so pairing leaves can be organised by fixing the LCA on both sides and merging per-level arrays.
problems.nudge: A cycle with two special edges is a pair of leaves: a path in tree 1, a hop across, a path in tree 2, a hop back. H is at most 18, so budget O(H) per leaf: walk tree 1 bottom-up fixing its LCA and combining the two child subtrees, carrying for each leaf an array indexed by its at most 18 ancestors in tree 2 holding the accumulated path product. Pair the two sides level by level, requiring the two leaves to enter an ancestor from different children so that it really is their LCA in tree 2.

ladders.name: String Algorithms & Palindromes
ladders.blurb: Twenty rungs that build the string toolkit in the order you actually need it: first counting occurrences by hand and keeping that count correct under edits, then the prefix structures — tries, borders, the Z-function — that let you compare prefixes and suffixes in bulk, then rolling hashes and segment trees for substring queries, and finally the automata (Aho-Corasick, the period structure of a string) that turn 'which patterns occur where' into a state machine you can run a DP or a matrix power on. Palindromes appear throughout, first as a window you must avoid, then as a hashed equality test, then as a reversal you have to locate.

tiers.name: Scanning and Counting
tiers.note: Occurrences you can count with a single pass, and the discipline of keeping that count correct when the string changes underneath you. Nothing here needs a named algorithm — it needs you to say exactly which positions a change can affect.

problems.label: ABC 346 B
problems.title: Piano
problems.teaches: That a question about an infinite periodic string is a question about a bounded window of it, once you bound how long the answer can be.
problems.nudge: The pattern `wbwbwwbwbwbw` has period 12 and `W + B <= 200`, so any substring you care about fits inside a couple of dozen periods. Build the repeated string once, long enough, and brute-force every start and end.

problems.label: ABC 372 C
problems.title: Count ABC Again
problems.teaches: The standard move for occurrence counts under point updates: subtract the windows a change can touch, apply the change, add them back.
problems.nudge: Changing position `X` can only create or destroy an occurrence of `ABC` that starts at `X-2`, `X-1` or `X`. Keep a running total, remove those three windows' contributions, write the new character, then re-add them.

problems.label: ABC 307 D
problems.title: Mismatched Parentheses
problems.teaches: That repeated 'delete the innermost matched thing' rules are a stack, and the order of deletions never matters.
problems.nudge: Push every character onto a stack. When you read `)`, pop back to the most recent unmatched `(` and throw that whole block away; if there is no `(` on the stack, the `)` survives. What is left on the stack, bottom to top, is the answer.

problems.label: ABC 381 D
problems.title: 1122 Substring
problems.teaches: Reindexing a string by blocks so that a two-pointer window can enforce a 'no repeated value' condition.
problems.nudge: A 1122 subarray is a run of equal adjacent pairs, so first mark every position `i` with `A[i] == A[i+1]` as a candidate pair. A valid answer starts at an even offset from its first pair, so run two separate sliding windows (one for each start parity) over the pair positions and shrink whenever a value repeats inside the window.

problems.label: ABC 430 E
problems.title: Shift String
problems.teaches: The doubling trick — every rotation of A is a substring of A+A — and your first real use of linear-time pattern search.
problems.nudge: Rotating A by k gives the length-|A| substring of `A + A` starting at index k, so the answer is the smallest index where B occurs in `A + A`. With |A| up to 10^6 you cannot compare rotations one by one; run KMP or the Z-function of `B + '#' + A + A` and take the first hit.

tiers.name: Tries, Windows, and Borders
tiers.note: The first structures that compare prefixes in bulk instead of one pair at a time: the trie, a DP whose state is the last few characters, and the Z-function. This is where 'shared prefix' stops being a loop and becomes a node.

problems.label: ABC 353 E
problems.title: Yet Another Sigma Problem
problems.teaches: That a sum over all pairs of longest-common-prefix lengths is really a sum over trie nodes, counting how many pairs pass through each one.
problems.nudge: Insert every string into a trie and let `c[v]` be the number of strings passing through node `v`. A pair contributes 1 for each node of depth >= 1 that both strings pass through, so the answer is the sum of `c[v] * (c[v] - 1) / 2` over all non-root nodes.

problems.label: ABC 359 D
problems.title: Avoid K Palindrome
problems.teaches: The core palindrome-avoidance DP: carry the last K-1 characters as the state, because that is exactly what you need to test the next window.
problems.nudge: `K <= 10`, so encode the last `K-1` characters as a bitmask over {A, B} — at most 512 states. Move left to right; when you append a character you form one new window of length K, so reject the transition if that window is a palindrome, and respect the fixed characters of S.

problems.label: ABC 403 E
problems.title: Forbidden Prefix
problems.teaches: That 'has some string as a prefix' is 'lies in that node's subtree', so forbidding a prefix is deactivating a subtree once and for all.
problems.nudge: Put both multisets in one trie. A Y-string is alive unless some node on its root path is marked by an X-string. When an X-string arrives, walk to its node and kill its whole subtree once (subtract the live Y-count stored there and mark it dead so you never descend again); total work stays linear in the summed lengths.

problems.label: ABC 415 F
problems.title: Max Combo
problems.teaches: How to design a mergeable summary for a range query: store just enough at each node that two children combine in O(1).
problems.nudge: Each segment tree node needs the length of the segment, its leading run, its trailing run, the characters those runs use, and the best run inside. Merging two nodes is mostly copying, plus the one extra case where the left node's trailing run and the right node's leading run share a character and join.

problems.label: ABC 284 F
problems.title: ABCBAC
problems.teaches: Reading a construction backwards into two prefix/suffix match questions, and answering all N+1 of them at once with the Z-function.
problems.nudge: If `T = S[1..i] + reverse(S) + S[i+1..N]`, then `T[1..i]` must equal the reverse of `T[N+i+1..2N]`, and `T[i+1..N+i]` is the reverse of the rest. Concretely: `T` and `reverse(T)` must agree as a prefix of length `i` and as a suffix of length `N-i`, so compute the Z-arrays of `reverse(T) + '#' + T` and of `T + '#' + reverse(T)` and test every `i` in O(1).

tiers.name: Hashes, Queries, and Automata
tiers.note: Substring equality as an O(1) test, structures over many strings at once, and the first genuine automaton. The theme is turning a property of a substring into something you can look up rather than recompute.

problems.label: ABC 331 F
problems.title: Palindrome Query
problems.teaches: The canonical rolling-hash setup: a substring is a palindrome exactly when its forward hash equals the backward hash of the mirrored range.
problems.nudge: Keep two segment trees of polynomial hashes, one over S and one over reverse(S), each node storing the hash of its range so a point update costs O(log N). `S[L..R]` is a palindrome iff its forward hash equals the hash of the same range read from the reversed string, which sits at positions `N+1-R .. N+1-L`.

problems.label: AGC 047 B
problems.title: First Second
problems.teaches: Characterising a reachability relation as 'a shared suffix plus one earlier character', then grouping by that suffix in a trie built on reversed strings.
problems.nudge: Deleting one of the first two characters repeatedly means T is reachable from S exactly when `T[2..]` is a suffix of S and `T[1]` occurs somewhere in the first `|S| - |T| + 1` characters of S. Insert all strings reversed into a trie; at the node of depth `|T|-1` you need to know which first characters are still available from the longer strings passing through, so carry 26 counters down the DFS.

problems.label: ABC 285 F
problems.title: Substring of Sorted String
problems.teaches: Decomposing a compound predicate into independently maintainable counters — here 'sorted' and 'uses up all of each interior letter'.
problems.nudge: `S[l..r]` is a substring of sorted(S) iff it is non-decreasing and, for every character strictly between its first and last character, the whole of S's supply of that character sits inside `[l, r]`. Keep 26 Fenwick trees of character counts plus one Fenwick tree counting descent positions `S[i] > S[i+1]`; a point update touches only O(1) of each.

problems.label: ABC 305 G
problems.title: Banned Substrings
problems.teaches: The standard pipeline for counting long strings avoiding patterns: build the automaton, write the transitions as a matrix, exponentiate.
problems.nudge: Every banned string has length at most 6, so the last 5 characters are all the state you need — or equivalently build the Aho-Corasick automaton of the banned set and delete the accepting nodes. With `N` up to 10^18, write the surviving transitions as a matrix over the states and raise it to the `N`-th power.

problems.label: AGC 055 B
problems.title: ABC Supremacy
problems.teaches: That deciding reachability under a local rewrite rule is usually 'compute a canonical form and compare' — and that finding the canonical form is the whole problem.
problems.nudge: `ABC`, `BCA` and `CAB` are the rotations of one block, and the key observation is that such a block can be pushed past any single neighbouring character (check `ABCA -> AABC` by hand). So the block's position carries no information: reduce each string with a stack, deleting the top three whenever they form one of the three patterns, and compare the leftovers.

tiers.name: Periods, Overlaps, and Multi-Pattern Machinery
tiers.note: Where borders stop being a trick and become the object of study: prefix covers, maximal overlaps between strings, the primitive period of a string, and Aho-Corasick driving a greedy. Each rung here is a technique you will reuse rather than a puzzle.

problems.label: ABC 257 G
problems.title: Prefix Concatenation
problems.teaches: That 'cover T with prefixes of S' becomes a jump-game once you know, for every position of T, how far a prefix of S can reach from there.
problems.nudge: Run the Z-function on `S + '#' + T`; for each index `i` of T that gives you `len[i]`, the longest prefix of S starting at `i`. From `i` you may jump anywhere in `[i+1, i+len[i]]`, and since the reachable set is always a contiguous interval, a greedy sweep (extend the current furthest reach, bump the count when you pass the old one) gives the minimum k. Report -1 the moment some `len[i]` is 0.

problems.label: ABC 343 G
problems.title: Compress Strings
problems.teaches: The shortest-superstring recipe: drop contained strings, compute maximal overlaps with a border computation, then run a Hamiltonian-path DP over the subsets.
problems.nudge: First discard any `S_i` that already occurs inside another `S_j`. Then `overlap(i, j)` — the longest suffix of `S_i` that is a prefix of `S_j` — is the border length you get from running KMP on `S_j + '#' + S_i` and reading the final failure value. With `N <= 20`, finish with a bitmask DP over (set used, last string).

problems.label: ABC 268 G
problems.title: Random Student ID
problems.teaches: Linearity of expectation on an ordering: the expected rank is a sum of pairwise comparison probabilities, and each probability depends only on the first place two strings differ.
problems.nudge: Expected ID of `S_i` is `1 + sum over j != i of P(S_j < S_i)`. If neither string is a prefix of the other, the comparison is decided by two distinct letters and the random permutation makes it 1/2; if `S_j` is a proper prefix of `S_i` it is always smaller, and if `S_i` is a proper prefix of `S_j` never. So you only need, per string, how many others are its proper prefixes and how many it is a proper prefix of — one trie pass.

problems.label: ABC 312 Ex
problems.title: snukesnuke
problems.teaches: The primitive root of a string, read straight off the prefix function, and why two strings collide under repetition exactly when their roots agree.
problems.nudge: `S^a = T^b` is possible only when S and T are powers of the same primitive string, so reduce each `S_i` to its primitive root: compute the prefix function, and if `n % (n - pi[n]) == 0` the shortest period is `n - pi[n]`. Group people by root; inside a group `S_i = R^{e_i}` and its k-th nickname uses `e_i * k` copies of R, so keep one 'next free multiple' pointer per (root, e) and advance it.

problems.label: ABC 268 Ex
problems.title: Taboo
problems.teaches: Aho-Corasick as an occurrence stream, plus the interval-stabbing exchange argument that makes the greedy choice provably optimal.
problems.nudge: Every occurrence of some `T_i` is an interval of S that you must hit with at least one `*`, so this is minimum points stabbing all intervals — sweep left to right and always stab at the right endpoint of the earliest-ending unstabbed interval. Feed S through the Aho-Corasick automaton of the `T_i`; at each position you want the shortest match ending there, which you precompute per node as the minimum pattern length along its suffix-link chain.

ladders.name: Bitwise Operations & XOR
ladders.guide_label: Bit Manipulation — XOR Properties & Linear Basis
ladders.blurb: A climb through the two habits that make bitwise problems easy: treating a number as a set you can enumerate, and treating each bit as a problem you can solve on its own. It starts with subset brute force and top-bit comparisons, moves to prefix XOR and per-bit counting, then to XOR as an invariant — Grundy values and GF(2) algebra — and finishes with binary tries, per-bit counting under floor sums, and bitset DP.

tiers.name: Bits you can enumerate
tiers.note: Small N means you can walk every subset, and a single number can be read from its most significant bit down. These rungs build the habit of seeing a number as a mask and a comparison as a question about one bit.

problems.label: ABC 358 C
problems.title: Popcorn
problems.teaches: Encoding a set of items as an integer mask and enumerating all 2^N subsets — the base move of every bitmask solution.
problems.nudge: N and M are at most 10. Turn each stand's string into an M-bit mask, loop over all `1 << N` subsets of stands, OR their masks together, and keep the smallest popcount whose OR is the full mask.

problems.label: ARC 129 A
problems.title: Smaller XOR
problems.teaches: That comparing `x ^ N` with `N` is settled entirely by one bit position, turning a comparison into a union of ranges.
problems.nudge: XORing only ever changes bits where x has a 1, and the most significant of those decides the comparison: `x ^ N < N` exactly when N has a 1 at the highest set bit of x. So the valid x are the union of the 60 intervals `[2^b, 2^(b+1) - 1]` over bits b where N is 1; intersect each with [L, R].

problems.label: ABC 301 D
problems.title: Bitmask
problems.teaches: The high-to-low greedy: fix bits from the most significant end, taking a 1 whenever it keeps the value feasible.
problems.nudge: Set every `?` to 0 first — if that already exceeds N the answer is -1. Then sweep the `?` positions from most significant to least and flip each to 1 only when the resulting value is still at most N; a high bit is always worth more than every lower bit combined.

problems.label: ABC 365 E
problems.title: Xor Sigma Problem
problems.teaches: The two workhorses together: XOR is its own inverse so a subarray XOR is a difference of prefixes, and each bit can then be counted separately.
problems.nudge: Let P_0 = 0 and P_j = A_1 ^ ... ^ A_j; the XOR of A_i..A_j is `P_(i-1) ^ P_j`. For each bit independently, a pair of prefixes contributes only when their bits differ, so the count is (number of prefixes with that bit 0) times (number with it 1). The sum you want excludes single elements, so subtract sum of A_i at the end.

problems.label: ABC 412 D
problems.title: Make 2-Regular Graph
problems.teaches: Enumerating structured objects over a vertex bitmask when N is tiny, and turning an edit-distance objective into a maximisation.
problems.nudge: A 2-regular graph on N vertices is a disjoint union of cycles of length at least 3, and it always has exactly N edges. So the cost is `N + M - 2 * (edges you keep)` — enumerate partitions of the at most 8 vertices into cycles (subsets plus a cyclic order inside each) and maximise the kept edges.

tiers.name: Splitting a number into independent bits
tiers.note: Here the statement is about whole numbers but the solution is about one bit at a time — decide each bit alone, then reassemble. Two of these also lean on XOR being its own inverse.

problems.label: ABC 310 E
problems.title: NAND repeatedly
problems.teaches: That when values live in {0,1} you never track which prefixes give what — only how many of each, so a quadratic sum collapses to a linear scan.
problems.nudge: Sweep j from left to right keeping c0 and c1, the number of i with f(i,j) = 0 and = 1. The NAND table does the transition: if A_j is 0 every value becomes 1, and if A_j is 1 the two counts swap. Add the singleton f(j,j) = A_j at each step and accumulate c1.

problems.label: ABC 396 E
problems.title: Min of Restricted Sum
problems.teaches: That `A_x ^ A_y = Z` constraints form a graph where one free value per component fixes everything, and the free choice is then made bit by bit.
problems.nudge: Treat each constraint as an edge and BFS each component with the root set to 0, propagating `A_v = A_u ^ Z`; any edge that disagrees means -1. The whole component can then be XORed by any single value, so for each bit independently flip it when more than half the component's vertices currently have that bit set.

problems.label: ARC 135 C
problems.title: XOR to All
problems.teaches: That repeating a self-inverse operation buys nothing — the reachable states collapse to a set of size N, which per-bit counting then evaluates fast.
problems.nudge: After XORing everything by A_k the array is `A_i ^ A_k`, and any second operation uses a value `A_m ^ A_k` currently present, giving `A_i ^ A_m`. So every reachable array is the original or `A_i ^ A_j` for one original j — score all N candidates in O(30N) using per-bit counts of how many A_i have each bit set.

tiers.name: XOR as an invariant
tiers.note: XOR stops being an operation in the statement and becomes the quantity that describes the state: Grundy values of independent subgames, and linear algebra over GF(2). The bit view is what makes these tractable at all.

problems.label: ARC 219 D
problems.title: Grid Game
problems.teaches: Reindexing a game so that only half the piles matter, and how a per-move cap of K turns a pile into its size mod (K+1).
problems.nudge: Index each cell by `d = i + j`; a move always sends stones from d to d - 1, so this is staircase nim — moves from even d can be mirrored and only cells with i + j odd count. With at most K stones per move each such pile behaves as bounded nim, so XOR `A[i][j] mod (K+1)` over those cells.

problems.label: ABC 297 G
problems.title: Constrained Nim 2
problems.teaches: Deriving a closed-form Grundy value for a single pile by brute-forcing small cases and spotting the period, then XORing across independent piles.
problems.nudge: Piles are independent, so compute the Grundy number of one pile and XOR. Brute force small A with a given L and R and the pattern is periodic with period L + R: the value is `floor((A mod (L + R)) / L)`.

problems.label: ARC 151 C
problems.title: 01 Game
problems.teaches: Cutting a huge board into independent subgames at the fixed cells, and handling N up to 10^18 by finding the period of the Grundy sequence.
problems.nudge: The pre-filled cells split the line into runs of empty squares that never interact, so the position is a sum of games. A run's Grundy value depends only on its length and on which of its two ends are fixed (and whether those two fixed digits agree) — brute force short runs for each of those few cases, find the period, and XOR.

problems.label: ARC 137 D
problems.title: Prefix XORs
problems.teaches: That iterating a prefix-XOR map k times weights each input by a binomial coefficient mod 2, and Kummer's carry rule turns that weight into a submask test.
problems.nudge: After k rounds A_N is the XOR of A_(N-j) weighted by `C(k-1+j, j) mod 2`, and `C(a+b, b)` is odd exactly when `a AND b == 0` (no carries when adding a and b). So the weight is 1 precisely when j is a submask of the complement of k-1 — get all M answers at once with a subset-sum (SOS) transform over bitmasks.

problems.label: ABC 206 F
problems.title: Interval Game 2
problems.teaches: Grundy on a range where a move splits the region into two independent halves — the mex-over-splits pattern that shows up all over game DP.
problems.nudge: Once an interval is taken, the region left of its L and the region right of its R can never interact, so define g(l, r) over coordinate ranges (all at most 100) and set it to the mex over every input interval contained in [l, r) of `g(l, L_i) XOR g(R_i, r)`. The answer is g over the whole range.

tiers.name: Tries, digit sums and bitsets
tiers.note: The hard end: descending the bits as a data structure. A binary trie or a bitwise divide and conquer answers pair questions, a Euclidean-like floor sum answers per-bit counting questions, and a bitset turns an infeasible DP into a fast one.

problems.label: ARC 122 D
problems.title: XOR Game
problems.teaches: Reading a minimax over pairings as a parity argument on the top bit: counts decide whether any pair is forced to cross the split.
problems.nudge: Split the multiset by the current top bit. If both sides have even size, no pair is forced to cross, the answer's bit is 0, and you recurse into each side. If both sides are odd, exactly one pair must cross — Alice can force that bit to 1 and Bob then picks the cheapest crossing pair, so the answer is the minimum XOR between the two sides, found with a binary trie.

problems.label: ARC 127 D
problems.title: Sum of Min of Xor
problems.teaches: Turning a min of two XORs into a single comparison key, then splitting all pairs by the bits of that key so each pair's winner is known.
problems.nudge: Which of `A_i^A_j` and `B_i^B_j` is smaller is decided at their highest differing bit, which is the highest set bit of `C_i ^ C_j` where `C = A ^ B`. So recurse on the bits of C: for pairs that split at a node you know from that bit which of A or B is the smaller XOR, and you can total those XORs with per-bit counts. Pairs with equal C give equal values, so sum either.

problems.label: ABC 283 Ex
problems.title: Popcount Sum
problems.teaches: The clean form of solving each bit independently: bit b of x is `floor(x / 2^b) - 2 * floor(x / 2^(b+1))`, so popcount sums become sums of floors over an arithmetic progression.
problems.nudge: Write x = M*j + R and sum over j. Bit b of x is `floor(x / 2^b) - 2 * floor(x / 2^(b+1))`, so the total popcount is a fixed number of sums of the form `sum_j floor((M*j + R) / 2^k)` — exactly what the Euclidean-like floor_sum routine computes in O(log), and with T up to 10^5 you need that per query.

problems.label: ABC 221 G
problems.title: Jumping sequence
problems.teaches: Decoupling two coordinates by a 45-degree rotation and then pushing a 2000 x 3.6 million subset-sum DP through with a bitset.
problems.nudge: Rotate: with `u = x + y` and `v = x - y`, each jump contributes independently `+D_i` or `-D_i` to u and independently to v, so the four directions become two separate sign choices. Each coordinate is then a subset sum — pick S with `2*sum(S) = total + target` (check parity and range) — solved by shifting a bitset, keeping per-step states so you can backtrack the signs and recombine them into U/D/L/R.

ladders.name: Number Theory
ladders.guide_label: Number Theory & Combinatorics — GCD / Extended Euclidean
ladders.blurb: Twenty rungs that build the standard number-theory toolkit in the order it actually becomes useful. It opens with the Euclidean algorithm and the two things it really is - an invariant and a fast loop - then moves to counting over divisors and multiples with sieve-shaped passes, then to problems that only open once you rewrite the quantity (an exponent modulo p-1, a gcd as a gcd of differences, a number as digits with carries), and closes on multiplicative order, shift lattices, CRT alignment and rational approximation.

tiers.name: The Euclidean Spine
tiers.note: Everything here rests on gcd and on division with remainder. The goal is to stop seeing gcd as a library call and start seeing it as an invariant you can reason with, plus the reflex of replacing a loop of subtractions with one division.

problems.label: ABC 297 D
problems.title: Count Subtractions
problems.teaches: That the Euclidean algorithm is exactly repeated subtraction, and that turning the subtractions into one division is what makes it fast enough for 10^18.
problems.nudge: Subtracting the smaller from the larger over and over is `A % B`, done one step at a time. Replace each run of identical subtractions with `A / B` operations and set `A = A % B`, then swap; stop when the remainder is 0, and remember the very last block does one subtraction fewer because the process ends when the two become equal, not when one hits zero.

problems.label: ARC 137 A
problems.title: Coprime Pair
problems.teaches: That a common divisor of x and y also divides y - x, which bounds how far the answer can fall short of the whole interval.
problems.nudge: If `d` divides both `x` and `y` then `d` divides `y - x`, so a pair at distance `g` can only be non-coprime through a divisor of `g`. That makes the answer sit within a handful of steps of `R - L`: loop the gap `g` downward from `R - L` and test every pair `(x, x+g)` inside the range, stopping at the first coprime one. Consecutive integers are always coprime, so the loop always ends.

problems.label: ABC 313 C
problems.title: Approximate Equalization 2
problems.teaches: The habit of reading `S = N*q + r` as an exact statement about the target configuration, not just as arithmetic.
problems.nudge: The move preserves the sum, so the final multiset is forced: with `S = N*q + r`, exactly `r` elements end at `q+1` and `N-r` end at `q`. Sort A, hand the `q+1` targets to the largest `r` elements, and the answer is the total surplus, i.e. the sum of the positive `A[i] - target[i]`.

problems.label: ABC 226 D
problems.title: Teleportation
problems.teaches: Canonicalising a vector by dividing out the gcd, so that 'same direction' becomes 'equal after normalisation' and can be counted with a set.
problems.nudge: A single spell `(a,b)` gets you from town i to town j only if `(dx,dy)` is a positive integer multiple of `(a,b)`, so the cheapest spell for that pair is the primitive vector `(dx/g, dy/g)` with `g = gcd(|dx|,|dy|)`. With N at most 500 you can afford all ordered pairs: normalise each difference and count distinct results in a set.

problems.label: ABC 215 D
problems.title: Coprime 2
problems.teaches: That coprimality with a whole set depends only on the set of primes involved, and that marking multiples of those primes is a harmonic-cost sieve pass.
problems.nudge: `gcd(A_i, k) = 1` for all i is the same as: no prime dividing any `A_i` divides `k`. Collect that set of primes once (a smallest-prime-factor sieve up to 10^5 factorises every `A_i` fast), then cross out every multiple of each collected prime up to M. Whatever is left is the answer.

tiers.name: Divisors and Multiples
tiers.note: The step up is counting over the divisor lattice instead of over the input. Enumerate divisors in O(sqrt n), sweep multiples in harmonic time, and use gcd to describe the shape of a process rather than just a number.

problems.label: ABC 290 D
problems.title: Marking
problems.teaches: That stepping by D around a ring of N visits exactly the multiples of gcd(N,D), which turns a simulation of 10^9 steps into a closed-form index.
problems.nudge: Let `g = gcd(N,D)`. Starting from 0 and jumping by D you can only ever land on multiples of `g`, and you hit all `N/g` of them before getting stuck; the collision rule then bumps you to 1 and repeats the same cycle on the residue class 1, then 2, and so on. So the K-th mark is decided by which block and which position inside it: with `L = N/g`, block `b = (K-1)/L` and offset `i = (K-1)%L`, the answer is `(b + i*D) % N`.

problems.label: ARC 118 C
problems.title: Coprime Set
problems.teaches: Designing numbers by their prime signature: pick a tiny set of primes and let each number carry a pair of them, so pairwise overlap is forced while global overlap is not.
problems.nudge: You need every pair to share a prime while no prime is shared by all. Three primes are enough: give each number exactly two of them, so any two numbers must collide in at least one. Take multiples of 6, 10 and 15 up to 10000 - there are well over 2500 of them - and just make sure all three families are represented so the overall gcd drops to 1.

problems.label: ABC 200 D
problems.title: Happy Birthday! 2
problems.teaches: Reading the modulus as a bound on how many distinct residues exist, which caps how much of the input you ever need to search.
problems.nudge: There are only 200 residues mod 200, so among 201 subsets two must collide. Subsets of the first 8 elements already give 256 of them - enumerate those, record the first index-set seen for each residue, and the first repeat is your answer. The two subsequences are allowed to overlap, so you do not have to remove common elements.

problems.label: ABC 393 E
problems.title: GCD of Subset
problems.teaches: The sieve-shaped counting pattern: for every candidate divisor d, sweep its multiples once, and the whole thing costs O(V log V) rather than O(N sqrt V).
problems.nudge: Turn the question around: instead of asking what the best gcd for `A_i` is, ask for which `d` the answer can be `d` at all. Count `cnt[d]` = how many `A_i` are divisible by `d` with one multiples sweep, then do a second multiples sweep that pushes each `d` with `cnt[d] >= K` onto all of its multiples, keeping the largest. Read the answer off at value `A_i`.

problems.label: ARC 124 C
problems.title: LCM of GCDs
problems.teaches: That a gcd over a whole collection must divide any single member, so one element's O(sqrt n) divisor list is a complete candidate set.
problems.nudge: Pack 1 puts one of its cards in each bag, so X divides `a_1` or `b_1` and Y divides the other. Enumerate the divisors of `a_1` and of `b_1` (there are at most about 1300 each), and for each candidate pair `(X,Y)` check every pack: it is placeable iff `X | a_i and Y | b_i` or `X | b_i and Y | a_i`. Maximise `lcm(X,Y)` over the pairs that survive.

tiers.name: Rewriting the Quantity
tiers.note: Each of these is unreachable head-on and easy once the object is restated: an exponent reduced mod p-1, a gcd rewritten as a gcd of differences, a number seen as digits with carries, a forward process run backwards.

problems.label: ABC 228 E
problems.title: Integer Sequence Fair
problems.teaches: Fast exponentiation plus Fermat's little theorem: the base lives mod p, the exponent lives mod p-1, and those are different worlds.
problems.nudge: The count is `M^(K^N)` mod 998244353. You cannot reduce `K^N` mod p - reduce it mod `p-1 = 998244352` by Fermat, then power `M` by that. The one trap is `M % p == 0`: Fermat does not apply, and the answer is 0.

problems.label: ABC 423 F
problems.title: Loud Cicada
problems.teaches: Counting 'exactly M' from 'at least these' data: subset sums of floor(Y/lcm) combined with binomial-weighted inclusion-exclusion.
problems.nudge: For a subset S, the years divisible by every `A_i` in S number `Y / lcm(S)` - and with N at most 20 you can walk all 2^20 subsets, capping the running lcm above Y so it cannot overflow. Group those by subset size into `g_k`, then exactly-M is `sum over k >= M of (-1)^(k-M) * C(k,M) * g_k`.

problems.label: ABC 254 F
problems.title: Rectangle GCD
problems.teaches: The identity gcd(x,y) = gcd(x, y-x) as a data-structure enabler: differencing turns a 2D gcd query into one corner value plus two static range gcds.
problems.nudge: Every entry is `A_i + B_j`, and subtracting the top-left corner leaves `(A_i - A_h1) + (B_j - B_w1)`. Since gcd is unchanged by subtracting one element from the others, the rectangle's gcd is `gcd` of the corner value, the gcd of consecutive differences of A over `[h1, h2-1]`, and the same for B. Build a sparse table over each difference array and each query is O(1) gcds.

problems.label: ARC 123 C
problems.title: 1, 2, 3 - Decomposition
problems.teaches: Deciding a global property one decimal place at a time, with the carry as the only state that crosses between places.
problems.nudge: The answer is tiny, so loop K upward and ask only 'is K feasible?'. For a fixed K, walk N's digits from the least significant carrying a small value: if `j` of the terms still reach this place, their contribution is between `j` and `3j`, and it plus the carry must end in the required digit. The number of live terms only ever shrinks as you move to higher places, so that plus the carry is the whole DP state.

problems.label: ABC 188 F
problems.title: +1-1x2
problems.teaches: Running an operation set backwards when the forward branching factor is unbounded but the reverse one is not.
problems.nudge: Forwards you could double at any moment; backwards from Y there is essentially one move, halving, and it needs Y even. So define `f(Y)`: if `Y <= X` the answer is `X - Y`; otherwise take the best of `Y - X` and one step of halving, where an odd Y first costs one `+1` or `-1`. Memoise on Y - only O(log Y) distinct values ever appear.

tiers.name: Orders and Lattices
tiers.note: The final tier is about the structure a modulus carries: which shifts a process can reach, what the multiplicative order of an element is, how to align many cycles at once with CRT, and how to approximate a real by a bounded-denominator rational.

problems.label: ARC 152 C
problems.title: Pivot
problems.teaches: Compressing a whole orbit of operations into two numbers - a sign and a shift living in a coset of gcd*Z - so optimisation becomes picking one residue.
problems.nudge: Write the state as `eps * a_i + c` with `eps` in {+1,-1}. Pivoting on the term whose current value is `s` sends this to `-eps * a_i + (c + 2*eps*a_j)`, so every operation flips the sign and adds twice some element. Chaining them, the even-length case reaches exactly the shifts that are multiples of `2g` with `g = gcd(a_i - a_1)`, and the odd case a coset of that. Then in each of the two sign classes pick the smallest shift keeping the minimum non-negative, and compare the two resulting maxima.

problems.label: ARC 191 C
problems.title: A^n - 1
problems.teaches: Building an element of prescribed multiplicative order by hand, using the binomial expansion of (1+m)^n modulo m^2.
problems.nudge: Stop searching and construct. Expand `(N+1)^n` by the binomial theorem modulo `N^2`: every term from the quadratic one onward vanishes, so it is `1 + n*N`. That is 1 mod `N^2` exactly when `N | n`, so the order is precisely N - and both numbers stay inside 10^18 because N is at most 10^9.

problems.label: ABC 222 G
problems.teaches: That the smallest n with a^n = 1 mod m divides phi(m), so you factorise phi and test its divisors instead of iterating n.
problems.nudge: The n-th term is `2*(10^n - 1)/9`, so `K` divides it exactly when `10^n = 1 mod M` for `M = 9K / gcd(9K, 2)`. If `gcd(10, M) > 1` no power of 10 is ever 1 mod M, so print -1. Otherwise the answer is the multiplicative order of 10 mod M: compute `phi(M)` by trial division, enumerate its divisors, and take the smallest `d` with `10^d = 1 mod M`.

problems.label: ABC 371 G
problems.title: Lexicographically Smallest Permutation
problems.teaches: CRT-shaped reconstruction: a greedy left-to-right choice fixes the operation count modulo one cycle length at a time, and the constraints are merged as congruences.
problems.nudge: Applying P rotates each of its cycles independently, so a whole state is described by one number t - the number of operations. Fix positions left to right: at each position, among the t still allowed by the congruences you have accumulated, pick the one giving the smallest value there, which pins t modulo that position's cycle length. Merge with CRT, and store the running modulus as a map from prime to exponent so it never has to be an actual integer.

problems.label: ABC 333 G
problems.title: Nearest Fraction
problems.teaches: Best rational approximation with a bounded denominator, and the mediant/continued-fraction descent that is the extended Euclidean algorithm wearing a different hat.
problems.nudge: Keep r as the exact fraction it is given as - up to 18 decimals means a denominator of 10^18 - and compare everything by cross multiplication in 128-bit. Then descend the Stern-Brocot tree between `0/1` and `1/1`, but never one step at a time: binary search how many copies of the current mediant you can add before crossing r or pushing the denominator past N, which is exactly one continued-fraction quotient. At the end only the two fractions bracketing r are candidates; compare their distances and break ties toward the smaller value.

ladders.name: Combinatorics & Inclusion–Exclusion
ladders.guide_label: Number Theory & Combinatorics — nCr under Modulo and Inclusion-Exclusion
ladders.blurb: Twenty rungs on counting things you cannot enumerate. It starts with counts you can write as a formula or a single subtraction, moves to the habit of changing what you count — a canonical representative, one bit at a time, one pair at a time — and then to inclusion-exclusion proper: signed sums over forbidden conditions. The last tier is where the signed sum is too big to write down and has to be run as a DP over blocks, subtrees, or subsets.

tiers.name: Direct Counts
tiers.note: Counts that close in a formula, a single scan, or one subtraction of overlaps. The habit to build here is describing the set you are counting precisely enough that a formula falls out.

problems.label: ABC 196 C
problems.title: Doubled
problems.teaches: That when every object you want is built from a smaller object, you should enumerate the smaller object instead of testing every candidate.
problems.nudge: You cannot walk 1..N when N is up to 10^12, but every valid x is exactly some k written twice. So enumerate k from 1 to 10^6, build the number k * 10^(digits of k) + k, and count the ones that are at most N.

problems.label: ABC 253 D
problems.title: FizzBuzz Sum Hard
problems.teaches: The two-set inclusion-exclusion identity in its plainest form, and that a sum over a set of multiples is an arithmetic series you never have to iterate.
problems.nudge: Take the whole sum 1..N and remove what you do not want: subtract the multiples of A, subtract the multiples of B, then add back the multiples of lcm(A, B) because you removed those twice. The sum of multiples of d up to N is d * m * (m+1) / 2 with m = N / d, so nothing is looped over. Watch for overflow.

problems.label: ABC 449 D
problems.title: Make Target 2
problems.teaches: Reducing a query rectangle to a fixed corner-anchored counter, then reassembling the answer from four such counts — the 2D form of a prefix sum.
problems.nudge: Colour depends only on max(|x|, |y|), so it is symmetric in both axes: fold the rectangle into the first quadrant and build one counter cnt(a, b) = number of points with 0 <= x <= a, 0 <= y <= b and max(x, y) even, which has a closed form. Then the rectangle [L,R] x [D,U] is assembled from corner-anchored pieces added and subtracted, splitting the x range and the y range at 0 first.

problems.label: ABC 441 E
problems.title: A > B substring
problems.teaches: Turning a condition on a substring into a comparison between two prefix values, so counting substrings becomes counting ordered pairs.
problems.nudge: Weight A as +1, B as -1 and C as 0, and let P be the prefix sums with P_0 = 0. The substring (i, j] is good exactly when P_j > P_i, so the answer is the number of pairs i < j with P_j > P_i. Sweep j left to right and ask a Fenwick tree over the P values how many earlier prefixes are smaller — this is inversion counting with the inequality flipped.

problems.label: ABC 307 E
problems.title: Distinct Adjacent
problems.teaches: The path-to-cycle correction: count the easy linear version, then fix up the one wrap-around constraint with a recurrence that carries an alternating sign.
problems.nudge: On a line the count is trivial, M * (M-1)^(N-1); the cycle only adds the constraint that the two ends differ. Let f(N) be the cycle answer and split the line colourings by whether the ends agree: that gives f(N) + f(N-1) = (M-1)^N, whose solution is (M-1)^N + (-1)^N * (M-1). Everything is one modular power.

tiers.name: Change the Object
tiers.note: Each rung here is unlocked by counting something other than what the statement names — a canonical representative, a single bit, a divisor class, a tree. The arithmetic only gets easy after the object is chosen well.

problems.label: ABC 436 F
problems.title: Starry Landscape Photo
problems.teaches: Counting distinct results rather than distinct recipes, by pinning each result to one canonical way of producing it — here, fixing the maximum.
problems.nudge: Many (l, r, b) triples give the same set, so charge each set to exactly one of them. A set S is reproducible at threshold b = the largest brightness rank inside it, and there S is a contiguous run of the positions with rank <= b that contains the position of that rank. So insert positions in order of rank b = 1..N and add (number inserted at or left of position of b) * (number inserted at or right of it), which a Fenwick tree gives in O(log N).

problems.label: ARC 135 C
problems.title: XOR to All
problems.teaches: Summing a XOR-transformed array by counting each bit's contribution across all elements instead of evaluating each element.
problems.nudge: Two ideas stack. First, more than one operation is pointless: after xoring everything by A_i, the available values are A_j xor A_i, and applying one of those returns A_j xor A_k — the same array you would have got from a single operation with A_k. So the answer is the best of the original sum and the sum after xoring by some A_i. Second, precompute for each of the 30 bits how many A_j have it set; then the sum after xoring by x is read off those counts in O(30) per candidate.

problems.label: ABC 390 D
problems.title: Stone XOR
problems.teaches: Recognising that a merge process is just a set partition, and that enumerating all partitions of 12 elements is small enough to do by brute force.
problems.nudge: Any sequence of moves ends with the bags grouped: each group's stones sit in one bag and the rest are empty, contributing 0 to the XOR. So the reachable values are exactly the XOR of block sums over all set partitions of the N bags. Enumerate partitions by always putting the lowest unassigned index into a new block and choosing which of the remaining indices join it; collect results in a hash set. Bell(12) is about 4.2 million, which fits.

problems.label: ARC 186 B
problems.title: Typical Permutation Descriptor
problems.teaches: Reading a constraint array as a tree shape, and the hook-length count N! / product of subtree sizes for permutations respecting that shape.
problems.nudge: The two conditions together say exactly that A_i is the index of the previous smaller element of P at position i, so P's min-Cartesian tree is completely determined: node i is the minimum of the interval from A_i + 1 up to just before the first j > i with A_j < i. Once the tree is fixed, the number of permutations realising it is N! divided by the product of all subtree sizes — compute that product with modular inverses.

problems.label: ABC 206 E
problems.title: Divide Both
problems.teaches: Counting pairs bucketed by their gcd via a downward sieve — Mobius inversion written as subtraction of multiples — then peeling off degenerate cases separately.
problems.nudge: Let c(g) be the count of multiples of g in [L, R]. Then c(g)^2 counts pairs whose gcd is a multiple of g, so sweeping g from R down to 2 and setting f(g) = c(g)^2 - sum of f over proper multiples of g gives the pairs with gcd exactly g in O(R log R). Summing f(g) for g >= 2 overcounts: for each g in [L, R] you must still remove the pairs where x = g or y = g, which is 2*c(g) - 1 of them.

tiers.name: Signed Sums
tiers.note: Inclusion-exclusion proper: a set of forbidden conditions, a sum over which of them you deliberately violate, and an alternating sign. These rungs are about finding the right conditions to index the sum by, and keeping the sum small enough to evaluate.

problems.label: ABC 217 G
problems.title: Groups
problems.teaches: The surjection formula: count into labelled boxes that may be empty, strip the empty ones with an alternating binomial sum, then divide by k! to unlabel.
problems.nudge: Residue classes mod M are the only thing that matters: within a class all people must land in different groups, and classes are otherwise independent. So with k labelled groups allowed to be empty, the count is the product over classes of the falling factorial k*(k-1)*...*(k-n_r+1). Call that F(k). Then the number of ways with all k groups non-empty is sum over j of (-1)^j * C(k,j) * F(k-j), and the answer for k is that divided by k!.

problems.label: ABC 243 F
problems.title: Lottery
problems.teaches: Deferring the multinomial coefficient: build a DP over items carrying probabilities divided by the per-item factorials, and multiply the K! back in only at the end.
problems.nudge: Decide, prize by prize, how many of the K draws it wins. Let dp[i][j][k] be the sum over ways to use the first i prizes, having won j distinct prizes with k draws spent, of the product of p^c / c! over those prizes. Transition by choosing c = 0 or c >= 1 copies of prize i. Because the per-prize factorials were divided out, the multinomial coefficient is restored in one shot: the answer is K! * dp[N][M][K]. Everything is mod 998244353 with p_i = W_i * inverse(sum W).

problems.label: ABC 462 G
problems.title: Completely Wrong
problems.teaches: The derangement pattern generalised: count placements avoiding a forbidden board by an alternating sum over j forbidden matches, with the j-counts built as a polynomial product.
problems.nudge: Drawing without replacement means the outcome is a uniformly random permutation of the balls, and score 0 means the ball at step k never has colour G_k. Let r_j be the number of ways to pick j (step, ball) pairs that are all forbidden, with distinct steps and distinct balls; then the good permutations number sum over j of (-1)^j * r_j * (N-j)!. The forbidden board is a disjoint union of full rectangles, one per colour c of size (steps wanting c) x (balls having c), whose own generating polynomial is sum over j of C(g_c,j)*C(cnt_c,j)*j! * x^j — so r is the product of those polynomials, which you multiply together with divide-and-conquer plus NTT.

problems.label: ARC 115 E
problems.title: LEQ and NEQ
problems.teaches: The moment inclusion-exclusion stops being a formula: there are 2^(N-1) subsets of violated constraints, so the signed sum has to be swept as a DP over the blocks they induce.
problems.nudge: Index the inclusion-exclusion by which of the N-1 adjacency constraints you force to be violated. Forcing a set of them cuts the sequence into blocks of positions that must all be equal, and a block [l, r] admits min(A_l..A_r) values with sign (-1)^(r-l). So dp[i] = sum over j < i of dp[j] * (-1)^(i-j-1) * min(A_{j+1..i}), with dp[0] = 1. Evaluate that in O(N) by keeping a monotonic stack of minima together with the running weighted sum over each stack segment.

problems.label: ABC 456 G
problems.title: Count Holidays
problems.model: Exactly k via at most k
problems.teaches: That 'the maximum is exactly k' is almost never counted directly — you count 'the maximum is at most k' and subtract consecutive values.
problems.nudge: Answer(k) = AtMost(k) - AtMost(k-1), where AtMost(k) counts schedules whose every holiday run has length <= k. The forced workdays cut S into independent maximal blocks of dots, so AtMost(k) is the product over blocks of f(L, k) = the number of binary strings of length L with no run of holidays longer than k. Any block with L <= k contributes a free 2^L, so only the blocks longer than k need real work.

tiers.name: Counting Over Structures
tiers.note: The signed sum is now indexed by something with shape — subtrees, orbits, weak orderings, set partitions — and is evaluated by a DP over that structure. These are the hardest rungs and each one is a different structure to sum over.

problems.label: ARC 121 E
problems.title: Directed Tree
problems.teaches: The standard permutation-with-forbidden-positions inclusion-exclusion, where the count of k forbidden choices is itself produced by a tree knapsack.
problems.nudge: The bad event for index i is that a_i is a proper ancestor of i. Let g_k be the number of ways to pick k indices and give each a distinct proper-ancestor value; then the answer is sum over k of (-1)^k * g_k * (N-k)!. Build g with a tree knapsack: merge children into dp[v][j] = ways to make j such pairs inside the subtree of v, then let v itself serve as the ancestor of one unused descendant, dp[v][j+1] += dp[v][j] * (sz_v - 1 - j).

problems.label: ARC 218 E
problems.title: Reverse and Reverse
problems.teaches: Collapsing an exponential space of operation sequences to the small group of end states it can reach, then counting how many sequences land on each one.
problems.nudge: Reversing the prefix of length i and the suffix separately is the same as reversing the whole permutation and then rotating it by N-i, and rotations commute past a second reversal — so after M operations the array is a cyclic rotation of P (M even) or of reverse(P) (M odd), and only the total rotation matters. Each step contributes a uniformly random non-zero shift, so the number of sequences with total shift 0 is ((N-1)^M + (N-1)*(-1)^M)/N and every other shift shares the rest equally. That leaves you needing the inversion count of the base array and the sum of inversion counts over all N of its rotations, both maintainable under an adjacent swap.

problems.label: ARC 126 E
problems.title: Infinite Operations
problems.teaches: Finding the potential function a process is draining, and then maintaining a sum over all pairs under point updates by contribution rather than recomputation.
problems.nudge: Take Phi = (1/2) * sum over i < j of |A_i - A_j| as a potential: one operation gaining x points lowers Phi by at least x, and by exactly x when you only ever move between values that are adjacent in sorted order — so the limit is just Phi. Now the whole problem is maintaining Phi under point updates: sort values into a Fenwick tree holding counts and sums, and read a value v's contribution as v*(count below) - (sum below) plus (sum above) - v*(count above).

problems.label: ARC 104 E
problems.title: Random LIS
problems.teaches: When N is tiny but values are huge, enumerate the order type instead of the values, and count how many value assignments realise each order type.
problems.nudge: The LIS depends only on the relative order of the X_i, including which are equal — that is a weak ordering of at most 6 elements, and there are only 4683 of them. Fix one: it groups the positions into levels that must take strictly increasing distinct values, each level capped by the minimum A over its group. Counting assignments is then counting strictly increasing sequences with per-level upper bounds, which you can do by compressing the at most 6 distinct A values into segments and running a small DP with binomials over how many levels sit in each segment.

problems.label: ABC 236 Ex
problems.title: Distinct Multiples
problems.teaches: Inclusion-exclusion over the partition lattice: the all-distinct condition is removed by summing over which indices are forced equal, with Mobius weight (-1)^(b-1)*(b-1)! per block, evaluated as a subset DP.
problems.nudge: Drop the distinctness and instead sum over set partitions of the N indices, where a block B means 'these entries are all forced equal'. Such a block has floor(M / lcm of D over B) choices and carries the partition-lattice Mobius weight (-1)^(|B|-1) * (|B|-1)!. With N <= 16, run the sum as a subset DP over the 2^16 masks, always extending by the block containing the lowest unused index so each partition is generated once; guard the lcm against overflow past M.

ladders.name: Game Theory: Nim & Grundy
ladders.guide_label: Game Theory — Nim and the XOR Winning Condition
ladders.blurb: A climb through the three ways a two-player game gets decided: search the state graph backwards, reduce the position to an invariant, or split it into independent games and XOR their Grundy numbers. It starts with tiny games you can exhaust, builds Nim and the mex, then breaks harder positions into piles, segments and subtrees, and finishes with games on graphs with cycles and with counting how many starting positions are wins.

tiers.name: Winners you can compute directly
tiers.note: Games small enough to exhaust, or shaped so that the answer is a one-line property of the position. These rungs build the two reflexes everything else needs: evaluate a state from its successors, and look for an invariant before you look for a search.

problems.label: ABC 239 D
problems.title: Prime Sum Game
problems.teaches: That a game with one move each and tiny option sets is settled by a double loop: does some choice of mine survive every reply.
problems.nudge: A, B, C, D are all at most 100, so sieve primes up to 200 and ask directly: does there exist a in [A, B] such that a + c is composite for every c in [C, D]? If yes Takahashi wins, otherwise Aoki does.

problems.label: ABC 418 C
problems.title: Flush
problems.teaches: Turning 'guarantee a win against any opponent choice' into a concrete count of the adversary's best sabotage.
problems.nudge: The dealer's best play is to hand you as many bags as possible while keeping every flavor below b, which is `min(A_i, b-1)` of each flavor. So the answer is `sum of min(A_i, b-1) over all i, plus 1`, and it is -1 exactly when no flavor has at least b bags. Sort A once and use prefix sums so each query is a binary search.

problems.label: ABC 427 D
problems.title: The Simple Game
problems.teaches: The core move of game DP: a state is winning for a player if some successor is, and losing if every successor is losing — computed backwards from the terminal layer.
problems.nudge: The game lasts exactly 2K plies with K at most 10, so the state is (vertex, plies remaining) and the layers never loop. Set `dp[0][v] = (S_v == 'A')`, then fill layer t from layer t-1: at an Alice ply take OR over out-edges, at a Bob ply take AND. Read the answer at `dp[2K][1]`.

problems.label: ARC 225 B
problems.title: Independent Nim
problems.teaches: That a game whose moves look complicated can collapse to a shape condition on the position, found by brute-forcing small cases first.
problems.nudge: Write a brute force over all 0/1 arrays of length up to 10 and list the positions the mover loses. The pattern is exact: the mover loses precisely when every maximal block of consecutive 1s has length exactly 2. So Bob wins if and only if each run of 1s is a run of two, and Alice wins otherwise.

problems.label: ARC 131 C
problems.title: Zero XOR
problems.teaches: Combining an immediate-win check with a parity argument about how long the game must last — no state search at all.
problems.nudge: Let X be the XOR of all A_i. If some A_i equals X you eat it and the remaining XOR is 0, so you win at once. Otherwise argue the game cannot end early and runs to the last cookie — and eating the last cookie leaves the empty XOR 0 — so the parity of N decides it: you win when N is odd.

tiers.name: Nim, Grundy, and the XOR condition
tiers.note: Where the Sprague-Grundy machinery arrives: give each independent component a Grundy number as the mex of its options, XOR the components, and nonzero means the mover wins. Two rungs deliberately step outside it, to keep the habit of asking whether a plain parity count or a memoized search is enough.

problems.label: ABC 368 F
problems.title: Dividing Game
problems.teaches: The full Sprague-Grundy pipeline on its cleanest example: name the Grundy value of one component, XOR across components, nonzero means the first player wins.
problems.nudge: Replacing A_i by a proper divisor removes at least one prime factor and can remove any number of them, so the Grundy value of A_i is Omega(A_i), the count of prime factors with multiplicity — from k you can reach every value 0..k-1, so mex gives k. Sieve smallest prime factors up to 1e5, XOR all Omega(A_i), and Anna wins if the XOR is nonzero.

problems.label: ABC 398 E
problems.title: Tree Game
problems.teaches: That when no move ever removes an option from anyone, the winner is just the parity of the number of legal moves — and how to run that as an interactive game.
problems.nudge: 'No odd cycle' means the graph stays bipartite, and the 2-coloring is already fixed by the tree. So the legal edges are exactly the pairs with different colors, and adding one never invalidates another: the game always lasts `c0 * c1 - (N - 1)` moves. Go first when that is odd, then play any remaining legal edge each turn and flush after every output.

problems.label: ARC 168 B
problems.title: Arbitrary Nim
problems.teaches: Bounded Nim: capping a move at k makes each pile's Grundy value `A_i mod (k+1)`, and then the question becomes which k the first player should want.
problems.nudge: With cap k the Grundy of a pile is `A_i mod (k+1)`, so Alice wins for that k exactly when the XOR of `A_i mod (k+1)` is nonzero. If the XOR of the A_i themselves is nonzero, every k above max A works, so print -1. Otherwise note that two equal piles cancel for every modulus, so delete values appearing an even number of times; the answer is the largest remaining value minus 1, or 0 if nothing remains.

problems.label: ABC 298 E
problems.title: Unfair Sugoroku
problems.teaches: The same backward evaluation as win/lose DP, but the value of a state is a probability averaged over the die instead of an OR over moves.
problems.nudge: The state is (Takahashi's square, Aoki's square, whose turn), at most 100 * 100 * 2 of them, and it always advances, so there is no cycle. `f(a, b, T) = (1/P) * sum over i of f(min(a+i, N), b, A)` with an immediate 1 when a reaches N; symmetric for Aoki with a 0. Do all arithmetic modulo 998244353 using the modular inverse of P and Q.

problems.label: ABC 349 E
problems.title: Weighted Tic-Tac-Toe
problems.teaches: That when the state space is small but unstructured, plain memoized minimax is the right tool — and how to fold a scoring tiebreak into a win/lose value.
problems.nudge: There are only 3^9 colorings of the grid, so recurse on the state (which cells are red, which are blue) and memoize. After each move check the eight lines for an immediate win; if the board fills with no line, the odd total guarantees no tie, so compare the two accumulated scores. Each player picks any move whose value says they win.

tiers.name: Splitting a game into independent parts
tiers.note: Real positions rarely arrive as a list of piles. These rungs practise finding the piles: cells at odd distance, segments between fixed cells, phases of a two-stage game, or a matching that lets the second player mirror forever.

problems.label: ARC 219 D
problems.title: Grid Game
problems.teaches: Staircase Nim: when tokens move toward a sink, only the cells at odd distance are real piles, because moves onto even cells can always be mirrored away.
problems.nudge: Give cell (i, j) the distance `d = (i-1) + (j-1)` to the corner. Stones on even d are worthless — whatever the opponent pushes onto an even cell you push straight on again — so only odd d counts, and the cap K makes each such cell a bounded-Nim pile. Alice wins exactly when the XOR of `A[i][j] mod (K+1)` over all cells with odd `i+j` is nonzero.

problems.label: ABC 297 G
problems.title: Constrained Nim 2
problems.teaches: Deriving a closed-form Grundy value for a modified subtraction game instead of tabulating it, so piles of size 1e9 are still fine.
problems.nudge: Tabulate the Grundy values of a single pile for small L and R and the pattern is clean: `g(a) = (a mod (L + R)) / L`, integer division. The intuition is that a block of L stones is one 'unit' and the L+R period comes from the opponent being able to complete any block you start. XOR the g(A_i); Taro wins on nonzero.

problems.label: ARC 105 D
problems.title: Let's Play Nim
problems.teaches: Analysing a game that has a forced setup phase before the real game: count the setup moves, then ask who is on move when Nim actually starts.
problems.nudge: Phase one is exactly N moves — every bag must be dumped once — so the parity of N fixes who opens the Nim phase, and the players are really fighting over which dish sums appear. Brute-force small cases: the second player wins whenever N is odd, and for even N whenever the multiset of a_i splits into pairs of equal values (he mirrors the first player's dumps onto the same dish). Otherwise the first player wins.

problems.label: ARC 151 C
problems.title: 01 Game
problems.teaches: Decomposing a line into independent segments cut by the fixed cells, then handling N up to 1e18 by finding the period of each segment's Grundy sequence.
problems.nudge: The M pre-filled squares cut the row into independent runs of empty squares, and writing a digit inside a run splits it into two smaller runs — a sum of games. A run is characterised only by its length and by its two boundary digits being absent, equal, or different (relabelling 0 and 1 is a symmetry). Brute-force the Grundy value of each of those four families for small lengths, spot the period, then XOR over the runs.

problems.label: ARC 148 D
problems.title: mod M Game
problems.teaches: That a draw-seeking second player wins exactly when a pairing of the objects lets him answer every move with its partner, and how to state the condition that pairing must satisfy.
problems.nudge: Bob's only real strategy is to fix a perfect matching of the 2N numbers and always take the partner of what Alice took. The running difference then telescopes: an equal pair contributes 0, and a pair differing by M/2 (only possible when M is even) contributes M/2. So Bob wins exactly when the numbers can be matched into equal pairs and M/2 pairs with an even number of the M/2 pairs; check that with counts per value and per residue class.

tiers.name: Grundy at scale, and counting games
tiers.note: The last tier keeps the same three ideas but pays for them with an algorithm: Grundy over O(N^2) sub-segments, a binary search over the game's value, a Dijkstra-like sweep on a graph that can cycle forever, an explicit mirroring construction, and XOR convolution to count winning starts.

problems.label: ABC 206 F
problems.title: Interval Game 2
problems.teaches: Grundy numbers indexed by a coordinate range: choosing an interval splits the free space into two independent games, so the recursion is over sub-ranges.
problems.nudge: Coordinates only go to 100, so define `g(l, r)` as the Grundy value of the free coordinate segment [l, r). A move is any given interval [L_i, R_i) contained in it, and it leaves `g(l, L_i) XOR g(R_i, r)`. Take the mex of those over all fitting intervals, memoize the O(100^2) states, and Alice wins when `g(1, 101)` is nonzero.

problems.label: ABC 246 G
problems.title: Game on Tree 3
problems.teaches: Turning an optimise-the-score game into a sequence of yes/no games by binary searching the answer and reducing the values to 0/1.
problems.nudge: Binary search X and mark each vertex 1 if `A_i >= X`, else 0; the question becomes whether Takahashi can reach a marked vertex. Aoki gets exactly one erase per Takahashi step, so let `f(v) = max(0, mark(v) + sum of f over children - 1)` count the surplus threats a subtree pushes upward. Takahashi achieves X exactly when the sum of f over the root's children is at least 1.

problems.label: ABC 261 Ex
problems.title: Game on Graph
problems.teaches: Solving a weighted game on a graph that may contain cycles: values are settled in increasing order like Dijkstra, with the two players finalised by different rules.
problems.nudge: States are (vertex, whose turn), and you relax them backwards along reversed edges in increasing order of value with a priority queue. Takahashi, who wants a finite game with small weight, is settled the moment his first successor is settled; Aoki, who prefers infinity, is settled only when the last of his successors is, so keep an out-degree counter per Aoki state. Anything never popped is INFINITY.

problems.label: ABC 278 G
problems.title: Generalized Subtraction Game
problems.teaches: The explicit mirroring construction: make the position symmetric on your first move, then copy the opponent forever — with a Grundy fallback for the case where symmetry is unreachable.
problems.nudge: If L < R you never need Grundy numbers: pick y in {L, L+1} with `N - y` even, remove that block from the middle so the two sides have equal length, then mirror every opponent move on the other side. If L == R the row is a sum of independent rows, so run the O(N^2) DP `g(n) = mex over x of g(x) XOR g(n - L - x)` up to N = 2000, and choose to go first exactly when `g(N)` is nonzero.

problems.label: ABC 212 H
problems.title: Nim Counting
problems.teaches: Counting how many starting positions are first-player wins: the Nim condition is a XOR constraint, and XOR-constrained counting is a Walsh-Hadamard transform.
problems.nudge: Removing 1..X stones from a heap of size X is plain Nim, so a position loses exactly when the XOR of heap sizes is 0; count those and subtract from `K + K^2 + ... + K^N`. Let f be the 2^16 indicator vector of A; the count of length-i sequences with XOR 0 is the 0-th entry of the inverse transform of `WHT(f)^i`, so transform once, sum the geometric series `t + t^2 + ... + t^N` pointwise (handling t = 1 separately), and transform back.

ladders.name: Geometry & Sweep Line
ladders.blurb: A climb through coordinate reasoning that never needs a floating-point library: integer distances on grids and lines, gcd-normalised directions, the 45-degree rotation that decouples Manhattan and diagonal moves, and sweep lines carrying segment trees over the second axis. The progression goes from brute force over points, to sorting along one coordinate, to event sweeps with lazy range structures, and finally to rotations, convex-polygon point location and offline sweeps where the geometry collapses into pure counting.

tiers.name: Points, Grids and Manhattan Distance
tiers.note: Small inputs where the whole job is to read the statement as integer coordinates and compute distances honestly. These rungs build the habit of asking what the coordinate actually is before reaching for a technique.

problems.label: ABC 383 B
problems.title: Humidifier 2
problems.teaches: Reading a grid as a set of integer points and computing Manhattan distance directly, with no geometry machinery at all.
problems.nudge: `H` and `W` are at most 10, so there are under 100 floor cells and fewer than 5000 placements; for each pair just scan every floor cell and count it if its Manhattan distance to either humidifier is at most `D`. Note a humidifier cell has distance 0 to itself, so it always counts.

problems.label: ABC 185 C
problems.title: Duodecim Ferra
problems.model: Stars and bars on cut points
problems.teaches: A statement about physically cutting a bar is really a choice of positions on a line, so the geometry evaporates into a single binomial coefficient.
problems.nudge: The only freedom is which integer positions carry the 11 cuts, and there are `L-1` interior positions to choose from. The answer is `C(L-1, 11)` — build it as a product so nothing overflows before the final value.

problems.label: ABC 240 C
problems.title: Jumping Takahashi
problems.teaches: Reachability along a coordinate axis as a boolean table over positions — the one-dimensional ancestor of the subset-sum step the ladder ends on.
problems.nudge: Keep a boolean array over positions `0..X`. After jump `i`, position `p` is reachable exactly when `p - a_i` or `p - b_i` was reachable before it, so sweep the array once per jump. `X` is only 10000, so the whole table is tiny.

problems.label: ABC 226 D
problems.title: Teleportation
problems.teaches: Normalising an integer displacement by its gcd, so two directions can be compared exactly without ever forming a slope or a float.
problems.nudge: One spell `(a,b)` used repeatedly reaches only positive multiples of `(a,b)`, so it serves the ordered pair `(i,j)` exactly when the difference `(dx,dy)` is such a multiple. Divide each of the `N*(N-1)` differences by `gcd(|dx|,|dy|)` and count how many distinct reduced vectors appear.

problems.label: ABC 266 D
problems.title: Snuke Panic (1D)
problems.teaches: A speed limit on a moving point becomes a purely local transition once you index the DP by both time and coordinate.
problems.nudge: There are only 5 positions, so carry `dp[t][x]` = best total collected by time `t` while standing at `x`. Waiting is free and one time unit lets you shift by one, so between consecutive events relax `dp[x]` against `dp[x-1]` and `dp[x+1]` once per elapsed unit — or note that a gap of `g` units lets you move up to `g`, which with 5 slots is a handful of relaxations.

tiers.name: One Coordinate at a Time
tiers.note: The pivot from brute force to structure: sort or bucket along one axis, keep an aggregate as points arrive, and repair only the part that changed. This is also where the 45-degree rotation first appears.

problems.label: ABC 430 D
problems.title: Neighbor Distance
problems.teaches: Maintaining a global aggregate over a sorted set of coordinates under insertions by touching only the entries whose value actually moved.
problems.nudge: Hold the occupied coordinates in an ordered set and keep a running total. Inserting a new point only changes three contributions — its predecessor's, its successor's, and its own — so subtract the two old ones and add the three new ones. Everything else is untouched.

problems.label: ABC 176 E
problems.title: Bomber
problems.teaches: Splitting a 2D placement into independent per-axis counts, then paying attention to the single cell where the two axes interact.
problems.nudge: Compute the best row count `R` and best column count `C` separately. The answer is `R + C` if some best-row / best-column intersection is empty, otherwise `R + C - 1`. There are at most `M` occupied cells, so if the number of (best row, best column) pairs exceeds `M` an empty intersection must exist; otherwise check those pairs directly.

problems.label: ABC 437 F
problems.title: Manhattan Christmas Tree 2
problems.teaches: The rewrite of Manhattan distance as a maximum over four sign choices, which turns a distance query into ordinary min/max range queries.
problems.nudge: Store `u = x + y` and `v = x - y` per tree. Then `max |x-a| + |y-b|` over a set equals the largest of `max(u) - (a+b)`, `(a+b) - min(u)`, `max(v) - (a-b)`, `(a-b) - min(v)`. A segment tree over indices holding min and max of `u` and `v` handles both the point update and the range query.

problems.label: ABC 223 E
problems.title: Placing Rectangles
problems.teaches: An existence question over dimensions up to 1e9 that is settled by exhaustive case analysis plus ceiling division, with no search anywhere.
problems.nudge: If a packing exists, one full-width or full-height cut separates one rectangle from the other two, and the same argument applies recursively to the remaining strip. Try all 6 assignments of `A,B,C` to slots and both cut orientations, and use `ceil(A/X) = (A + X - 1) / X` for the minimum strip a given area needs. Areas reach 1e18, so keep everything in 64-bit integers.

problems.label: ABC 306 F
problems.title: Merge Sets
problems.teaches: Turning a pairwise merge-and-sum-positions quantity into a count of cross pairs, then answering that count by sweeping one coordinate while a Fenwick tree indexes the other.
problems.nudge: For an element `a` of `S_i`, its position after merging with `S_j` is its rank inside `S_i` plus the number of elements of `S_j` below it. So the answer is `C(N,2) * M(M+1)/2` plus, over all `N*M` values in increasing order, the number of already-inserted elements whose set index is greater than `a`'s — one Fenwick tree over set indices, swept by value.

tiers.name: Events and Segment Trees
tiers.note: The core sweep-line tier: each object becomes an interval or a rectangle of parameters, and a segment tree riding the sweep answers the aggregate. Two rungs deliberately break the pattern to show when discretising or a plain window beats a sweep.

problems.label: ABC 327 F
problems.title: Apples
problems.teaches: Mapping each item to the axis-aligned rectangle of parameter choices that capture it, so 'pick the best parameters' becomes 'find the most-covered point'.
problems.nudge: Apple `(T,X)` is caught exactly when `S` lies in `[T-D+1, T]` and `L` lies in `[X-W+1, X]` — an axis-aligned rectangle in the `(S,L)` plane. Sweep `S` upward with add/remove events and keep a lazy segment tree over `L` doing range `+1` / `-1` with a global maximum.

problems.label: ABC 179 F
problems.title: Simplified Reversi
problems.teaches: Representing a shrinking grid frontier by two arrays of 'first blocking coordinate', updated with range-chmin and read with point queries.
problems.nudge: You never need the board. Keep one tree over columns giving the smallest row that already blocks that column, and one over rows giving the smallest blocking column. A query from the top at column `x` reads its blocking row `m`, flips `m - 2` stones, and then blocks rows `2..m-1` at column `x` — a range chmin on the other tree. The symmetric query mirrors this.

problems.label: ABC 334 F
problems.title: Christmas Present 2
problems.teaches: A DP whose transition is a minimum over a fixed-width window of earlier states, made linear by a monotone deque or a segment tree.
problems.nudge: Let `dp[i]` be the best cost once child `i` has a present and Santa is free to continue. Walking straight from child to child telescopes into a prefix sum, so subtract that prefix from the state: `dp[i]` is then a minimum over the last `K` values of `dp[j] - prefix[j] + d(house_j, home) + d(home, house_{j+1})`. That is a window minimum of width `K`.

problems.label: ARC 164 D
problems.title: 1D Coulomb
problems.teaches: A physical simulation on a line collapsing to the prefix sums of a +1 / -1 sequence, after which summing over all completions is pure counting.
problems.nudge: Read `+` as `+1` and `-` as `-1`. The total distance travelled for a fixed string depends only on the prefix sums of that sequence — equivalently on the bracket-matching structure — not on the actual coordinates. So instead of enumerating strings, count for each prefix position and each balance value how many valid completions pass through it, which is a product of two binomial-style counts. `N <= 3000` makes the `O(N^2)` table fine.

problems.label: ABC 312 E
problems.title: Tangency of Cuboids
problems.teaches: When coordinates are bounded by a small constant, discretising space into unit cells beats every clever geometric argument.
problems.nudge: Every coordinate is at most 100, so allocate a `100 x 100 x 100` array and paint each unit cell with the id of the cuboid containing it (cuboids do not overlap, so this is well defined). Two cuboids share positive face area exactly when some pair of face-adjacent unit cells carries their two ids; collect those into a per-cuboid set and report its size.

tiers.name: Rotations, Polygons and Offline Sweeps
tiers.note: The hard tier, where the right coordinate change is the whole solution: exact integer orientation tests, Mo's ordering of query points, and the 45-degree rotation that splits coupled moves into independent one-dimensional ones.

problems.label: ABC 296 G
problems.title: Polygon and Points
problems.teaches: Point location in a strictly convex polygon by binary searching the fan of triangles from one vertex, decided entirely by integer cross products.
problems.nudge: Anchor at vertex 1. Because the polygon is strictly convex, the rays from it to the other vertices are already sorted by angle, so a binary search on cross-product signs finds the single wedge containing the query point; one more cross product against that wedge's outer edge separates IN, ON and OUT, plus a special check for the two boundary rays. Coordinates reach 1e9, so cross products need 64-bit integers and must never touch floating point.

problems.label: ABC 384 G
problems.title: Abs Sum
problems.teaches: Treating prefix-pair queries as points in a plane and reordering them offline so each pointer step is one Fenwick update plus one Fenwick query.
problems.nudge: Each query is the point `(X_k, Y_k)`; sort them in Mo's order and move two pointers. Adding one `A_i` against the current `B` prefix contributes `cnt_below * A_i - sum_below + sum_above - cnt_above * A_i`, so keep two Fenwick trees over compressed `B` values (and two more over `A` for the symmetric move). Each of the `O((N+K) sqrt(N))` steps costs a log.

problems.label: ABC 240 G
problems.title: Teleporting Takahashi
problems.teaches: Decoupling a lattice walk into independent one-dimensional walks by rotating the plane 45 degrees, turning a path count into a sum of binomial products.
problems.nudge: Split the `N` steps into those along `z` and the rest. For the steps left in the `xy`-plane, substitute `u = x + y` and `v = x - y`: each such step changes `u` by `+-1` and `v` by `+-1` independently, so the count for a fixed number of `xy` steps is a product of two central-binomial terms. Sum over the split (parity and the target pin most of it) with factorials precomputed to 1e7.

problems.label: ABC 360 F
problems.title: InterSections
problems.teaches: Counting properly crossing intervals — not merely overlapping ones — with a sweep over the left endpoint and a lazy range-add / range-max tree over the right endpoint.
problems.nudge: Interval `i` is crossed by `[l,r]` only when exactly one endpoint of each lies strictly inside the other. Fix `l` and sweep it upward: each interval then contributes `+1` to a contiguous range of `r` values, and that contribution is switched on and off at two specific values of `l`. So it is two events on the `l` axis plus a range add on a lazy max segment tree over `r`. Remember `(0,0)` with value 0 is always available, and ties break by smallest `l` then smallest `r`.

problems.label: ABC 221 G
problems.title: Jumping sequence
problems.teaches: The capstone rotation: four-direction moves of fixed length become two independent sign choices, reducing a 2D reachability question to two bitset subset sums with reconstruction.
problems.nudge: Substitute `u = x + y` and `v = x - y`. Every move changes `u` by `+-D_i` and `v` by `+-D_i`, and the two signs are independent — so you need signs summing to `A+B` in `u` and to `A-B` in `v`, separately. Each is 'choose a subset of `D` to be positive', i.e. subset sum for `(target + sum D) / 2`; check the parity, run a bitset DP, then walk the DP backwards to recover which jumps were positive and map the two sign patterns back to U/D/L/R.
